$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-de337785-0bed-5d88-927f-c04df51fff3b"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-de337785-0bed-5d88-927f-c04df51fff3b" :answer-field/id #uuid "de337785-0bed-5d88-927f-c04df51fff3b" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-96a52254-ea30-53d5-b2d5-8fa3a1d84466" :answer-field/choices ["answer-96a52254-ea30-53d5-b2d5-8fa3a1d84466" "answer-2150377d-9170-5e26-8c05-6932a47baf31" "answer-78a5e0b0-0aff-56f5-b302-e96894a6e57c" "answer-01c03964-bbb3-565c-bfcb-c6ed69ba5e55" "answer-8ff6cccd-26e2-5560-99d7-944b84007b58"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-96a52254-ea30-53d5-b2d5-8fa3a1d84466" :answer/id #uuid "96a52254-ea30-53d5-b2d5-8fa3a1d84466" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "{(\frac{1}{9})}^{18}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-2150377d-9170-5e26-8c05-6932a47baf31" :answer/id #uuid "2150377d-9170-5e26-8c05-6932a47baf31" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "{(\frac{1}{9})}^{3}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-78a5e0b0-0aff-56f5-b302-e96894a6e57c" :answer/id #uuid "78a5e0b0-0aff-56f5-b302-e96894a6e57c" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "{(\frac{1}{9})}^{9}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-01c03964-bbb3-565c-bfcb-c6ed69ba5e55" :answer/id #uuid "01c03964-bbb3-565c-bfcb-c6ed69ba5e55" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "{9}^{18}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-8ff6cccd-26e2-5560-99d7-944b84007b58" :answer/id #uuid "8ff6cccd-26e2-5560-99d7-944b84007b58" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "{9}^{9}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186101969 :tutorial/content "To raise a power to another power, we multiply the exponents. This is the **power rule for exponents**. 

To demonstrate, let's simplify the expression $\left( 3^5\right)^4$ by applying the power rule:

$$
\left( 3^5\right)^4 = 3^{5\cdot 4} = 3^{20}
$$

**Note:** The power rule for exponents is just a quicker alternative to using repeated multiplication, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{({3}^{5})}^{4} & = \\ {{{3}^{5}\times {3}^{5}\times {3}^{5}\times {3}^{5}}_{⏟}}_{4\text{ copies}} & = \\ {3}^{5+5+5+5} & = \\ {3}^{5\cdot 4} & = \\ {3}^{20}\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186101076 :activity/expected-seconds 420.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]} [:db/retract 17592186123212 :answer-field/choices 17592186123217] [:db/retract 17592186123212 :answer-field/choices 17592186123213] [:db/retract 17592186123212 :answer-field/choices 17592186123214] [:db/retract 17592186123212 :answer-field/choices 17592186123215] {:db/id 17592186124533 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-7f2c9542-25be-572a-a669-8d12401722e1"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186125102 :question/problem "Consider the matrix $A,$ given by

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & -5 \\ 11 & 8 & 1 \\ 4 & 0 & -7\end{aligned}]
$$

Determine whether $A=PD{P}^{-1}$ for some invertible matrix $P$ and a diagonal matrix $D,$ where $P$ and $D$ are both real. In the affirmative case, find a possible diagonal matrix $D.$" :question/worked-solution "First, we need to determine whether $D$ is diagonalizable over $R.$

We start by computing the eigenvalues of $A.$ To do that, we solve the characteristic equation, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A-\lambda I) & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}1-\lambda  & 0 & -5 \\ 11 & 8-\lambda  & 1 \\ 4 & 0 & -7-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (8-\lambda )|\begin{aligned}1-\lambda  & -5 \\ 4 & -7-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (8-\lambda )((1-\lambda )(-7-\lambda )+20) & =0 \\ (8-\lambda )({\lambda }^{2}+6\lambda +13) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

For the quadratic polynomial ${\lambda }^{2}+6\lambda +13=0,$ we have that the discriminant $D<0.$ So, it doesn't have real roots. 

Therefore, $A$ is not diagonalizable over $R.$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186123212 :answer-field/correct 17592186123216 :answer-field/choices ["answer-2b774372-51ae-5bda-8eff-29ba0b1a454a" "answer-45c01a88-e97e-59fa-b369-0c03e469bc6a" "answer-6757aa5b-9c37-5abb-9da9-6dbe52e7e8f9" "answer-8a24d661-bdd6-5639-9e9f-991e9c96a769"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-2b774372-51ae-5bda-8eff-29ba0b1a454a" :answer/id #uuid "2b774372-51ae-5bda-8eff-29ba0b1a454a" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "D=[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -7\end{aligned}]" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-45c01a88-e97e-59fa-b369-0c03e469bc6a" :answer/id #uuid "45c01a88-e97e-59fa-b369-0c03e469bc6a" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "D=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 8 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -7\end{aligned}]" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-6757aa5b-9c37-5abb-9da9-6dbe52e7e8f9" :answer/id #uuid "6757aa5b-9c37-5abb-9da9-6dbe52e7e8f9" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "D=[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 5\end{aligned}]" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-8a24d661-bdd6-5639-9e9f-991e9c96a769" :answer/id #uuid "8a24d661-bdd6-5639-9e9f-991e9c96a769" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "D=[\begin{aligned}8 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-7f2c9542-25be-572a-a669-8d12401722e1" :question/id #uuid "7f2c9542-25be-572a-a669-8d12401722e1" :question/math-academy-id "q-84600" :question/problem "Consider the matrix $A,$ given by

Determine whether $A=PD{P}^{-1}$ for some invertible matrix $P$ and a diagonal matrix $D,$ where $P$ and $D$ are both real. In the affirmative case, find a possible diagonal matrix $D.$" :question/worked-solution "First, we need to determine whether $D$ is diagonalizable over $R.$

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A-\lambda I) & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}4-\lambda  & 0 & 3 \\ 2 & 4-\lambda  & -9 \\ -8 & 0 & -4-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (4-\lambda )|\begin{aligned}4-\lambda  & 3 \\ -8 & -4-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (4-\lambda )((4-\lambda )(-4-\lambda )+24) & =0 \\ (4-\lambda )({\lambda }^{2}+8) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

For the quadratic polynomial $\,{\lambda }^{2}+8\,$ we have that the discriminant $D<0.$ So, it doesn't have real roots.

[:step/validate]} {:db/id 17592186172309 :question/worked-solution "Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $F=P\,i+Q\,j,$ and $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first derivatives on an open region containing $D,$ then the flux form of Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={∬}_{D}\text{div}\,F\,\text{d}A,
$$

which is equivalent to

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dy-Q\,dx={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\,\text{d}A.
$$

The region $D$ and the curve $C$ for this case are shown below.

![](images/26/265d27ad87a7f114bd2a32a5f48cbfedb13192abf48f9b759c4ed635e71ff144.png)

We have that $P(x,y)={x}^{2}y$ and $Q(x,y)=5xy.$ So,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂x}=2xy,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂y} & =5x.\end{aligned}
$$

We can express the region $D$ as a type I region as follows:

$$
D=\{(x,y):-1\le x\le 2,\,0\le y\le 2\}
$$

Therefore, applying Green's theorem in flux form, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}P\,dy-Q\,dx & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(2xy+5x)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{2}x(2y+5)\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186387803 :question/worked-solution "Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $F=P\,i+Q\,j,$ and $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first derivatives on an open region containing $D,$ then the flux form of Green's theorem states that

$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186262736 :question/worked-solution "Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $F=P\,i+Q\,j,$ and $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first derivatives on an open region containing $D,$ then the flux form of Green's theorem states that

:question/id #uuid "08715ccd-f649-5c84-af70-2145bc128aa0" :question/math-academy-id "q-162396" :question/problem "Find the radius of curvature for the curve $r(t)={t}^{2}\,i+({t}^{2}-t)\,j$ at $t=0.$" :question/worked-solution "The curvature $κ(t)$ of a plane curve $r(t)=x(t)\,i+y(t)\,j$ is given by

$$
κ(t)=\frac{|{x}^{′}(t){y}^{″}(t)-{y}^{′}(t){x}^{″}(t)|}{([{x}^{′}(t)]^{2}+[{y}^{′}(t)]^{2})^{3/2}}.
$$

The radius of curvature $R$ is defined as
$R(t)=\frac{1}{κ(t)}.$

Along our curve, we have

$$
x(t)={t}^{2},\,y(t)={t}^{2}-t.
$$

First, we calculate the derivatives of the components:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t) & =2t,\, & {y}^{′}(t) & =2t-1 \\ {x}^{″}(t) & =2,\, & {y}^{″}(t) & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting these into the formula for the curvature, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}κ(t) & =\frac{|2t\cdot 2-(2t-1)\cdot 2|}{{((2t)^{2}+(2t-1)^{2})}^{3/2}} \\  & =\frac{2}{{(8{t}^{2}-4t+1)}^{3/2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the curvature at $t=0$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}κ(0) & =\frac{2}{{(8(0)^{2}-4(0)+1)}^{3/2}} \\  & =\frac{2}{{(0-0+1)}^{3/2}} \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the radius of curvature at $t=0$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}R(0) & =\frac{1}{κ(0)}=\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-e5755c53-01de-5e40-9f46-4f16d8b88aa1"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id curve $r(t)=(1+{t}^{2})^{2}\,i+t\,j$ at $t=0.$" :question/worked-solution "The curvature $κ(t)$ of a plane curve $r(t)=x(t)\,i+y(t)\,j$ is given by

$$
κ(t)=\frac{|{x}^{′}(t){y}^{″}(t)-{y}^{′}(t){x}^{″}(t)|}{([{x}^{′}(t)]^{2}+[{y}^{′}(t)]^{2})^{3/2}}.
$$

The radius of curvature $R$ is defined as
$R(t)=\frac{1}{κ(t)}.$

Along our curve, we have

$$
x(t)=(1+{t}^{2})^{2},\,y(t)=t.
$$

First, we calculate the derivatives of the components:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t) & =4t(1+{t}^{2}),\, & {y}^{′}(t) & =1 \\ {x}^{″}(t) & =12{t}^{2}+4,\, & {y}^{″}(t) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting these into the formula for the curvature, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}κ(t) & =\frac{|4t(1+{t}^{2})\cdot 0-1\cdot (12{t}^{2}+4)|}{{((4t(1+{t}^{2}))^{2}+{1}^{2})}^{3/2}} \\  & =\frac{12{t}^{2}+4}{{((4t(1+{t}^{2}))^{2}+1)}^{3/2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the curvature at $t=0$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}κ(0) & =\frac{12(0)^{2}+4}{{((4(0)(1+(0)^{2}))^{2}+1)}^{3/2}} \\  & =\frac{4}{{(0+1)}^{3/2}} \\  & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the radius of curvature at $t=0$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}R(0) & =\frac{1}{κ(0)}=\frac{1}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-21292018-ea56-5ae6-a7f5-dac08271bdff"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id Find the moment of inertia of this lamina about the $y$-axis." :question/worked-solution "For a plane lamina $D$ with mass density function $\lambda (x,y),$ we have the following definitions:

- The moment of inertia about the $x$-axis is given by

$$
{I}_{x}={∬}_{D}{y}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A.
$$

- The moment of inertia about the $y$-axis is given by

$$
{I}_{y}={∬}_{D}{x}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A.
$$

- The moment of inertia about the origin is given by

$$
{I}_{0}={∬}_{D}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A={I}_{x}+{I}_{y}.
$$

Using the formula for ${I}_{y},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{y} & ={∬}_{D}{x}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}{\int }_{2}^{4}{x}^{2}\cdot x{e}^{2y}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}[{\int }_{2}^{4}{x}^{3}{e}^{2y}\,\text{d}x]\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}{e}^{2y}{[\frac{1}{4}{x}^{4}]}_{2}^{4}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}60{e}^{2y}\,\text{d}y \\  & =[30{e}^{2y}]_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡2} \\  & =120-30 \\  & =90.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the moment of inertia of the lamina about the $y$-axis is $90\,\text{kg}\cdot {\text{m}}^{2}.$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "94.2\,\text{kg}\cdot {\text{m}}^{2}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186281622 :question/worked-solution "For a plane lamina $D$ with mass density function $\lambda (x,y),$ we have the following definitions:

- The moment of inertia about the $x$-axis is given by

$$
{I}_{x}={∬}_{D}{y}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A.
$$

- The moment of inertia about the $y$-axis is given by

$$
{I}_{y}={∬}_{D}{x}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A.
$$

- The moment of inertia about the origin is given by

$$
{I}_{0}={∬}_{D}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A={I}_{x}+{I}_{y}.
$$

First, notice that $D$ is a type I region with representation

$$
D=\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le 4,\,\,0\le y\le \sqrt{x}\},
$$

as shown below.

![](images/dd/dd5ee021dd73317a775c0ea653212f7ee5545f8c6854e6a9daabdc93b5c3b9c0.png)

Using the formula for ${I}_{0},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{0} & ={∬}_{D}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{4}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{x}}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\cdot 3y\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{4}[{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{x}}3{x}^{2}y+3{y}^{3}\,\text{d}y]\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{4}{[\frac{3}{2}{x}^{2}{y}^{2}+\frac{3}{4}{y}^{4}]}_{y=0}^{y=\sqrt{x}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{4}\frac{3}{2}{x}^{3}+\frac{3}{4}{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={[\frac{3}{8}{x}^{4}+\frac{1}{4}{x}^{3}]}_{0}^{4} \\  & =96+16 \\  & =112.\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186281636 :question/worked-solution "For a plane lamina $D$ with mass density function $\lambda (x,y),$ we have the following definitions:

- The moment of inertia about the $x$-axis is given by

$$
{I}_{x}={∬}_{D}{y}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A.
$$

- The moment of inertia about the $y$-axis is given by

$$
{I}_{y}={∬}_{D}{x}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A.
$$

- The moment of inertia about the origin is given by

$$
{I}_{0}={∬}_{D}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A={I}_{x}+{I}_{y}.
$$

First, notice that $D$ is a type II region with representation

$$
D=\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le y\le 3,\,\,\frac{y}{3}\le x\le 4-y\},
$$

as shown below.

![](images/47/47c897bd58a23965d9c36f683553c0817afa8bc2e37ed53a432edcd62b386e55.png)

The area of the triangular plate $D$ is 

$$
A=\frac{1}{2}\cdot 4\cdot 3=6.
$$

Since the plate has uniform density, every unit of area contains the same amount of mass. Therefore, the mass density is constant and is given by the total mass divided by the total area:

$$
\lambda (x,y)=\frac{M}{A}=\frac{M}{6}.
$$

Therefore, the moment of inertia about the $x$-axis is

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{x} & ={∬}_{D}{y}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A \\  & =\frac{M}{6}{\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{y/3}^{4-y}{y}^{2}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{M}{6}{\int }_{0}^{3}{y}^{2}[{\int }_{y/3}^{4-y}\,\text{d}x]\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{M}{6}{\int }_{0}^{3}{y}^{2}(4-y-\frac{1}{3}y)\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{M}{6}{\int }_{0}^{3}4{y}^{2}-\frac{4}{3}{y}^{3}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{M}{6}{[\frac{4}{3}{y}^{3}-\frac{1}{3}{y}^{4}]}_{0}^{3} \\  & =\frac{M}{6}(36-27) \\  & =\frac{3M}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186281637 :question/worked-solution "For a plane lamina $D$ with mass density function $\lambda (x,y),$ we have the following definitions:

+ (3^2-5).$" :question/worked-solution "To evaluate the given expression, we use PEMDAS.

First, we compute the expression inside the parentheses:

$$
\begin{aligned}10÷{5}^{0}+(9-5)=10÷{5}^{0}+4\end{aligned}
$$

Next, notice that $5^0=1.$ So, we obtain:

$$
\begin{aligned}10÷{5}^{0}+4 & = \\ 10÷1+4 & = \\ 10+4 & = \\ 14\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186129309 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-372dbe69-5a97-5673-bcbc-f7d304887030" "question-6433a3cf-883a-54aa-9f03-bdc753346e58"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186128871 :question/problem "What is the value of  $\dfrac{4}{3} \times (-5+3)^{-2} + \dfrac{2}{3} ?$" :question/worked-solution "To evaluate the given expression, we use PEMDAS.

First, we compute the expression inside the parentheses:

$$
\dfrac{4}{3} \times ({\color{red}-5} + {\color{red}3})^{-2} + \dfrac{2}{3} = \dfrac{4}{3} \times ({\color{red}-2})^{-2} + \dfrac{2}{3}
$$

Next, notice that $(-2)^{-2}=\dfrac{1}{(-2)^2} = \dfrac{1}{4}.$ So, we obtain:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{4}{3}\times (-2)^{-2}+\frac{2}{3} & = \\ \frac{4}{3}\times \frac{1}{4}+\frac{2}{3} & = \\ \frac{4\times 1}{3\times 4}+\frac{2}{3} & = \\ \frac{\cancel{4}\times 1}{3\times \cancel{4}}+\frac{2}{3} & = \\ \frac{1}{3}+\frac{2}{3} & = \\ 1\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186129310 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-2dbc86c1-eb39-5436-87d8-eb16a5d4d270" "question-5e5e796d-b724-597d-a614-e8af03095fdf"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186128872 :question/problem "Find the value of $2 + \left(-4\right)^{-2} \div \left( 1.5 + \dfrac{2}{15} \right)^0.$" :question/worked-solution "To evaluate the given expression, we use PEMDAS.

2+(5+1)^{-2}=${{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "To evaluate the given expression, we use PEMDAS.

$$

$$

$$

Next, notice that ${(\frac{1}{10})}^{0}=1.$ So, we obtain:

$$
\begin{aligned}{2}^{-4}+{(\frac{1}{10})}^{0} & = \\ {2}^{-4}+1\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, notice that ${2}^{-4}=\frac{1}{{2}^{4}}=\frac{1}{16}.$ So, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{2}^{-4}+1 & = \\ \frac{1}{16}+1 & = \\ \frac{1+16}{16} & = \\ \frac{17}{16}. & \end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-c9a275f8-e12f-531b-9ed6-2c3eda31cf0e"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-c9a275f8-e12f-531b-9ed6-2c3eda31cf0e" :answer-field/id #uuid "c9a275f8-e12f-531b-9ed6-2c3eda31cf0e" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank :answer-field/correct "answer-ff37ba3f-b657-5468-a046-c7a885ae86ed" :answer-field/choices ["answer-ff37ba3f-b657-5468-a046-c7a885ae86ed"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-ff37ba3f-b657-5468-a046-c7a885ae86ed" :answer/id #uuid "ff37ba3f-b657-5468-a046-c7a885ae86ed" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{17}{16}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-5e5e796d-b724-597d-a614-e8af03095fdf" :question/id #uuid "5e5e796d-b724-597d-a614-e8af03095fdf" :question/math-academy-id "q-100301" :question/problem "Calculate ${(\frac{8}{7}-\frac{1}{16})}^{0}-11\times {(\frac{1}{2})}^{-3}.$" :question/worked-solution "To evaluate the given expression, we use PEMDAS.

$$
{(\frac{8}{7}-\frac{1}{16})}^{0}=1.
$$

$$
{(\frac{1}{2})}^{-3}={(\frac{2}{1})}^{3}={2}^{3}=8.

$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-93d546fe-e93e-5d3c-8f24-4f640019211e"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-93d546fe-e93e-5d3c-8f24-4f640019211e" :answer-field/id #uuid "93d546fe-e93e-5d3c-8f24-4f640019211e" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-2f5e6d20-6d83-5a4b-9919-511354ddc37f" :answer-field/choices ["answer-fdeff659-436b-5f34-ac81-a6409e40fce1" "answer-2f5e6d20-6d83-5a4b-9919-511354ddc37f" "answer-b381b4b1-c1bc-52ab-8b7e-21ef5860d874" "answer-76d69649-f0c6-5771-848d-71954873581b" "answer-e6602306-1f53-57b5-91c7-8b39e35659a8"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-fdeff659-436b-5f34-ac81-a6409e40fce1" :answer/id #uuid "fdeff659-436b-5f34-ac81-a6409e40fce1" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-121" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-2f5e6d20-6d83-5a4b-9919-511354ddc37f" :answer/id #uuid "2f5e6d20-6d83-5a4b-9919-511354ddc37f" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-87" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-b381b4b1-c1bc-52ab-8b7e-21ef5860d874" :answer/id #uuid "b381b4b1-c1bc-52ab-8b7e-21ef5860d874" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-89" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-76d69649-f0c6-5771-848d-71954873581b" :answer/id #uuid "76d69649-f0c6-5771-848d-71954873581b" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "87" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-e6602306-1f53-57b5-91c7-8b39e35659a8" :answer/id #uuid "e6602306-1f53-57b5-91c7-8b39e35659a8" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "89" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186130481 :tutorial/content "As we know already, to evaluate numerical expressions with a mix of different operations, we follow the order of operations (PEMDAS).

The same rules apply to numerical expressions with zero and negative exponents. To demonstrate, let's compute the value of

$$
(-3)^0 +2^2 \div 2.
$$

To evaluate the given expression, we use PEMDAS.

Notice that $\left(-3\right)^{0}=1.$ So, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{(-3)}^{0}+{2}^{2}÷2 & = \\ 1+{2}^{2}÷2 & = \\ 1+4÷2 & = \\ 1+2 & = \\ 3 & .\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186129335 :activity/expected-seconds 540.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]} {:db/id 17592186124591 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-75f0d82a-dd66-5d66-8858-8e85c7e74ab7"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id "question-75f0d82a-dd66-5d66-8858-8e85c7e74ab7" :question/id #uuid "75f0d82a-dd66-5d66-8858-8e85c7e74ab7" :question/math-academy-id "q-94610" :question/problem "Consider the vector space ${R}_{3}[t]$ of all polynomials in the variable $t$ of degree at most $3,$ and its subset $B=\{a{t}^{3}+bt+1\,|\,a,b\in R\}.$

Which of the following statements are true?

I. $B$ is closed under polynomial addition

II. $B$ is closed under scalar multiplication

III. $B$ is a subspace of ${R}_{3}[t]$

IV. $B$ is **not** a subspace of ${R}_{3}[t]$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that a subset of a vector space is a subspace if it's closed under addition and scalar multiplication.

With that in mind, let's examine each statement in turn.

- Statement I is false. For example, if $f(t)=g(t)=t+1,$ then

$$
\begin{aligned}f(t)+g(t) & =(t+1)+(t+1) \\  & =2t+2,\end{aligned}
$$

which is not a polynomial from $B.$ So, $B$ is *not* closed under addition.

- Statement II is false. For example, if $f(t)=t+1$ and $k=2,$ then 

$$
\begin{aligned}kf(t) & =2(t+1)=2t+2,\end{aligned}
$$

which is not a polynomial from $B.$ So, $B$ is *not* closed under scalar multiplication.

- Statement III is false, while statement IV is true. $B$ is *not* a subspace because it's not closed under addition and scalar multiplication.

Therefore, the correct answer is "IV only."" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-a24ecf47-9c4a-5174-a968-bb79cd6b4d3c"] :db/ensure We proceed to find an orthogonal basis using the Gram-Schmidt process, as follows.

**Step 1**: We set ${v}_{1}={a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ 3\end{aligned}].$

**Step 2**: Next, we find ${v}_{2}$, by using the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{2} & ={a}_{2}-\frac{{a}_{2}\cdot {v}_{1}}{{v}_{1}\cdot {v}_{1}}{v}_{1}.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the formula for ${v}_{2}$ in our case gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{2} & ={a}_{2}-\frac{2\cdot (-1)+7\cdot 1+2\cdot 3}{(-1)^{2}+{1}^{2}+{3}^{2}}{v}_{1} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 7 \\ 2\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 6 \\ -1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we normalize each vector to get an orthonormal basis:

- ${u}_{1}=\frac{{v}_{1}}{‖{v}_{1}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{(-1)^{2}+{1}^{2}+{3}^{2}}}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ 3\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}\frac{-\sqrt{11}}{11} \\ \frac{\sqrt{11}}{11} \\ \frac{3\sqrt{11}}{11}\end{aligned}].$

- ${u}_{2}=\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{{3}^{2}+{6}^{2}+(-1)^{2}}}[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 6 \\ -1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}\frac{3\sqrt{46}}{46} \\ \frac{3\sqrt{46}}{23} \\ -\frac{\sqrt{46}}{46}\end{aligned}].$

Therefore, $B=\{{u}_{1},{u}_{2}\}=\{[\begin{aligned}\frac{-\sqrt{11}}{11} \\ \frac{\sqrt{11}}{11} \\ \frac{3\sqrt{11}}{11}\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}\frac{3\sqrt{46}}{46} \\ \frac{3\sqrt{46}}{23} \\ -\frac{\sqrt{46}}{46}\end{aligned}]\}$ is an orthonormal basis of $V.$

Finally, $a=\frac{3\sqrt{46}}{46},$ $b=\frac{3\sqrt{46}}{23},$ $c=-\frac{\sqrt{46}}{46}$ and  

$$
|a|+|b|+|c|=|\frac{3\sqrt{46}}{46}|+|\frac{3\sqrt{46}}{23}|+|-\frac{\sqrt{46}}{46}|=\frac{5\sqrt{46}}{23}.
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-7d04279b-ec75-5254-bd55-34cd8f8839e1"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-7d04279b-ec75-5254-bd55-34cd8f8839e1" :answer-field/id #uuid "7d04279b-ec75-5254-bd55-34cd8f8839e1" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-a891591d-a9eb-53fe-8982-96c9b063fffc" :answer-field/choices ["answer-c2214cfa-1da7-5079-9e10-7f06971759ac" "answer-a891591d-a9eb-53fe-8982-96c9b063fffc" "answer-85a5f849-bfe1-54f4-a472-2f3b1a9f7def" "answer-7f1f7ef1-8ffa-5d79-89f5-0f699ae92a81" "answer-b8569b62-9dc0-5a84-afdd-7c7913cb7cbd"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-c2214cfa-1da7-5079-9e10-7f06971759ac" :answer/id #uuid "c2214cfa-1da7-5079-9e10-7f06971759ac" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{10\sqrt{46}}{23}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-a891591d-a9eb-53fe-8982-96c9b063fffc" :answer/id #uuid "a891591d-a9eb-53fe-8982-96c9b063fffc" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{5\sqrt{46}}{23}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-85a5f849-bfe1-54f4-a472-2f3b1a9f7def" :answer/id #uuid "85a5f849-bfe1-54f4-a472-2f3b1a9f7def" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{5\sqrt{46}}{46}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-7f1f7ef1-8ffa-5d79-89f5-0f699ae92a81" :answer/id #uuid "7f1f7ef1-8ffa-5d79-89f5-0f699ae92a81" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{\sqrt{46}}{23}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-b8569b62-9dc0-5a84-afdd-7c7913cb7cbd" :answer/id #uuid "b8569b62-9dc0-5a84-afdd-7c7913cb7cbd" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{\sqrt{46}}{46}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186135054 :tutorial/content "The **Gram-Schmidt process** is an algorithm that we can use to construct an *orthogonal* basis if we are given a non-orthogonal basis to start with.

For example, consider the basis $\{ \mathbf{a}_1, \mathbf{a}_2 \}$ for the subspace $V=\textrm{Span} \{ \mathbf{a}_1, \mathbf{a}_2 \},$ where
![](images/c2/c2543117bc661286a5965534dfeeaaf6a066281ee58e2f39ea35143971d6837f.svg)

We can use the above basis to construct an *orthogonal* basis for the given $2$-dimensional subspace. To do this, we use the Gram-Schmidt process, which involves $2$ steps:

- **Step 1:** Set ${\color{blue}\mathbf{v}_1}=\mathbf{a}_1.$

- **Step 2:** Find a vector $\color{blue}\mathbf{v}_2$ in $V$ that's orthogonal to $\color{blue}\mathbf{v}_1.$ This can be achieved by computing

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{2} & ={a}_{2}\,-\,{\text{proj}}_{{v}_{1}}\,{a}_{2} \\  & ={a}_{2}-\frac{{a}_{2}\cdot {v}_{1}}{{v}_{1}\cdot {v}_{1}}{v}_{1}.\end{aligned}
$$

![](images/67/678cc056e3c9d3fbf17423ac591b3e85d84ee8060c0637840fe1c4c9e87aa878.png)

Notice that $\color{blue}\mathbf{v}_2$ is written as a linear combination of $\mathbf{a}_1(={\color{blue}\mathbf{v}_1})$ and $\mathbf{a}_2.$ So this means that ${\color{blue}\mathbf{v}_2} \in V,$ and also ${\color{blue}\mathbf{v}_2} \perp {\color{blue}\mathbf{v}_1}.$
Moreover, 

$$
\textrm{Span}\{\mathbf{a}_1,\mathbf{a}_2\} = V = \textrm{Span}\{ {\color{blue}\mathbf{v}_1}, {\color{blue}\mathbf{v}_2} \}.
$$

After applying the Gram-Schmidt process, we get the set $\mathcal{B}=\{{\color{blue}\mathbf{v}_1}, {\color{blue}\mathbf{v}_2}\},$ which is an orthogonal basis for $V.$

So, in our example, we start by setting ![](images/72/7221215504f7dc7a831501ee23c0563434dd414ac05c1ef7e5761c2719e7d24d.svg) Then, we find the vector $\mathbf{v}_2$ that's orthogonal to $\textrm{Span}\{\mathbf{v}_1\}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{2} & ={a}_{2}-\frac{{a}_{2}\cdot {v}_{1}}{{v}_{1}\cdot {v}_{1}}{v}_{1} \\  & ={a}_{2}-\frac{4\cdot 1+6\cdot (-1)}{{1}^{2}+(-1)^{2}}{v}_{1} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 6\end{aligned}]-(-1)\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 5\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, ![](images/59/5944c42ffd5e609dcec914718180be9652a817de6b8cf84439d57cb106f03353.svg) is an orthogonal basis for $V.$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186135089 :tutorial/content "Sometimes it's helpful to "clean up" the result of a Gram-Schmidt process by scaling the resulting vectors.

For example, suppose that the set $\mathcal B,$ given by

![](images/79/79d1a4963f0e8a2e47dda0acf5c6031571574b1631d57c15d757f94b4f25468b.svg)

is an orthogonal basis for $\textrm{Span} \{ \mathbf{v}_1, \mathbf{v}_2 \}.$

Since the vector $\mathbf{v}_2$ lies in $\textrm{Span} \{ \mathbf{v}_1, \mathbf{v}_2 \}$ and $\mathbf{v}_1 \perp \mathbf{v}_2,$ the vector $3\mathbf{v}_2$ also lies in $\textrm{Span} \{ \mathbf{v}_1, \mathbf{v}_2 \}$ and $\mathbf{v}_1 \perp 3\mathbf{v}_2.$ Therefore, taking

17592186151932 :question/worked-solution "The fractional exponent $x^{1/n}$ can be written as the radical $\sqrt[n]{x}.$

Comparing $x^{1/n}$ with $8^{1/5},$ we get $x = 8$ and $n = 5.$ Therefore,

- To find the square root of a number, we need to find another that multiplies by itself $2$ times to give the original number. For example,

$$
\sqrt{9} = \sqrt{3 \cdot 3} = \sqrt{3^2} = 3.
$$

- To find the cube root of a number, we need to find another that multiplies by itself $3$ times to give the original number. For example,

$$
\sqrt[3]{8} = \sqrt[3]{2 \cdot 2 \cdot 2} = \sqrt[3]{2^3} = 2.
$$

We can extend this to any root. In general, to find the $n$th root of a number, we needed to find another number that multiplies by itself $n$ times to give the original number. We express the $n$th root as the radical $\sqrt[n]{\phantom{0}}.$ For instance,

$$
\sqrt[{\color{blue}4}]{16} = \sqrt[{\color{blue}4}]{\underbrace{2\cdot 2\cdot 2\cdot 2}_{{\color{blue}4}\text{ times}}} = \sqrt[{\color{blue}4}]{2^4} = 2.
$$

Given a radical $\sqrt[n]{x},$ we can write an equivalent expression using the fractional exponent $x^{1/n}.$ To demonstrate, let's write an equivalent expression for $\sqrt[7]{3}.$

Comparing $\sqrt[n]{x}$ with $\sqrt[7]{3},$ we get $x = 3$ and $n = 7.$ Therefore,

$$
\sqrt[7]{3} = 3^{1/7}.
$$

The reverse is also true: the fractional exponent $x^{1/n}$ can be written as the radical $\sqrt[n]{x}.$

**Note:** Remember that the square root of a number corresponds to the case of $n=2.$ So, for example, we have

$$
\sqrt{3} = 3^{1/2}.
$$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186152321 :activity/expected-seconds 420.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]} [:db/retract 17592186163900 :answer-field/choices 17592186163905] [:db/retract 17592186163900 :answer-field/choices 17592186163901] [:db/retract 17592186163900 :answer-field/choices 17592186163903] {:db/id 17592186166883 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-65bd6053-5f41-5a6f-ac31-815596c779fb" "question-a130ee36-c4fa-557a-b62c-af4b4bf44ed4" "question-510822f4-2240-59da-8db4-5275b43b2562" "question-a8b13a1a-6bdb-56d5-b06e-dfa9901c1db1" "question-d1845eab-f52b-5f23-bd27-faf40f79c71a"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186166884 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-bbfd9077-09aa-55c5-a7ec-ce238f7922af" "question-0fd9a9b1-ea5c-5d82-ac2e-6cadd4a02789" "question-a3d12aa9-7854-5ac5-a883-81ef95d3c722"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186166885 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-3b9226c2-67e0-5858-9c64-ae46c4147a95" "question-b2ff4fa5-a334-50b5-9869-f8e569ec5011" "question-b0a81f04-6f59-512d-aa20-c54e3b26a51d"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id "question-65bd6053-5f41-5a6f-ac31-815596c779fb" :question/id #uuid "65bd6053-5f41-5a6f-ac31-815596c779fb" :question/math-academy-id "q-163208" :question/problem "Consider the function $f(x,y)$ and the region $D$ given by

$$
f(x,y)=3y-2x,\,D=\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le y,\,0\le y\le 3\}.
$$

According to the mean value theorem for double integrals, there exists a point $(a,b)\in D$ such that the volume of the solid enclosed between the surface $z=f(x,y)$ and the $xy$-plane over the region $D$ equals the volume of the right cylinder with base $D$ and height $f(a,b).$ Find $b$ given that $a=1.$" :question/worked-solution "According to the mean value theorem for double integrals, there exists a point $(a,b)\in D$ such that

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A=f(a,b)\cdot \text{Area}(D).
$$

Evaluating the integral on the left-hand side, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{D}(3y-2x)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{0}^{y}(3y-2x)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}[3xy-{x}^{2}]_{x=0}^{x=y}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}2{y}^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={[\frac{2{y}^{3}}{3}]}_{y=0}^{y=3} \\  & =18.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Area}(D) & ={∬}_{D}\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{0}^{y}\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}[x]_{x=0}^{x=y}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}y\,\text{d}y \\  & ={[\frac{{y}^{2}}{2}]}_{y=0}^{y=3} \\  & =\frac{9}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Also, we are told that $a=1.$ So, our initial equation simplifies to

$$
\begin{aligned}18 & =f(1,b)\cdot \frac{9}{2} \\ 18 & =(3b-2\cdot 1)\cdot \frac{9}{2} \\ 4 & =3b-2 \\ 6 & =3b \\ b & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that $(1,2)\in D.$ Therefore, the answer is $b=2.$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-efe2ad41-143d-5a5f-9acb-57cf8643ab94"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-efe2ad41-143d-5a5f-9acb-57cf8643ab94" :answer-field/id #uuid "efe2ad41-143d-5a5f-9acb-57cf8643ab94" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-e1a845bb-0954-584e-b542-37d3783851e0" :answer-field/choices ["answer-a7b6ca86-eebb-5760-b9bd-8e54ad1102c8" "answer-e1a845bb-0954-584e-b542-37d3783851e0" "answer-071427db-1ab5-5a7b-8ab5-fd9f44da6576" "answer-b5822c67-2544-5801-8e37-04b814eeeae7" "answer-38e562f4-0b20-5eaa-a03e-6faae7854a82"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-a7b6ca86-eebb-5760-b9bd-8e54ad1102c8" :answer/id #uuid "a7b6ca86-eebb-5760-b9bd-8e54ad1102c8" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "1" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-e1a845bb-0954-584e-b542-37d3783851e0" :answer/id #uuid "e1a845bb-0954-584e-b542-37d3783851e0" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "2" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-071427db-1ab5-5a7b-8ab5-fd9f44da6576" :answer/id #uuid "071427db-1ab5-5a7b-8ab5-fd9f44da6576" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "3" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-b5822c67-2544-5801-8e37-04b814eeeae7" :answer/id #uuid "b5822c67-2544-5801-8e37-04b814eeeae7" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{3}{2}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-38e562f4-0b20-5eaa-a03e-6faae7854a82" :answer/id #uuid "38e562f4-0b20-5eaa-a03e-6faae7854a82" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{5}{2}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-a130ee36-c4fa-557a-b62c-af4b4bf44ed4" :question/id #uuid "a130ee36-c4fa-557a-b62c-af4b4bf44ed4" :question/math-academy-id "q-163151" :question/problem "Consider the function $f(x,y)$ and the region $D$ given by

$$
f(x,y)=2x+{y}^{2},\,D=\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le 2,\,0\le y\le 3\}.
$$

According to the mean value theorem for double integrals, there exists a point $(a,b)\in D$ such that the volume of the solid enclosed between the surface $z=f(x,y)$ and the $xy$-plane over the region $D$ equals the volume of the right cylinder with base $D$ and height $f(a,b).$ Find $a$ given that $b=1.$" :question/worked-solution "According to the mean value theorem for double integrals, there exists a point $(a,b)\in D$ such that

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A=f(a,b)\cdot \text{Area}(D).
$$

Evaluating the integral on the left-hand side, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{D}(2x+{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{3}(2x+{y}^{2})\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}[2xy+\frac{{y}^{3}}{3}]_{y=0}^{y=3}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}(6x+9)\,\text{d}x \\  & =[3{x}^{2}+9x]_{x=0}^{x=2} \\  & =(3\cdot {2}^{2}+9\cdot 2)-0 \\  & =30.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we have

$$
\text{Area}(D)=2\cdot 3=6.
$$

Also, we are told that $b=1.$ So, our initial equation simplifies to

$$
\begin{aligned}30 & =f(a,1)\cdot 6 \\ 30 & =(2a+{1}^{2})\cdot 6 \\ 30 & =12a+6 \\ 24 & =12a \\ a & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

#uuid "a8b13a1a-6bdb-56d5-b06e-dfa9901c1db1" :question/math-academy-id "q-163149" :question/problem "Consider the function $f(x,y)$ and the region $D$ given by

$$
f(x,y)=2x+3{y}^{2},\,D=\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le 2,\,0\le y\le 2\}.
$$

According to the mean value theorem for double integrals, there exists a point $(a,b)\in D$ such that the volume of the solid enclosed between the surface $z=f(x,y)$ and the $xy$-plane over the region $D$ equals the volume of the right cylinder with base $D$ and height $f(a,b).$ Find $a$ given that $b=1.$" :question/worked-solution "According to the mean value theorem for double integrals, there exists a point $(a,b)\in D$ such that

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A=f(a,b)\cdot \text{Area}(D).
$$

Evaluating the integral on the left-hand side, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{D}(2x+3{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{2}(2x+3{y}^{2})\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}[2xy+{y}^{3}]_{y=0}^{y=2}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}(4x+8)\,\text{d}x \\  & =[2{x}^{2}+8x]_{x=0}^{x=2} \\  & =(2\cdot {2}^{2}+8\cdot 2)-0 \\  & =24.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we have

$$
\text{Area}(D)=2\cdot 2=4.
$$

Also, we are told that $b=1.$ So, our initial equation simplifies to

$$
\begin{aligned}24 & =f(a,1)\cdot 4 \\ 24 & =(2a+3\cdot {1}^{2})\cdot 4 \\ 6 & =2a+3 \\ 3 & =2a \\ a & =\frac{3}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that $(\frac{3}{2},1)\in D.$ Therefore, the answer is $a=\frac{3}{2}.$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields $$

$$

$$

Evaluating the integral on the left-hand side, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{D}(2x+y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{6}{\int }_{y/2}^{y}(2x+y)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{6}[{x}^{2}+xy]_{x=y/2}^{x=y}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{6}([{y}^{2}+{y}^{2}]-[\frac{{y}^{2}}{4}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{2}])\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{6}\frac{5{y}^{2}}{4}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={[\frac{5{y}^{3}}{12}]}_{y=0}^{y=6} \\  & =90.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Area}(D) & ={∬}_{D}\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{6}{\int }_{y/2}^{y}\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{6}[x]_{x=y/2}^{x=y}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{6}\frac{y}{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={[\frac{{y}^{2}}{4}]}_{y=0}^{y=6} \\  & =9.\end{aligned}
$$

Also, we are told that $b=4.$ So, our initial equation simplifies to

$$
\begin{aligned}90 & =f(a,4)\cdot 9 \\ 90 & =(2a+4)\cdot 9 \\ 10 & =2a+4 \\ 6 & =2a \\ a & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

$f(x,y)={y}^{2}$ on the disk of radius $2$ centered at the origin." :question/worked-solution "First, notice that 

$$
\text{Area}(D)=\pi \cdot {2}^{2}=4\pi .
$$

The average value of the function over a region $D$ is given by

$$
{f}_{\text{ave}}=\frac{1}{\text{Area}(D)}\,{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A.
$$

We will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .
$$

In polar coordinates $(r,\theta ),$ the region can be expressed as 

$$
Δ=\{(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le 2,\,0\le \theta <2\pi \}.
$$

Using the change of variables formula, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}{y}^{2}\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2}\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{2}{r}^{3}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{sin}^{2}⁡\theta {\int }_{0}^{2}{r}^{3}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{sin}^{2}⁡\theta \,{[\frac{{r}^{4}}{4}]}_{0}^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{sin}^{2}⁡\theta (4-0)\text{d}\theta  \\  & =4{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{sin}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =4{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\frac{1}{2}(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta )\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =2{[\theta -\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta ]}_{0}^{2\pi } \\  & =2[(2\pi -0)-\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{sin}⁡4\pi -\operatorname{sin}⁡0)] \\  & =2\cdot 2\pi  \\  & =4\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$f(x,y)={e}^{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}$ on the disk of radius $\frac{1}{2}$ centered at the origin." :question/worked-solution "First, notice that 

$$
\text{Area}(D)=\pi \cdot {(\frac{1}{2})}^{2}=\frac{\pi }{4}.
$$

The average value of the function over a region $D$ is given by

$$
{f}_{\text{ave}}=\frac{1}{\text{Area}(D)}\,{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A.
$$

We will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .
$$

In polar coordinates $(r,\theta ),$ the region can be expressed as 

$$
Δ=\{(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le \frac{1}{2},\,0\le \theta <2\pi \}.
$$

Using the change of variables formula, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}{e}^{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}{e}^{(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2}}\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={∬}_{Δ}{e}^{{r}^{2}}\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\,{[\frac{{e}^{{r}^{2}}}{2}]}_{0}^{1/2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(\frac{{e}^{1/4}}{2}-\frac{1}{2})\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{\sqrt[4]{e}-1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{\sqrt[4]{e}-1}{2}[\theta ]_{0}^{2\pi } \\  & =\frac{\sqrt[4]{e}-1}{2}(2\pi -0) \\  & =(\sqrt[4]{e}-1)\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
{f}_{\text{ave}}=\frac{4}{\pi }\cdot (\sqrt[4]{e}-1)\pi =4(\sqrt[4]{e}-1).
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-d1136c19-2541-5007-b027-75b59e3253ba"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-d1136c19-2541-5007-b027-75b59e3253ba" :answer-field/id #uuid "d1136c19-2541-5007-b027-75b59e3253ba" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-aaec5f62-9f91-57f5-b958-6eca6bd1c1da" :answer-field/choices ["answer-ff8cb142-efbd-5919-b474-a1189a94a948" "answer-9d49fd2e-9748-5870-a942-7855eab45dc3" "answer-c378d23d-c433-57b0-a302-3ca7d194c79d" "answer-aaec5f62-9f91-57f5-b958-6eca6bd1c1da" "answer-3d66d8b4-c0c5-583c-9422-a56fec563fa4"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-ff8cb142-efbd-5919-b474-a1189a94a948" :answer/id #uuid "ff8cb142-efbd-5919-b474-a1189a94a948" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "2(\sqrt[2]{e}+2)" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-9d49fd2e-9748-5870-a942-7855eab45dc3" :answer/id #uuid "9d49fd2e-9748-5870-a942-7855eab45dc3" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "2(\sqrt[4]{e}+1)" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-c378d23d-c433-57b0-a302-3ca7d194c79d" :answer/id #uuid "c378d23d-c433-57b0-a302-3ca7d194c79d" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "4(\sqrt[2]{e}-1)" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-aaec5f62-9f91-57f5-b958-6eca6bd1c1da" :answer/id #uuid "aaec5f62-9f91-57f5-b958-6eca6bd1c1da" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "4(\sqrt[4]{e}-1)" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-3d66d8b4-c0c5-583c-9422-a56fec563fa4" :answer/id #uuid "3d66d8b4-c0c5-583c-9422-a56fec563fa4" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\sqrt[8]{e}-2" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-b0a81f04-6f59-512d-aa20-c54e3b26a51d" :question/id #uuid "b0a81f04-6f59-512d-aa20-c54e3b26a51d" :question/math-academy-id "q-163277" :question/problem "![](images/06/06a853735916ae3219eea02fa7e7e30d9e941106600cd5b642d951f553aace59.png)

Find the average value of the function $f(x,y)=5y({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})$ on the semicircle shown above." :question/worked-solution "First, notice that 

$$
\text{Area}(D)=\frac{1}{2}\cdot \pi \cdot {1}^{2}=\frac{\pi }{2}.
$$

The average value of the function over a region $D$ is given by

$$
{f}_{\text{ave}}=\frac{1}{\text{Area}(D)}\,{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A.
$$

We will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .
$$

Notice that the region $D$ represents a portion of the disk of radius $1$ centered at 
$(1,0).$

Cartesian and polar coordinates are connected by the following equations:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \end{aligned}
$$

With that is mind, let's now write the $y=-\sqrt{2x-{x}^{2}}$ in polar coordinates:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =-\sqrt{2x-{x}^{2}} \\ {y}^{2} & =2x-{x}^{2} \\ {x}^{2}+{y}^{2} & =2x \\ (r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2} & =2r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ {r}^{2}({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta ) & =2r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ {r}^{2} & =2r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ {r}^{2}-2r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =0 \\ r(r-2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

 

Since $r$ cannot be identical to zero on the entire semicircle, we must have $r=2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .$

Therefore, in polar coordinates $(r,\theta ),$ the region can be expressed as 

$$
Δ=\{(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le 2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,-\frac{\pi }{2}\le \theta \le 0\}.
$$

Therefore, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}5y({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}5r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ((r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2})\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{0}{\int }_{0}^{2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }5{r}^{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{0}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta {\int }_{0}^{2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }5{r}^{4}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{0}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta [{r}^{5}]_{0}^{2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{0}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ((2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{5}-0)\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =32{\int }_{-\pi /2}^{0}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta {cos}^{5}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =32{[-\frac{1}{6}{cos}^{6}⁡\theta ]}_{-\pi /2}^{0} \\  & =-\frac{16}{3}[{cos}^{6}⁡(0)-{cos}^{6}⁡(-\frac{\pi }{2})] \\  & =-\frac{16}{3}(1-0) \\  & =-\frac{16}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
{f}_{\text{ave}}=\frac{1}{(\frac{\pi }{2})}\cdot (-\frac{16}{3})=-\frac{32}{3\pi }.
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-7e8c2182-159c-53aa-a9ec-6a0270a24944"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-7e8c2182-159c-53aa-a9ec-6a0270a24944" :answer-field/id #uuid "7e8c2182-159c-53aa-a9ec-6a0270a24944" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-e979451f-00ff-5ed9-83e8-7aff07a87414" :answer-field/choices ["answer-07e40d47-7a70-5f2c-ba24-6a855b1d6eb7" "answer-e1b2263d-a0be-566e-8984-74cc5d983449" "answer-e979451f-00ff-5ed9-83e8-7aff07a87414" "answer-e83a9fc3-1293-5456-b3e0-ca1e41eb01ee" "answer-43bff162-e0e6-5e6e-b559-7547ee7c72a5"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-07e40d47-7a70-5f2c-ba24-6a855b1d6eb7" :answer/id #uuid "07e40d47-7a70-5f2c-ba24-6a855b1d6eb7" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-\frac{16}{3\pi }" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-e1b2263d-a0be-566e-8984-74cc5d983449" :answer/id #uuid "e1b2263d-a0be-566e-8984-74cc5d983449" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-\frac{16}{5\pi }" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-e979451f-00ff-5ed9-83e8-7aff07a87414" :answer/id #uuid "e979451f-00ff-5ed9-83e8-7aff07a87414" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-\frac{32}{3\pi }" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-e83a9fc3-1293-5456-b3e0-ca1e41eb01ee" :answer/id #uuid "e83a9fc3-1293-5456-b3e0-ca1e41eb01ee" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-\frac{32}{3}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-43bff162-e0e6-5e6e-b559-7547ee7c72a5" :answer/id #uuid "43bff162-e0e6-5e6e-b559-7547ee7c72a5" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-\frac{8}{3}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186167137 :question/problem "Find the average value of the function $f(x,y)=2x+y$ on the portion of the disk of radius $2$ centered at the origin, where $y\ge 0.$" :question/worked-solution "First, let's sketch our region $D:$ 

![](images/b5/b5ba69ab02aa13e201b7b9113f6a36e705ad19e6412499504afc4f239459a8f3.png)

Notice that 

$$
\text{Area}(D)=\frac{1}{2}\cdot \pi \cdot {2}^{2}=2\pi .
$$

The average value of the function over a region $D$ is given by

$$
{f}_{\text{ave}}=\frac{1}{\text{Area}(D)}\,{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A.
$$

We will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .
$$

In polar coordinates $(r,\theta ),$ the region can be expressed as 

$$
Δ=\{(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le 2,\,0\le \theta \le \pi \}.
$$

Using the change of variables formula, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}(2x+y)\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}(2r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{2}{r}^{2}(2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }(2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ){\int }_{0}^{2}{r}^{2}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }(2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,{[\frac{{r}^{3}}{3}]}_{0}^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }(2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )(\frac{{2}^{3}}{3}-0)\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{8}{3}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }(2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{8}{3}[2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ]_{0}^{\pi } \\  & =\frac{8}{3}((2\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi )-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi ))-(2\operatorname{sin}⁡(0)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(0))) \\  & =\frac{8}{3}(1+1) \\  & =\frac{16}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
{f}_{\text{ave}}=\frac{1}{2\pi }\cdot \frac{16}{3}=\frac{8}{3\pi }.
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186163900 :answer-field/correct "answer-932abe94-bffd-5dad-a100-ed7dd0878970" :answer-field/choices ["answer-a461f542-25f5-59e6-a3ba-329bd57b7ee7" "answer-3243821a-d8ad-5dd7-aced-e15740550519" "answer-932abe94-bffd-5dad-a100-ed7dd0878970"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-a461f542-25f5-59e6-a3ba-329bd57b7ee7" :answer/id #uuid "a461f542-25f5-59e6-a3ba-329bd57b7ee7" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{4}{3\pi }" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-3243821a-d8ad-5dd7-aced-e15740550519" :answer/id #uuid "3243821a-d8ad-5dd7-aced-e15740550519" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{6}{\pi }" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-932abe94-bffd-5dad-a100-ed7dd0878970" :answer/id #uuid "932abe94-bffd-5dad-a100-ed7dd0878970" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{8}{3\pi }" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186281653 :question/worked-solution "First, let's sketch our region $D:$ 

![](images/25/25c1f00e588ddaa130f854d9f4e9dfe9b1158d7952a01bae8108ea4b94d3c347.png)

Notice that 

$$
\text{Area}(D)=\frac{1}{2}\cdot \pi \cdot {3}^{2}=\frac{9\pi }{2}.
$$

The average value of the function over a region $D$ is given by

$$
{f}_{\text{ave}}=\frac{1}{\text{Area}(D)}\,{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A.
$$

We will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .
$$

In polar coordinates $(r,\theta ),$ the region can be expressed as 

$$
Δ=\{(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le 3,\,\frac{\pi }{2}\le \theta \le \frac{3\pi }{2}\}.
$$

Using the change of variables formula, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\frac{2}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+1}\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}\frac{2}{(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2}+1}\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{3\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{3}\frac{2r}{{r}^{2}+1}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{3\pi /2}[\operatorname{ln}⁡({r}^{2}+1)]_{0}^{3}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{3\pi /2}(\operatorname{ln}⁡10-\operatorname{ln}⁡1)\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡10{\int }_{\pi /2}^{3\pi /2}\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡10[\theta ]_{\pi /2}^{3\pi /2} \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡10(\frac{3\pi }{2}-\frac{\pi }{2}) \\  & =\pi \operatorname{ln}⁡10.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
{f}_{\text{ave}}=\frac{2}{9\pi }\cdot \pi \operatorname{ln}⁡10=\frac{2\operatorname{ln}⁡10}{9}.
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186168150 :tutorial/content "Given a continuous function $f(x)$ on a closed interval $[a, b],$ the mean value theorem for integrals guarantees that there exists a number $c \in [a,b]$ such that

$$
\int_a^b f(x)\, \textrm d x = f(c) \cdot (b-a),
$$

which can be visualized as shown below.

![](images/0a/0afb9b15787eb89f73f322290bdbe2288027c54924d274c438773ce151a17291.png)

 

We have a similar theorem for functions with two variables. The so-called **mean value theorem for double integrals** states:

*If the function $f(x,y)$ is continuous on a closed and bounded region $D,$ then there exists a point $(a,b) \in D$ such that*

$$
\iint\limits_D f(x,y) \: \textrm{d}A = f(a,b) \cdot \textrm{Area}(D).
$$

This has a nice geometrical interpretation when $f$ is non-negative on $D.$ In this case, the theorem tells us that there exists a point $(a,b) \in D$ such that the volume of the solid enclosed between the surface $z=f(x,y)$ and the $xy$-plane over the region $D$ equals the volume of the right cylinder with base $D$ and height $f(a,b).$ 

The diagram below shows the case when $D$ is rectangular, and the corresponding cylinder is a rectangular solid.

![](images/8e/8ed477207ee61fbdaf963ed8a127e3f1d4cf76707d2eeb4b450fd49f78e15b7e.png)

 

In general, the point $(a,b)$ mentioned in the theorem is not unique. Let's see an example." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186168151 :tutorial/content "Consider the continuous function 

$$
f(x,y) = x+3y^2+2
$$

and the region $D$ given by

$$
D = \big\{ (x,y) \: : \: 0 \leq x \leq 2, \: 0 \leq y \leq 2 \big\}.
$$

According to the mean value theorem for double integrals, there exists a point $(a,b) \in D$ such that

$$
\iint\limits_D f(x,y) \: \textrm{d}A = f(a,b) \cdot \textrm{Area}(D).
$$

Evaluating the integral on the left-hand side, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{D}(x+3{y}^{2}+2)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{2}(x+3{y}^{2}+2)\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{[xy+{y}^{3}+2y]}_{y=0}^{y=2}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}(2x+12)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={[{x}^{2}+12x]}_{x=0}^{x=2} \\  & =28.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we have

$$
\textrm{Area}(D) = 2 \cdot 2 = 4.
$$

So, our mean-value equation simplifies to

$$
\begin{aligned}28 & =f(a,b)\cdot 4 \\ 7 & =f(a,b) \\ 7 & =a+3{b}^{2}+2 \\ a & =5-3{b}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

This equation describes part of a parabola in the $xy$-plane, as shown below.

![](images/46/46873c4ecb290380488e589082fc0759324d3540494f5b83e2d64db5d9cdf62a.png)

  

To find a particular point that satisfies the mean value theorem, we can set, for example, $b=1 \in [0,2]$ and obtain $a=2.$ So, the point $(2,1)$ satisfies the mean value theorem for double integrals. Consequently, the two solids below must have the same volume.

![](images/82/82d3a762ab323339570e6010038e75ce95f3fdbde958a2ffa876972cbf91e8fb.png)" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186168149 :tutorial/content "Recall that the average value of a continuous function $f(x)$ on a closed interval $D = [a,b]$ is given by

$$

*Suppose $D$ is a closed and bounded region in $\mathbb{R}^2$ which has non-zero finite area $\textrm{Area}(D).$ If $f (x, y)$ is a continuous function on $D,$ then **the average value of $\boldsymbol f$ on $\boldsymbol D$** is given by*

$$

![](images/de/ded8743284f207bff35eba24617fd4245a69d439ed151d09eed564813f9d72fb.png)

The *distance* between the number $-3$ and $0$ is known as the **absolute value** of $-3.$ We write it as

$$
|-3| = {\color{red}3}.
$$

Similarly, $|\,2\,|$, the absolute value of the number $2$, is the distance between $2$ and $0$:

![](images/f4/f44fcd05fb0932083d48c8b11892247d8de8fbc46ccf7186fb12843702181aea.png)

We write $|\,2\,| = {\color{red}2}.$

So, the absolute value simply 

- *removes the minus sign*, if the number is negative, or

- does nothing, if the number is non-negative.

Sometimes, we can be asked to evaluate an expression involving the absolute value function, like $|x +1| + 5$ when $x=-3.$ In this case, we evaluate the expression inside the absolute value before simplifying the rest of the expression: 

$$
\begin{aligned}|x+1|+5 & = \\ |(-3)+1|+5 & = \\ |-2|+5 & = \\ 2+5 & = \\ 7 & \end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186054936 :activity/expected-seconds 420.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]} {:db/id 17592186157276 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-8702bab9-12cd-5dfe-a35e-1fe882de5059" "question-d1f6161d-c4cc-5098-b5d8-59c092ed97d0"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186157080 :question/problem "Given the orthogonal basis $\mathcal{B}$ of $\mathbb{R}^3$ and the vector $\mathbf{x}$ below, find the value of $x_2,$ the second component of $[\mathbf{x}]_{\mathcal{B}}.$

![](images/c7/c7ef03afd5772c8446f0864cc470d7375b5ddb30a97a0e19c48cec9c0dc755a4.svg)" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186158471 :tutorial/content "Given any vector $\mathbf{x}$ and any subspace $W$ in $\mathbb{R}^n,$ we can always write $\mathbf{x}$ as a sum of a vector from $W$ and a vector from $W^{\perp}.$ This fact is known as the **orthogonal decomposition theorem.** We can state it formally as follows:

*Let $W$ be a subspace of $\mathbb{R}^n.$ Then each $\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^n$ can be written uniquely in the form

$$
\mathbf{x}= \mathbf{y}+\mathbf{z}
$$

where $\mathbf{y} \in W$ and $\mathbf{z} \in W^{\perp}.$* 

*Moreover, since $\mathbf y$ is the orthogonal projection of $\mathbf x$ onto the subspace $W,$ if $\{\mathbf{u}_1\,\dots,\mathbf{u}_p\}$ is any orthogonal basis of $W,$ then* 

$$
\begin{aligned}y & ={\text{proj}}_{W}\,x \\  & ={\text{proj}}_{{u}_{1}}\,x+{\text{proj}}_{{u}_{2}}\,x+⋯+{\text{proj}}_{{u}_{p}}\,x \\  & =\frac{x\cdot {u}_{1}}{{u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{1}}{u}_{1}+\frac{x\cdot {u}_{2}}{{u}_{2}\cdot {u}_{2}}{u}_{2}+⋯+\frac{x\cdot {u}_{p}}{{u}_{p}\cdot {u}_{p}}{u}_{p}.\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186157482 :activity/expected-seconds 420.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]} {:db/id 17592186162124 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-40beaebe-e39b-5263-8664-2ca0bd457e93" "question-bf85ed85-426f-57b2-8e6b-2867b23718fe" "question-c34fa369-1de0-5740-997b-e34e018ecb92" "question-a1b40ecf-b8ac-57c2-a3f6-1fe3744073eb"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186161690 :question/problem "Let $X$ and $Y$ be discrete random variables with the joint probability mass function $f(x,y)$ shown below.

Let the joint CDF of $X$ and $Y$ be $F(x,y),$ where the supports of $X$ and $Y$, respectively, are

$$
{S}_{X}=\{1,3\},\,{S}_{Y}=\{1,2,3,4\}.
$$

Find an expression for the corresponding joint CDF when $x>3,y<1.$" :question/worked-solution "If $X$ and $Y$ are discrete random variables with the joint probability mass function $f(x,y),$ then the corresponding joint CDF is given by

$$
F(x,y)=P(X\le x,Y\le y)={\sum }_{{x}_{i}\le x}{\sum }_{{y}_{i}\le y}f({x}_{i},{y}_{i}).
$$

Note the following:

- We can think of each point where $f(x,y)\ne 0$ as a point mass in the plane, where the "probability mass" at each point equals the probability associated with that point.

- The joint CDF $F(x,y)=P(X\le x,Y\le y)$ is the total "probability mass" that lies in the infinite rectangular region that has its top-right corner at $(x,y)$ and whose sides are parallel to the coordinate axis.

Given the supports of $X$ and $Y,$ the joint support $S$ is a subset of

$$
{S}_{X}\times {S}_{Y}=\{1,3\}\times \{1,2,3,4\}.
$$

Let's sketch the points in ${S}_{X}\times {S}_{Y},$ which contains the joint support. Let's also consider a point $(x,y)$ where $x>3$ and $y<1,$ and a region $Δ$ that lies below and to the left of this point.

![](images/2e/2ef3347831324b55e1a8ddaff2b0eb6af7fb7fc171867906e70c4b51f0051b05.png)

Since every value in the support of $Y$ is at least $1$ and $y<1,$ no possible value of $Y$ satisfies $Y\le y.$ Therefore, there are no points in the joint support that lie in the region $Δ.$

Hence,

$$

$$

Find $P(X\le 1,-1<Y\le 1).$" :question/worked-solution "Note the following:

- For a given joint PMF $f(x,y),$ we can think of each point where $f(x,y)\ne 0$ as a point mass in the plane, where the "probability mass" at each point equals the probability associated with that point.

- The joint CDF $F(x,y)=P(X\le x,Y\le y)$ is the total "probability mass" that lies in the infinite rectangular region that has its top-right corner at $(x,y)$ and whose sides are parallel to the coordinate axis.

Given the supports of $X$ and $Y,$ the joint support $S$ is a subset of

$$
{S}_{X}\times {S}_{Y}=\{-2,-1,0,1,2\}\times \{-2,-1,0,1,2\}.
$$

Let's sketch the points in ${S}_{X}\times {S}_{Y},$ which contains the joint support.

![](images/dd/dd49cc4b7cb5cc80bb325819c5c8f3c31f8bc3ed762139c2c3b9567a24db2324.png)

Let's sketch the region corresponding to the probability we wish to find.

![](images/34/344fec686907843b4b9375db138592f93be9d0232500fb35dceb90086db503cc.png)

Geometrically, this region can be obtained by taking all points in the infinite rectangle that has its top-right corner at $(1,1)$ (the blue region below) and *subtracting* all points in the infinite rectangle that has its top-right corner at $(1,-1)$ (the red region below).

![](images/6e/6e3a7389008d67f4096fdaa6a98c0e3e2bdeda64ec1e47b93a6d3ba66a54b18d.png)

Therefore, we have

$$

$$

and the supports of $X$ and $Y$, respectively, are

$$
{S}_{X}=\{0,1,2,3,4,5\},\,{S}_{Y}=\{-2,-1,0,1,2\}.
$$

Find $P(1<X\le 4,-1<Y\le 1).$" :question/worked-solution "Note the following:

- For a given joint PMF $f(x,y),$ we can think of each point where $f(x,y)\ne 0$ as a point mass in the plane, where the "probability mass" at each point equals the probability associated with that point.

- The joint CDF $F(x,y)=P(X\le x,Y\le y)$ is the total "probability mass" that lies in the infinite rectangular region that has its top-right corner at $(x,y)$ and whose sides are parallel to the coordinate axis.

Given the supports of $X$ and $Y,$ the joint support $S$ is a subset of

$$
{S}_{X}\times {S}_{Y}=\{0,1,2,3,4,5\}\times \{-2,-1,0,1,2\}.
$$

Let's sketch the points in ${S}_{X}\times {S}_{Y},$ which contains the joint support.

![](images/01/01e04dfdac5f4abc16bd856dcfbe1b7361010cce2e7779658a33f293c1c52ae4.png)

Let's sketch the region corresponding to the probability we wish to find.

![](images/2d/2d2525118ca3b62c0829c0308fab168d0b806dfa13302c007a63cd354314d63f.png)

Geometrically, this region can be obtained as follows:

1\. Take the infinite rectangle that has its top-right corner at $(4,1).$

2\. Subtract the infinite rectangles that have their top-right corners at $(4,-1)$ and $(1,1).$

3\. Finally, we need to add back the infinite rectangle that has its top-right corner at $(1,-1).$ This is because we subtracted this region twice in step 2.

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}P(1<X\le 4,-1<Y\le 1) & =\overset{\text{top-right corner at }(4,1)}{\overset{⏞}{P(X\le 4,Y\le 1)}} \\  & \,-\overset{\text{top-right corner at }(4,-1)}{\overset{⏞}{P(X\le 4,Y\le -1)}}-\overset{\text{top-right corner at }(1,1)}{\overset{⏞}{P(X\le 1,Y\le 1)}} \\  & \,+\overset{\text{top-right corner at }(1,-1)}{\overset{⏞}{P(X\le 1,Y\le -1)}} \\  & =F(4,1)-F(4,-1)-F(1,1)+F(1,-1) \\  & =0.77-0.15-0.19+0.09 \\  & =0.52.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-0973e0ae-8949-52fe-9d14-7a1a4925ba53"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-0973e0ae-8949-52fe-9d14-7a1a4925ba53" :answer-field/id #uuid "0973e0ae-8949-52fe-9d14-7a1a4925ba53" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-ea93ddf2-c74d-5131-8f0c-698558bc1ccd" :answer-field/choices ["answer-fe0f133d-d936-51dc-8dad-167e59ac346b" "answer-05a1a33d-ed6a-57ac-b7c7-d80e7811473a" "answer-85b516c6-df16-5177-b323-6e0f55271ea3" "answer-ea93ddf2-c74d-5131-8f0c-698558bc1ccd" "answer-e248ad4f-2ddb-5621-a2c5-b027b720eeff"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-fe0f133d-d936-51dc-8dad-167e59ac346b" :answer/id #uuid "fe0f133d-d936-51dc-8dad-167e59ac346b" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "0.09" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-05a1a33d-ed6a-57ac-b7c7-d80e7811473a" :answer/id #uuid "05a1a33d-ed6a-57ac-b7c7-d80e7811473a" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "0.34" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-85b516c6-df16-5177-b323-6e0f55271ea3" :answer/id #uuid "85b516c6-df16-5177-b323-6e0f55271ea3" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "0.43" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-ea93ddf2-c74d-5131-8f0c-698558bc1ccd" :answer/id #uuid "ea93ddf2-c74d-5131-8f0c-698558bc1ccd" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "0.52" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-e248ad4f-2ddb-5621-a2c5-b027b720eeff" :answer/id #uuid "e248ad4f-2ddb-5621-a2c5-b027b720eeff" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "0.61" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186162413 :question/problem "Suppose $X$ and $Y$ are discrete random variables. Let the joint CDF of $X$ and $Y$ be $F(x,y),$ where

$$
F(5,1)=0.67,\,F(3,1)=0.43\,F(1,1)=0.2,
$$

and the supports of $X$ and $Y$, respectively, are

$$
{S}_{X}=\{1,2,3,4,5\},\,{S}_{Y}=\{-2,-1,0,1,2\}.
$$

Find $P(X>3,Y<2).$" :question/worked-solution "Note the following:

- For a given joint PMF $f(x,y),$ we can think of each point where $f(x,y)\ne 0$ as a point mass in the plane, where the "probability mass" at each point equals the probability associated with that point.

- The joint CDF $F(x,y)=P(X\le x,Y\le y)$ is the total "probability mass" that lies in the infinite rectangular region that has its top-right corner at $(x,y)$ and whose sides are parallel to the coordinate axis.

Given the supports of $X$ and $Y,$ the joint support $S$ is a subset of

$$
{S}_{X}\times {S}_{Y}=\{1,2,3,4,5\}\times \{-2,-1,0,1,2\}.
$$

Let's plot the points in ${S}_{X}\times {S}_{Y},$ which contains the joint support, and sketch the region corresponding to the probability we wish to find.

![](images/cd/cdb5c8084958ba3dc1175c1e92035d89fb4edcdf8ce333962b49f22b40552f71.png)

Notice that this region encompasses the same possible support points as the infinite rectangle with its top-right corner at $(5,1)$ and top-left corner at $(3,1),$ where the top and right boundaries are included, and the left boundary is excluded.

![](images/1c/1c28f3e2f820511a30aa64ccd3affacaa6d72e69da9c596827429b244bf1129a.png)

Geometrically, this region can be obtained by taking all points in the infinite rectangle that has its top-right corner at $(5,1)$ (the blue region below) and *subtracting* all points in the infinite rectangle that has its top-right corner at $(3,1)$ (the red region below).

![](images/ae/ae993ae6e8c0d71a42ca0e11ed5b30a8d762b3fab12771247eca262f0131c4f5.png)

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X>3,Y<2) & =\overset{\text{top-right corner at }(5,1)}{\overset{⏞}{P(X\le 5,Y\le 1)}}-\overset{\text{top-right corner at }(3,1)}{\overset{⏞}{P(X\le 3,Y\le 1)}} \\  & =F(5,1)-F(3,1) \\  & =0.67-0.43 \\  & =0.24.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-7b5302b1-965f-57a3-8e52-58216fd37b2b"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-7b5302b1-965f-57a3-8e52-58216fd37b2b" :answer-field/id #uuid "7b5302b1-965f-57a3-8e52-58216fd37b2b" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-e0f16e58-ba50-5519-b0c9-2c7d1935a069" :answer-field/choices ["answer-7d933f6f-e2c3-51e2-80f4-1f904b3bbf7b" "answer-04ed47b4-e775-566f-bc2c-56a2a7bded91" "answer-e0f16e58-ba50-5519-b0c9-2c7d1935a069" "answer-9d89dae4-9bbc-5113-9c23-1d88b96505c0" "answer-be91de9f-ef83-54e9-8ed1-7d56afbe15c5"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-7d933f6f-e2c3-51e2-80f4-1f904b3bbf7b" :answer/id #uuid "7d933f6f-e2c3-51e2-80f4-1f904b3bbf7b" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "0.086" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-04ed47b4-e775-566f-bc2c-56a2a7bded91" :answer/id #uuid "04ed47b4-e775-566f-bc2c-56a2a7bded91" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "0.23" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-e0f16e58-ba50-5519-b0c9-2c7d1935a069" :answer/id #uuid "e0f16e58-ba50-5519-b0c9-2c7d1935a069" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "0.24" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-9d89dae4-9bbc-5113-9c23-1d88b96505c0" :answer/id #uuid "9d89dae4-9bbc-5113-9c23-1d88b96505c0" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "0.47" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-be91de9f-ef83-54e9-8ed1-7d56afbe15c5" :answer/id #uuid "be91de9f-ef83-54e9-8ed1-7d56afbe15c5" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "0.63" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-9ab8b5f0-f462-5316-91ff-26b04644c742" :question/id #uuid "9ab8b5f0-f462-5316-91ff-26b04644c742" :question/math-academy-id "q-146848" :question/problem "Suppose $X$ and $Y$ are discrete random variables. Let the joint CDF of $X$ and $Y$ be $F(x,y),$ where

$$
F(10,9)=0.55,\,F(10,3)=0.15,\,F(4,9)=0.1,\,F(4,3)=0.05,
$$

and the supports of $X$ and $Y$, respectively, are

$$
{S}_{X}=\{2,4,6,8,10,12\},\,{S}_{Y}=\{3,6,9,12\}.
$$

Find $P(5<X<11,4<Y<10).$" :question/worked-solution "Note the following:

- For a given joint PMF $f(x,y),$ we can think of each point where $f(x,y)\ne 0$ as a point mass in the plane, where the "probability mass" at each point equals the probability associated with that point.

- The joint CDF $F(x,y)=P(X\le x,Y\le y)$ is the total "probability mass" that lies in the infinite rectangular region that has its top-right corner at $(x,y)$ and whose sides are parallel to the coordinate axis.

Given the supports of $X$ and $Y,$ the joint support $S$ is a subset of

$$
{S}_{X}\times {S}_{Y}=\{2,4,6,8,10,12\}\times \{3,6,9,12\}.
$$

Let's plot the points in ${S}_{X}\times {S}_{Y},$ which contains the joint support, and sketch the region corresponding to the probability we wish to find.

![](images/f4/f43c5ae8d27872c4aebe235c507600b7bf1806e22b52dd3b3ff2261509ac9925.png)

Notice that this region encompasses the same possible support points as the rectangular region with its top-right corner at $(10,9)$ and bottom-left corner at $(4,3)$ below, where the top and right boundaries are inclusive and the bottom and left boundaries are exclusive.

![](images/60/60bf5a958b682d513010c3eff9a8084072be62e286c0b0dfacb09960a3283e38.png)

Geometrically, this region can be obtained as follows:

1\. Take the infinite rectangle that has its top-right corner at $(10,9).$

2\. Subtract the infinite rectangles that have their top-right corners at $(10,3)$ and $(4,9).$

3\. Finally, we need to add back the infinite rectangle that has its top-right corner at $(4,3).$ This is because we subtracted this region twice in step 2.

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}P(5<X<11,4<Y<10) & =\overset{\text{top-right corner at }(10,9)}{\overset{⏞}{P(X\le 10,Y\le 9)}} \\  & \,-\overset{\text{top-right corner at }(10,3)}{\overset{⏞}{P(X\le 10,Y\le 3)}}-\overset{\text{top-right corner at }(4,9)}{\overset{⏞}{P(X\le 4,Y\le 9)}} \\  & \,+\overset{\text{top-right corner at }(4,3)}{\overset{⏞}{P(X\le 4,Y\le 3)}} \\  & =F(10,9)-F(10,3)-F(4,9)+F(4,3) \\  & =0.55-0.15-0.1+0.05 \\  & =0.35.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-23fa940f-fe5f-5cda-bceb-aaf37edf3942"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-23fa940f-fe5f-5cda-bceb-aaf37edf3942" :answer-field/id #uuid "23fa940f-fe5f-5cda-bceb-aaf37edf3942" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-ef6caa9c-a472-5218-9f51-793ff820cd6b" :answer-field/choices ["answer-87cd8823-38ea-50c5-94f7-78a13978c16c" "answer-76b02660-6e75-52ad-85ae-f40779aa5c78" "answer-ef6caa9c-a472-5218-9f51-793ff820cd6b" "answer-a704e947-f321-56a0-8e33-a84b3ace5f65" "answer-0270bd4d-b1c8-5184-b8a3-b42476109664"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-87cd8823-38ea-50c5-94f7-78a13978c16c" :answer/id #uuid "87cd8823-38ea-50c5-94f7-78a13978c16c" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "0.05" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-76b02660-6e75-52ad-85ae-f40779aa5c78" :answer/id #uuid "76b02660-6e75-52ad-85ae-f40779aa5c78" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "0.3" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-ef6caa9c-a472-5218-9f51-793ff820cd6b" :answer/id #uuid "ef6caa9c-a472-5218-9f51-793ff820cd6b" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "0.35" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-a704e947-f321-56a0-8e33-a84b3ace5f65" :answer/id #uuid "a704e947-f321-56a0-8e33-a84b3ace5f65" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "0.45" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-0270bd4d-b1c8-5184-b8a3-b42476109664" :answer/id #uuid "0270bd4d-b1c8-5184-b8a3-b42476109664" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "0.55" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-d10653a4-2ac5-5be4-9b7e-7dbc6ddafa84" :question/id #uuid "d10653a4-2ac5-5be4-9b7e-7dbc6ddafa84" :question/math-academy-id "q-146849" :question/problem "Suppose $X$ and $Y$ are discrete random variables. $$

Find $P(-1.5\le X\le 1.5,-1.5\le Y\le 1.5).$" :question/worked-solution "Note the following:

- For a given joint PMF $f(x,y),$ we can think of each point where $f(x,y)\ne 0$ as a point mass in the plane, where the "probability mass" at each point equals the probability associated with that point.

- The joint CDF $F(x,y)=P(X\le x,Y\le y)$ is the total "probability mass" that lies in the infinite rectangular region that has its top-right corner at $(x,y)$ and whose sides are parallel to the coordinate axis.

Given the supports of $X$ and $Y,$ the joint support $S$ is a subset of

$$
{S}_{X}\times {S}_{Y}=\{-2,-1,0,1,2\}\times \{-2,-1,0,1,2\}.
$$

Let's plot the points in ${S}_{X}\times {S}_{Y},$ which contains the joint support, and sketch the region corresponding to the probability we wish to find.

![](images/ae/ae7d480e52257825e679349ce185b4aa08ed3b096fd7a780ece56c90439798fe.png)

Notice that this region encompasses the same possible support points as the rectangular region with its top-right corner at $(1,1)$ and bottom-left corner at $(-2,-2)$ below, where the top and right boundaries are inclusive and the bottom and left boundaries are exclusive.

![](images/5b/5bcb1b0b518485dfcd4066a0259fea4a2dc050be47e95b4de0b925d8f1c997aa.png)

Geometrically, this region can be obtained as follows:

1\. Take the infinite rectangle that has its top-right corner at $(1,1).$

2\. Subtract the infinite rectangles that have their top-right corners at $(1,-2)$ and $(-2,1).$

3\. Finally, we need to add back the infinite rectangle that has its top-right corner at $(-2,-2).$ This is because we subtracted this region twice in step 2.

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}P(-1.5\le X\le 1.5,-1.5\le Y\le 1.5) & =\overset{\text{top-right corner at }(1,1)}{\overset{⏞}{P(X\le 1,Y\le 1)}} \\  & \,-\overset{\text{top-right corner at }(1,-2)}{\overset{⏞}{P(X\le 1,Y\le -2)}}-\overset{\text{top-right corner at }(-2,1)}{\overset{⏞}{P(X\le -2,Y\le 1)}} \\  & \,+\overset{\text{top-right corner at }(-2,-2)}{\overset{⏞}{P(X\le -2,Y\le -2)}} \\  & =F(1,1)-F(1,-2)-F(-2,1)+F(-2,-2) \\  & =0.7-0.3-0.4+0.1 \\  & =0.1.\end{aligned}

$$

Find $P(2<X\le 5,2\le Y<4).$" :question/worked-solution "Note the following:

- For a given joint PMF $f(x,y),$ we can think of each point where $f(x,y)\ne 0$ as a point mass in the plane, where the "probability mass" at each point equals the probability associated with that point.

- The joint CDF $F(x,y)=P(X\le x,Y\le y)$ is the total "probability mass" that lies in the infinite rectangular region that has its top-right corner at $(x,y)$ and whose sides are parallel to the coordinate axis.

Given the supports of $X$ and $Y,$ the joint support $S$ is a subset of

$$
{S}_{X}\times {S}_{Y}=\{1,2,3,4,5,6\}\times \{1,2,3,4\}.
$$

Let's plot the points in ${S}_{X}\times {S}_{Y},$ which contains the joint support, and sketch the region corresponding to the probability we wish to find.

![](images/2d/2dd2929b39c9d0357516ebea9f1f31ed2b5f64c6154184ec904996c51162c144.png)

Notice that this region encompasses the same possible support points as the rectangular region with its top-right corner at $(5,3)$ and bottom-left corner at $(2,1)$ below, where the top and right boundaries are inclusive and the bottom and left boundaries are exclusive.

![](images/db/db601c0b0d2931a61d2218e196ea7485fc8d258cb77c604dc44661687de43beb.png)

Geometrically, this region can be obtained as follows:

1\. Take the infinite rectangle that has its top-right corner at $(5,3).$

2\. Subtract the infinite rectangles that have their top-right corners at $(5,1)$ and $(2,3).$

$$
\begin{aligned}P(2<X\le 5,2\le Y<4) & =\overset{\text{top-right corner at }(5,3)}{\overset{⏞}{P(X\le 5,Y\le 3)}} \\  & \,-\overset{\text{top-right corner at }(5,1)}{\overset{⏞}{P(X\le 5,Y\le 1)}}-\overset{\text{top-right corner at }(2,3)}{\overset{⏞}{P(X\le 2,Y\le 3)}} \\  & \,+\overset{\text{top-right corner at }(2,1)}{\overset{⏞}{P(X\le 2,Y\le 1)}} \\  & =F(5,3)-F(5,1)-F(2,3)+F(2,1) \\  & =0.6-0.23-0.32+0.05 \\  & =0.1.\end{aligned}
