where $D=\{(x,y)\,:\,1\le {e}^{x}\le 2,\,1\le {e}^{y}\le 4\}.$" :question/worked-solution "Let's define a transformation $T$ as follows:

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{aligned}]
$$

This transformation maps some region $Δ$ in the $uv$-plane to our region $D$ in the $xy$-plane.

To compute the required integral, we can use the change of variables formula

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,dx\,dy={∬}_{Δ}f(x(u,v),y(u,v))|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|du\,dv
$$

where $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}$ is the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T.$

Note that the change of variables

$$
u={e}^{x},\,v={e}^{y}
$$

 

gives us the *inverse* function ${T}^{-1},$ that is

$$
{T}^{-1}:[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}u(x,y) \\ v(x,y)\end{aligned}].
$$

To compute the required integral, we proceed as follows:

**Step 1**: Find $Δ,$ which is the image of $D$ under the action of ${T}^{-1}.$ 

Our domain in the $uv$-plane is

$$
\begin{aligned}Δ & =\{(u,v)\,:\,1\le u\le 2,\,1\le v\le 4\}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}{e}^{x} & 0 \\ 0 & \text{ }\text{ }{e}^{y}\end{aligned}| \\  & ={e}^{x+y}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T$ is

$$
\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}={(\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)})}^{-1}=\frac{1}{{e}^{x+y}}=\frac{1}{uv}.
$$

Note that $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}\ne 0$ everywhere inside $Δ.$ In other words, $T$ has no critical points inside $Δ.$

**Step 4**: Perform the change of variables:

Performing the change of variables, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}y\,dx\,dy & ={∬}_{Δ}\operatorname{ln}⁡v\,|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\text{d}u\,\text{d}v \\  & ={∬}_{Δ}\operatorname{ln}⁡v\cdot |\frac{1}{uv}|\,\text{d}u\,\text{d}v \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}\frac{1}{u}[{\int }_{1}^{4}\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡v}{v}\,dv]du \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}\frac{1}{u}{[\frac{{ln}^{2}⁡v}{2}]}_{1}^{4}du \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{1}^{2}\frac{1}{u}[{ln}^{2}⁡4-{ln}^{2}⁡1]\,du \\  & =\frac{{ln}^{2}⁡4}{2}{\int }_{1}^{2}\frac{1}{u}\,du \\  & =2{ln}^{2}⁡2[\operatorname{ln}⁡u]_{1}^{2} \\  & =2{ln}^{2}⁡2(\operatorname{ln}⁡2-\operatorname{ln}⁡1) \\  & =2{ln}^{3}⁡2.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-f081c215-96de-53ac-b301-926b90ac00ff"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-f081c215-96de-53ac-b301-926b90ac00ff" :answer-field/id #uuid "f081c215-96de-53ac-b301-926b90ac00ff" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-68632396-ccfe-581e-8589-6ce419497b94" :answer-field/choices ["answer-0f4c86f2-5cfb-5693-a142-edc6be59008a" "answer-95eca681-53e5-51f4-8569-95f9733c2dbe" "answer-68632396-ccfe-581e-8589-6ce419497b94" "answer-79ad7697-010f-568d-851d-4911a16f499a" "answer-344eed9f-15e2-5d9d-a328-322b0adeb917"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-0f4c86f2-5cfb-5693-a142-edc6be59008a" :answer/id #uuid "0f4c86f2-5cfb-5693-a142-edc6be59008a" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "2\operatorname{ln}⁡2" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-95eca681-53e5-51f4-8569-95f9733c2dbe" :answer/id #uuid "95eca681-53e5-51f4-8569-95f9733c2dbe" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "2{ln}^{2}⁡2" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-68632396-ccfe-581e-8589-6ce419497b94" :answer/id #uuid "68632396-ccfe-581e-8589-6ce419497b94" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "2{ln}^{3}⁡2" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-79ad7697-010f-568d-851d-4911a16f499a" :answer/id #uuid "79ad7697-010f-568d-851d-4911a16f499a" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "{ln}^{2}⁡2" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-344eed9f-15e2-5d9d-a328-322b0adeb917" :answer/id #uuid "344eed9f-15e2-5d9d-a328-322b0adeb917" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "{ln}^{3}⁡2" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-ea750ce2-b7b3-5ba2-80fa-7d5a87470671" :question/id #uuid "ea750ce2-b7b3-5ba2-80fa-7d5a87470671" :question/math-academy-id "q-160850" :question/problem "Using the change of variables $u=x+y$ and $v=x-y,$ evaluate the double integral

$$
{∬}_{D}(x+y)(x-y)^{3/2}\,dx\,dy,
$$

where $D=\{(x,y)\,:\,1\le x+y\le 3,\,0\le x-y\le 1\}.$" :question/worked-solution "Let's define a transformation $T$ as follows:

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{aligned}]
$$

This transformation maps some region $Δ$ in the $uv$-plane to our region $D$ in the $xy$-plane.

To compute the required integral, we can use the change of variables formula

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,dx\,dy={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(x(u,v),y(u,v))|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|du\,dv
$$

where $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}$ is the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T.$

Note that the change of variables

$$
u=x+y,\,v=x-y
$$

 

gives us the *inverse* function ${T}^{-1},$ that is

$$
{T}^{-1}:[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}u(x,y) \\ v(x,y)\end{aligned}].
$$

To compute the required integral, we proceed as follows:

**Step 1**: Find $Δ,$ which is the image of $D$ under the action of ${T}^{-1}.$ 

Our domain in the $uv$-plane is

$$
\begin{aligned}Δ & =\{(u,v)\,:\,1\le u\le 3,\,0\le v\le 1\}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 1 & \text{ }\text{ }-1\end{aligned}| \\  & =-2.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T$ is

$$
\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}={(\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)})}^{-1}=-\frac{1}{2}.
$$

Note that $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}\ne 0$ everywhere inside $Δ.$ In other words, $T$ has no critical points inside $Δ.$

**Step 4**: Perform the change of variables:

Performing the change of variables, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}(x+y)(x-y)^{3/2}\,dx\,dy & ={∬}_{Δ}u{v}^{3/2}|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\text{d}u\,\text{d}v \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{1}^{3}u{v}^{3/2}|-\frac{1}{2}|du\,dv \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}{v}^{3/2}[{\int }_{1}^{3}u\,du]dv \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}{v}^{3/2}{[\frac{{u}^{2}}{2}]}_{1}^{3}\,dv \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}{v}^{3/2}[\frac{9}{2}-\frac{1}{2}]dv \\  & =2{\int }_{0}^{1}{v}^{3/2}\,dv \\  & =2{[\frac{2}{5}\,{v}^{5/2}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{4}{5}[1-0] \\  & =\frac{4}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-6b345d81-65d6-5a3f-9150-c97ad1b7b016"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-6b345d81-65d6-5a3f-9150-c97ad1b7b016" :answer-field/id #uuid "6b345d81-65d6-5a3f-9150-c97ad1b7b016" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-fc8d0347-5303-50ad-8ea6-72f1ba59d8dd" :answer-field/choices ["answer-8236c364-9a58-5bd5-bca8-e007796586fd" "answer-91e046c8-5b65-5972-9eef-cd8f897a8cd2" "answer-dbc70cb2-b436-5aca-b9d7-fabe9b0e5de6" "answer-6364af2a-3d6b-5851-9049-3595e8cfce71" "answer-fc8d0347-5303-50ad-8ea6-72f1ba59d8dd"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-8236c364-9a58-5bd5-bca8-e007796586fd" :answer/id #uuid "8236c364-9a58-5bd5-bca8-e007796586fd" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "2" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-91e046c8-5b65-5972-9eef-cd8f897a8cd2" :answer/id #uuid "91e046c8-5b65-5972-9eef-cd8f897a8cd2" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "3" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-dbc70cb2-b436-5aca-b9d7-fabe9b0e5de6" :answer/id #uuid "dbc70cb2-b436-5aca-b9d7-fabe9b0e5de6" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{1}{2}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-6364af2a-3d6b-5851-9049-3595e8cfce71" :answer/id #uuid "6364af2a-3d6b-5851-9049-3595e8cfce71" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{2}{3}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-fc8d0347-5303-50ad-8ea6-72f1ba59d8dd" :answer/id #uuid "fc8d0347-5303-50ad-8ea6-72f1ba59d8dd" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{4}{5}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-fee52d9d-67c4-5104-9f57-4122f892110d" :question/id #uuid "fee52d9d-67c4-5104-9f57-4122f892110d" :question/math-academy-id "q-82911" :question/problem "Using the change of variables $u=x+y$ and $v=x-y,$ evaluate the double integral

$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-7505a4fd-3c5e-5a38-a1f7-3891a3c2965c"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-7505a4fd-3c5e-5a38-a1f7-3891a3c2965c" :answer-field/id #uuid "7505a4fd-3c5e-5a38-a1f7-3891a3c2965c" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-bcd0ae49-abbe-5447-a383-493cedc60a77" :answer-field/choices ["answer-8273dafa-bda1-5a66-9cff-9b7575876a40" "answer-ec2a5b9c-1081-52b7-b89e-e7f3524f0dee" "answer-bcd0ae49-abbe-5447-a383-493cedc60a77" "answer-e59d2e21-5875-56c6-8566-91c968ba9e4a" "answer-0e55ce08-51f3-5f7d-9882-1ad73c59bda5"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-8273dafa-bda1-5a66-9cff-9b7575876a40" :answer/id #uuid "8273dafa-bda1-5a66-9cff-9b7575876a40" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "2" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-ec2a5b9c-1081-52b7-b89e-e7f3524f0dee" :answer/id #uuid "ec2a5b9c-1081-52b7-b89e-e7f3524f0dee" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "4" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-bcd0ae49-abbe-5447-a383-493cedc60a77" :answer/id #uuid "bcd0ae49-abbe-5447-a383-493cedc60a77" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "6" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-e59d2e21-5875-56c6-8566-91c968ba9e4a" :answer/id #uuid "e59d2e21-5875-56c6-8566-91c968ba9e4a" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "8" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-0e55ce08-51f3-5f7d-9882-1ad73c59bda5" :answer/id #uuid "0e55ce08-51f3-5f7d-9882-1ad73c59bda5" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{1}{2}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-f47eca8f-5f35-574c-b95e-5dc9a27cb04d" :question/id #uuid "f47eca8f-5f35-574c-b95e-5dc9a27cb04d" :question/math-academy-id "q-160916" :question/problem "Use a change of variables to evaluate the double integral

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡(y-2x)}{y-2x}\,\text{d}x\text{d}y & ={∬}_{Δ}\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡u}{u}\,|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & ={∬}_{Δ}\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡u}{u}\,|-\frac{1}{2}|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{2}[{\int }_{1}^{4}\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡u}{u}\,du]dv \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{2}{[\frac{{ln}^{2}⁡u}{2}]}_{1}^{4}dv \\  & =\frac{1}{4}{\int }_{0}^{2}({ln}^{2}⁡4-{ln}^{2}⁡1)\,dv \\  & =\frac{1}{4}{ln}^{2}⁡4{\int }_{0}^{2}dv \\  & =\frac{1}{4}(2\operatorname{ln}⁡2)^{2}\cdot [v]_{0}^{2} \\  & ={ln}^{2}⁡2\cdot (2-0) \\  & =2{ln}^{2}⁡2.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-a913f95c-4f3f-51d9-a609-d167776b85b5"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-a913f95c-4f3f-51d9-a609-d167776b85b5" :answer-field/id #uuid "a913f95c-4f3f-51d9-a609-d167776b85b5" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-f0d1564e-78dd-55a4-b512-a4adf4fcad56" :answer-field/choices ["answer-2ac193e9-56da-5e90-afd1-e67c5f8d1870" "answer-f0d1564e-78dd-55a4-b512-a4adf4fcad56" "answer-8be6f850-b0e1-5bd0-adfc-a35ba9264b99" "answer-b6110701-1956-577b-a189-4d9681a4e3ce" "answer-602828b8-7fa4-51b0-ae3e-ca2c02d7c8af"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-2ac193e9-56da-5e90-afd1-e67c5f8d1870" :answer/id #uuid "2ac193e9-56da-5e90-afd1-e67c5f8d1870" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "2\operatorname{ln}⁡2" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-f0d1564e-78dd-55a4-b512-a4adf4fcad56" :answer/id #uuid "f0d1564e-78dd-55a4-b512-a4adf4fcad56" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "2{ln}^{2}⁡2" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-8be6f850-b0e1-5bd0-adfc-a35ba9264b99" :answer/id #uuid "8be6f850-b0e1-5bd0-adfc-a35ba9264b99" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "3\operatorname{ln}⁡2" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-b6110701-1956-577b-a189-4d9681a4e3ce" :answer/id #uuid "b6110701-1956-577b-a189-4d9681a4e3ce" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "4{ln}^{2}⁡2" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-602828b8-7fa4-51b0-ae3e-ca2c02d7c8af" :answer/id #uuid "602828b8-7fa4-51b0-ae3e-ca2c02d7c8af" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "{ln}^{2}⁡2" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-ebe24ae4-1aba-5953-99d8-8533d35f69cf" :question/id #uuid "ebe24ae4-1aba-5953-99d8-8533d35f69cf" :question/math-academy-id "q-160918" :question/problem "Use a change of variables to evaluate the double integral 

$$
{∬}_{D}({x}^{2}+2xy+{y}^{2}){e}^{x-y}\,dxdy,
$$

where $D=\{(x,y)\,:\,1\le x+y\le 3,\,0\le x-y\le 2\}.$" :question/worked-solution "Let's define a transformation $T$ as follows:

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{aligned}]
$$

This transformation maps some region $Δ$ in the $uv$-plane to our region $D$ in the $xy$-plane.

To compute the required integral, we can use the change of variables formula

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dxdy={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(x(u,v),y(u,v))\,|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\text{ }dudv
$$

where $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}$ is the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T.$

To compute the required integral, we proceed as follows:

**Step 1**: Find a suitable change of variables.

The inequalities that define the region $D,$

$$
1\le x+y\le 3,\,0\le x-y\le 2,
$$

suggest that we use the change of variables 

$$
u=x+y\,\text{and}\,v=x-y.
$$

This change of variables gives us the *inverse* function ${T}^{-1},$ that is

$$
{T}^{-1}:[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}u(x,y) \\ v(x,y)\end{aligned}].
$$

**Step 2**: Find $Δ,$ which is the image of $D$ under the action of ${T}^{-1}.$ 

Our domain in the $uv$-plane is

$$
\begin{aligned}Δ & =\{(u,v)\,:\,1\le u\le 3,\,0\le v\le 2\}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}1 & \text{ }\text{ }\text{ }1 \\ 1 & -1\end{aligned}| \\  & =-2.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 4**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T:$

$$
\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}={(\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)})}^{-1}=-\frac{1}{2}
$$

Note that $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}\ne 0$ everywhere inside $Δ.$ In other words, $T$ has no critical points inside $Δ.$

**Step 5**: Perform the change of variables, and evaluate the integral:

Performing the change of variables, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}({x}^{2}+2xy+{y}^{2}){e}^{x-y}\,\text{d}x\text{d}y & ={∬}_{D}(x+y)^{2}{e}^{x-y}\,\text{d}x\text{d}y \\  & ={∬}_{Δ}{u}^{2}{e}^{v}|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & ={∬}_{Δ}{u}^{2}{e}^{v}|-\frac{1}{2}|\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{1}^{3}{u}^{2}[{\int }_{0}^{2}{e}^{v}\,dv]du \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{1}^{3}{u}^{2}[{e}^{v}]_{0}^{2}\,du \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{1}^{3}{u}^{2}\cdot ({e}^{2}-1)\,du \\  & =\frac{{e}^{2}-1}{2}{[\frac{1}{3}{u}^{3}]}_{1}^{3} \\  & =\frac{{e}^{2}-1}{2}\cdot \frac{26}{3} \\  & =\frac{13({e}^{2}-1)}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-5e6427b8-37d4-5988-9502-b3fd4454d9b3"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-5e6427b8-37d4-5988-9502-b3fd4454d9b3" :answer-field/id #uuid "5e6427b8-37d4-5988-9502-b3fd4454d9b3" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-71a05bae-9b38-579f-bf4d-77a5a3ed21ce" :answer-field/choices ["answer-ff742366-fc6b-51c9-9bb1-c3bf559e492f" "answer-c8d2beaf-f051-5e9a-a9bb-d9e392012d19" "answer-78a5344d-2607-521a-bc5c-b422c76ae208" "answer-71a05bae-9b38-579f-bf4d-77a5a3ed21ce" "answer-e262d3c6-319b-5ade-8d21-fe6baf79d69d"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-ff742366-fc6b-51c9-9bb1-c3bf559e492f" :answer/id #uuid "ff742366-fc6b-51c9-9bb1-c3bf559e492f" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "3{e}^{2}-2" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-c8d2beaf-f051-5e9a-a9bb-d9e392012d19" :answer/id #uuid "c8d2beaf-f051-5e9a-a9bb-d9e392012d19" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "4e-3" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-78a5344d-2607-521a-bc5c-b422c76ae208" :answer/id #uuid "78a5344d-2607-521a-bc5c-b422c76ae208" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "4{e}^{2}-1" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-71a05bae-9b38-579f-bf4d-77a5a3ed21ce" :answer/id #uuid "71a05bae-9b38-579f-bf4d-77a5a3ed21ce" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{13({e}^{2}-1)}{3}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-e262d3c6-319b-5ade-8d21-fe6baf79d69d" :answer/id #uuid "e262d3c6-319b-5ade-8d21-fe6baf79d69d" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{4(e-1)}{3}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-c8466ab0-fd66-5adb-8220-fa89c46bae69" :question/id #uuid "c8466ab0-fd66-5adb-8220-fa89c46bae69" :question/math-academy-id "q-38309" :question/problem "Use a change of variables to evaluate the double integral

where $D=\{(x,y)\,:\,|y-x|\le \frac{\pi }{2},\,0\le y\le \frac{\pi }{2}\}.$" :question/worked-solution "Let's define a transformation $T$ as follows:

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{aligned}]
$$

This transformation maps some region $Δ$ in the $uv$-plane to our region $D$ in the $xy$-plane.

To compute the required integral, we can use the change of variables formula

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dxdy={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(x(u,v),y(u,v))\,|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\text{ }dudv
$$

where $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}$ is the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T.$

To compute the required integral, we proceed as follows:

**Step 1**: Find a suitable change of variables.

The inequalities that define the region $D,$

$$
\frac{\pi }{2}\le y-x\le \frac{\pi }{2},\,0\le y\le \frac{\pi }{2},
$$

suggest that we use the change of variables 

$$
u=y-x\,\text{and}\,v=y.
$$

This change of variables gives us the *inverse* function ${T}^{-1},$ that is

$$
{T}^{-1}:[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}u(x,y) \\ v(x,y)\end{aligned}].
$$

**Step 2**: Find $Δ,$ which is the image of $D$ under the action of ${T}^{-1}.$ 

Our domain in the $uv$-plane is

$$
\begin{aligned}Δ & =\{(u,v)\,:\,-\frac{\pi }{2}\le u\le \frac{\pi }{2},\,0\le v\le \frac{\pi }{2}\}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}-1 & \text{ }\text{ }1 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}| \\  & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 4**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T:$

$$
\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}={(\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)})}^{-1}=-1.
$$

Note that $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}\ne 0$ everywhere inside $Δ.$ In other words, $T$ has no critical points inside $Δ.$

**Step 5**: Perform the change of variables, and evaluate the integral:

Performing the change of variables, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}y{cos}^{2}⁡(y-x)\,\text{d}x\text{d}y & ={∬}_{Δ}v{cos}^{2}⁡u\,|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & ={∬}_{Δ}v{cos}^{2}⁡u\cdot |-1|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}v[{\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}{cos}^{2}⁡u\,du]dv \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}v[{\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡2u+1)du]dv \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}v[\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡2u}{2}+u]_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}\,dv \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\pi v\,dv \\  & =\frac{\pi }{2}[\frac{{v}^{2}}{2}]_{0}^{\pi /2} \\  & =\frac{\pi }{2}\cdot \frac{{\pi }^{2}}{8} \\  & =\frac{{\pi }^{3}}{16}.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-be68da14-ad39-5dd8-8b81-96f9bc5c3b1f"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-be68da14-ad39-5dd8-8b81-96f9bc5c3b1f" :answer-field/id #uuid "be68da14-ad39-5dd8-8b81-96f9bc5c3b1f" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-f17962e7-50b9-5445-bd8a-61e21702bfc0" :answer-field/choices ["answer-062b1938-49ed-576d-84ed-09a8fb852cc9" "answer-9d25158d-398d-5c30-8fda-c6ddce1b0d76" "answer-34aac4ef-6b3d-5a11-9211-3216b95b6351" "answer-f17962e7-50b9-5445-bd8a-61e21702bfc0" "answer-365aa022-a66e-5c42-b417-e96430223091"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-062b1938-49ed-576d-84ed-09a8fb852cc9" :answer/id #uuid "062b1938-49ed-576d-84ed-09a8fb852cc9" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "1-\frac{{\pi }^{3}}{8}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-9d25158d-398d-5c30-8fda-c6ddce1b0d76" :answer/id #uuid "9d25158d-398d-5c30-8fda-c6ddce1b0d76" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{16}-1" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-34aac4ef-6b3d-5a11-9211-3216b95b6351" :answer/id #uuid "34aac4ef-6b3d-5a11-9211-3216b95b6351" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{4}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-f17962e7-50b9-5445-bd8a-61e21702bfc0" :answer/id #uuid "f17962e7-50b9-5445-bd8a-61e21702bfc0" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{{\pi }^{3}}{16}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-365aa022-a66e-5c42-b417-e96430223091" :answer/id #uuid "365aa022-a66e-5c42-b417-e96430223091" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{{\pi }^{3}}{8}-1" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186199007 :question/problem "Use a change of variables to evaluate the double integral 

$$
{∬}_{D}(x+2y){e}^{(x+2y)^{2}}\,dxdy,
$$

where $D=\{(x,y)\,:\,1\le x\le 5,\,0\le x+2y\le 1\}.$" :question/worked-solution "Let's define a transformation $T$ as follows:

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{aligned}]
$$

This transformation maps some region $Δ$ in the $uv$-plane to our region $D$ in the $xy$-plane.

To compute the required integral, we can use the change of variables formula

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dxdy={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(x(u,v),y(u,v))\,|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\text{ }dudv
$$

where $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}$ is the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T.$

To compute the required integral, we proceed as follows:

**Step 1**: Find a suitable change of variables.

The inequalities that define the region $D,$

$$
1\le x\le 5,\,0\le x+2y\le 1,
$$

suggest that we use the change of variables 

$$
u=x\,\text{and}\,v=x+2y.
$$

This change of variables gives us the *inverse* function ${T}^{-1},$ that is

$$
{T}^{-1}:[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}u(x,y) \\ v(x,y)\end{aligned}].
$$

**Step 2**: Find $Δ,$ which is the image of $D$ under the action of ${T}^{-1}.$ 

Our domain in the $uv$-plane is

$$
\begin{aligned}Δ & =\{(u,v)\,:\,1\le u\le 5,\,0\le v\le 1\}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}1 & \text{ }\text{ }0 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}| \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 4**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T:$

$$
\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}={(\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)})}^{-1}=\frac{1}{2}.
$$

Note that $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}\ne 0$ everywhere inside $Δ.$ In other words, $T$ has no critical points inside $Δ.$

**Step 5**: Perform the change of variables, and evaluate the integral:

Performing the change of variables, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}(x+2y){e}^{(x+2y)^{2}}\,\text{d}x\text{d}y & ={∬}_{Δ}v{e}^{{v}^{2}}\,|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & ={∬}_{Δ}v{e}^{{v}^{2}}\,|\frac{1}{2}|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{1}^{5}[{\int }_{0}^{1}v{e}^{{v}^{2}}\,dv]du \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{1}^{5}{[\frac{{e}^{{v}^{2}}}{2}]}_{0}^{1}du \\  & =\frac{1}{4}{\int }_{1}^{5}(e-1)\,du \\  & =\frac{1}{4}(e-1)[u]_{1}^{5} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}(e-1)(5-1) \\  & =e-1.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186197912 :answer-field/correct "answer-4cfe915e-292f-5afc-a987-feaf8645491b" :answer-field/choices ["answer-a5e7b49a-7376-5f77-b4cd-07e49c94ad93" "answer-69ed5ffb-e837-50a7-83fa-9b0d9378cfad" "answer-4cfe915e-292f-5afc-a987-feaf8645491b" "answer-50bbbf00-20cb-560c-a0ab-ee8b2c1c6005"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-a5e7b49a-7376-5f77-b4cd-07e49c94ad93" :answer/id #uuid "a5e7b49a-7376-5f77-b4cd-07e49c94ad93" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{e-2}{2}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-69ed5ffb-e837-50a7-83fa-9b0d9378cfad" :answer/id #uuid "69ed5ffb-e837-50a7-83fa-9b0d9378cfad" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{{e}^{2}-e}{4}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-4cfe915e-292f-5afc-a987-feaf8645491b" :answer/id #uuid "4cfe915e-292f-5afc-a987-feaf8645491b" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "e-1" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-50bbbf00-20cb-560c-a0ab-ee8b2c1c6005" :answer/id #uuid "50bbbf00-20cb-560c-a0ab-ee8b2c1c6005" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "{e}^{2}-1" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-d3e35845-58c1-5603-a038-b92edbbc2e02" :question/id #uuid "d3e35845-58c1-5603-a038-b92edbbc2e02" :question/math-academy-id "q-160906" :question/problem "Use a change of variables to evaluate the double integral 

$$

where $D$ is the quadrilateral region with vertices $(1,-\frac{1}{2}),$ $(\frac{3}{2},-\frac{3}{4}),$ $(\frac{3}{2},\frac{\pi -3}{4}),$ and $(1,\frac{\pi -2}{4}).$" :question/worked-solution "Let's define a transformation $T$ as follows:

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{aligned}]
$$

This transformation maps some region $Δ$ in the $uv$-plane to our region $D$ in the $xy$-plane.

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dxdy={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(x(u,v),y(u,v))\,|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\text{ }dudv
$$

where $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}$ is the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T.$

To compute the required integral, we proceed as follows:

**Step 1**: Find a suitable change of variables.

The integrand

$$
f(x,y)=2x\operatorname{cos}⁡(x+2y)
$$

suggests that we use the change of variables 

$$
u=2x,\,v=x+2y.
$$

This change of variables gives us the *inverse* function ${T}^{-1},$ that is

$$
{T}^{-1}:[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}u(x,y) \\ v(x,y)\end{aligned}].
$$

**Step 2**: Find $Δ,$ which is the image of $D$ under the action of ${T}^{-1}.$ 

The vertices of our domain $Δ$ in the $uv$-plane are as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{T}^{-1}(1,-\frac{1}{2}) & =(2\cdot 1,1+2(-\frac{1}{2})) \\  & =(2,0) \\ {T}^{-1}(\frac{3}{2},-\frac{3}{4}) & =(2\cdot \frac{3}{2},\frac{3}{2}+2(-\frac{3}{4})) \\  & =(3,0) \\ {T}^{-1}(\frac{3}{2},\frac{\pi -3}{4}) & =(2\cdot \frac{3}{2},\frac{3}{2}+2(\frac{\pi -3}{4})) \\  & =(3,\frac{\pi }{2}) \\ {T}^{-1}(1,\frac{\pi -2}{4}) & =(2\cdot 1,1+2(\frac{\pi -2}{4})) \\  & =(2,\frac{\pi }{2})\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our domain in the $uv$-plane is the following rectangle:

$$
Δ=\{(u,v)\,:\,2\le u\le 3,\,0\le v\le \frac{\pi }{2}\}
$$

![](images/dd/dd628fd99b4684d79e8c3b0f4e6696f72582abaef18eef729f5611711a2e42ec.png)

**Step 3**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}| \\  & =4.\end{aligned}

**Step 4**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T:$

$$

$$

**Step 5**: Perform the change of variables, and evaluate the integral:

$$

$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-848b178b-00cd-5964-8724-b50b402d0b68"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-848b178b-00cd-5964-8724-b50b402d0b68" :answer-field/id #uuid "848b178b-00cd-5964-8724-b50b402d0b68" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-47c7196f-be5c-55f4-aa25-27610bf7736c" :answer-field/choices ["answer-1761c3e4-c91a-57a8-9013-9b3654a234fa" "answer-ae180a90-3ca2-5c61-ac30-22916f24dea1" "answer-47c7196f-be5c-55f4-aa25-27610bf7736c" "answer-e5aa3207-9a4b-5442-a65a-773ebcb88f61" "answer-f081f9d6-ce8e-5bb4-8583-a147cbb0c2be"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-1761c3e4-c91a-57a8-9013-9b3654a234fa" :answer/id #uuid "1761c3e4-c91a-57a8-9013-9b3654a234fa" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "10" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-ae180a90-3ca2-5c61-ac30-22916f24dea1" :answer/id #uuid "ae180a90-3ca2-5c61-ac30-22916f24dea1" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{5}{2}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-47c7196f-be5c-55f4-aa25-27610bf7736c" :answer/id #uuid "47c7196f-be5c-55f4-aa25-27610bf7736c" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{5}{8}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-e5aa3207-9a4b-5442-a65a-773ebcb88f61" :answer/id #uuid "e5aa3207-9a4b-5442-a65a-773ebcb88f61" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{\pi }{2}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-f081f9d6-ce8e-5bb4-8583-a147cbb0c2be" :answer/id #uuid "f081f9d6-ce8e-5bb4-8583-a147cbb0c2be" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\pi " :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-b878a44e-123c-5f2f-a474-6dc1888b9c72" :question/id #uuid "b878a44e-123c-5f2f-a474-6dc1888b9c72" :question/math-academy-id "q-160938" :question/problem "Use a change of variables to evaluate the double integral

where $D$ is the quadrilateral region with vertices $(3,2),$ $(5,4),$ $(5,2),$ and $(3,0).$" :question/worked-solution "Let's define a transformation $T$ as follows:

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{aligned}]
$$

This transformation maps some region $Δ$ in the $uv$-plane to our region $D$ in the $xy$-plane.

To compute the required integral, we can use the change of variables formula

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dxdy={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(x(u,v),y(u,v))\,|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\text{ }dudv
$$

where $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}$ is the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T.$

To compute the required integral, we proceed as follows:

**Step 1**: Find a suitable change of variables.

The integrand

$$
f(x,y)={x}^{2}-xy=x(x-y)
$$

suggests that we use the change of variables 

$$
u=x,\,v=x-y.
$$

This change of variables gives us the *inverse* function ${T}^{-1},$ that is

$$
{T}^{-1}:[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}u(x,y) \\ v(x,y)\end{aligned}].
$$

**Step 2**: Find $Δ,$ which is the image of $D$ under the action of ${T}^{-1}.$ 

The vertices of our domain $Δ$ in the $uv$-plane are as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{T}^{-1}(3,2) & =(3,3-2) \\  & =(3,1) \\ {T}^{-1}(5,4) & =(5,5-4) \\  & =(5,1) \\ {T}^{-1}(5,2) & =(5,5-2) \\  & =(5,3) \\ {T}^{-1}(3,0) & =(3,3-0) \\  & =(3,3)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our domain in the $uv$-plane is the following rectangle:

$$
Δ=\{(u,v)\,:\,3\le u\le 5,\,1\le v\le 3\}
$$

![](images/e0/e0b810c03e7e3210fcff3a739e3781ad5ff694bfe44d5f73d7782c3b4108a286.png)

**Step 3**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 1 & -1\end{aligned}| \\  & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 4**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T:$

$$
\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}={(\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)})}^{-1}=-1
$$

Note that $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}\ne 0$ everywhere inside $Δ.$ In other words, $T$ has no critical points inside $Δ.$

**Step 5**: Perform the change of variables, and evaluate the integral:

Performing the change of variables, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}({x}^{2}-xy)\,\text{d}x\text{d}y & ={∬}_{D}x(x-y)\,\text{d}x\text{d}y \\  & ={∬}_{Δ}uv\,|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & ={∬}_{Δ}uv\,|-1|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{3}{\int }_{3}^{5}uv\,\text{d}u\,\text{d}v \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{3}v\,\text{d}v{\int }_{3}^{5}u\,\text{d}u \\  & ={[\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}]}_{1}^{3}\cdot {[\frac{1}{2}{u}^{2}]}_{3}^{5} \\  & =4\cdot 8 \\  & =32.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-e051d3d7-1ee2-505b-957c-b010b42121b8"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-e051d3d7-1ee2-505b-957c-b010b42121b8" :answer-field/id #uuid "e051d3d7-1ee2-505b-957c-b010b42121b8" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-31768ff6-9f0c-50bd-9796-46c6ac637b1f" :answer-field/choices ["answer-14aeda53-bc0f-5285-a152-aac2c1de7b55" "answer-31768ff6-9f0c-50bd-9796-46c6ac637b1f" "answer-11e03497-2478-5699-b8c8-60dc8393efd3" "answer-328e9ba1-7166-5fcf-9c18-bf5334f7dc30" "answer-c05027eb-9d67-552f-950c-d7aa5524cbba"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-14aeda53-bc0f-5285-a152-aac2c1de7b55" :answer/id #uuid "14aeda53-bc0f-5285-a152-aac2c1de7b55" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "24" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-31768ff6-9f0c-50bd-9796-46c6ac637b1f" :answer/id #uuid "31768ff6-9f0c-50bd-9796-46c6ac637b1f" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "32" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-11e03497-2478-5699-b8c8-60dc8393efd3" :answer/id #uuid "11e03497-2478-5699-b8c8-60dc8393efd3" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "4" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-328e9ba1-7166-5fcf-9c18-bf5334f7dc30" :answer/id #uuid "328e9ba1-7166-5fcf-9c18-bf5334f7dc30" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "8" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-c05027eb-9d67-552f-950c-d7aa5524cbba" :answer/id #uuid "c05027eb-9d67-552f-950c-d7aa5524cbba" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{1}{2}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-e4b188aa-dc23-5bc9-90f6-b5a36b6d8b4b" :question/id #uuid "e4b188aa-dc23-5bc9-90f6-b5a36b6d8b4b" :question/math-academy-id "q-160902" :question/problem "Use a change of variables to evaluate the double integral

where $D$ is the quadrilateral region with vertices $(1,-1),$ $(2,0),$ $(3,-2),$ and $(2,-3).$" :question/worked-solution "Let's define a transformation $T$ as follows:

$$

where $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}$ is the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T.$

To compute the required integral, we proceed as follows:

**Step 1**: Find a suitable change of variables.

The integrand

$$
f(x,y)=2{x}^{2}-xy-{y}^{2}=(2x+y)(x-y)
$$

suggests that we use the change of variables 

$$
u=2x+y,\,v=x-y.

$$
{T}^{-1}:[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}u(x,y) \\ v(x,y)\end{aligned}].
$$

**Step 2**: Find $Δ,$ which is the image of $D$ under the action of ${T}^{-1}.$ 

The vertices of our domain $Δ$ in the $uv$-plane are as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{T}^{-1}(1,-1) & =(2(1)+(-1),1-(-1)) \\  & =(1,2) \\ {T}^{-1}(2,0) & =(2(2)+0,2-0) \\  & =(4,2) \\ {T}^{-1}(3,-2) & =(2(3)+(-2),3-(-2)) \\  & =(4,5) \\ {T}^{-1}(2,-3) & =(2(2)+(-3),2-(-3)) \\  & =(1,5)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our domain in the $uv$-plane is the following rectangle:

$$
Δ=\{(u,v)\,:\,1\le u\le 4,\,2\le v\le 5\}
$$

![](images/9f/9f5030bc3437fbc4431dd5350620bc7f9133d2bf910654607c0c5f7ef292f3a3.png)

**Step 3**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 1 & -1\end{aligned}| \\  & =-3.\end{aligned}

**Step 4**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T:$

$$

$$

**Step 5**: Perform the change of variables, and evaluate the integral:

Performing the change of variables, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}(2{x}^{2}-xy-{y}^{2})\,\text{d}x\text{d}y & ={∬}_{D}(2x+y)(x-y)\,\text{d}x\text{d}y \\  & ={∬}_{Δ}uv\,|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & ={∬}_{Δ}uv\,|-\frac{1}{3}|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & =\frac{1}{3}{\int }_{2}^{5}{\int }_{1}^{4}uv\,\text{d}u\,\text{d}v \\  & =\frac{1}{3}{\int }_{2}^{5}v\,\text{d}v{\int }_{1}^{4}u\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\cdot {[\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}]}_{2}^{5}\cdot {[\frac{1}{2}{u}^{2}]}_{1}^{4} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\cdot \frac{21}{2}\cdot \frac{15}{2} \\  & =\frac{105}{4}.\end{aligned}

$$

$$

where $D$ is the quadrilateral region with vertices $(1,0),$ $(2,1),$ $(3,0),$ and $(2,-1).$" :question/worked-solution "Let's define a transformation $T$ as follows:

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{aligned}]
$$

This transformation maps some region $Δ$ in the $uv$-plane to our region $D$ in the $xy$-plane.

To compute the required integral, we can use the change of variables formula

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dxdy={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(x(u,v),y(u,v))\,|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\text{ }dudv
$$

where $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}$ is the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T.$

To compute the required integral, we proceed as follows:

**Step 1**: Find a suitable change of variables.

The integrand

$$
f(x,y)=\frac{{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}{(x-y)^{2}}=\frac{x+y}{x-y}
$$

suggests that we use the change of variables 

$$
u=x+y,\,v=x-y.
$$

This change of variables gives us the *inverse* function ${T}^{-1},$ that is

$$
{T}^{-1}:[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}u(x,y) \\ v(x,y)\end{aligned}].
$$

**Step 2**: Find $Δ,$ which is the image of $D$ under the action of ${T}^{-1}.$ 

The vertices of our domain $Δ$ in the $uv$-plane are as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{T}^{-1}(1,0) & =(1+0,1-0) \\  & =(1,1) \\ {T}^{-1}(2,1) & =(2+1,2-1) \\  & =(3,1) \\ {T}^{-1}(3,0) & =(3+0,3-0) \\  & =(3,3) \\ {T}^{-1}(2,-1) & =(2+(-1),2-(-1)) \\  & =(1,3)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our domain in the $uv$-plane is the following rectangle:

$$
Δ=\{(u,v)\,:\,1\le u\le 3,\,1\le v\le 3\}
$$

![](images/f3/f34926c196b850fa22e0f918b27c8d25e5deb7f6aa7ec232e2eeaf4e46dd309c.png)

**Step 3**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1\end{aligned}| \\  & =-2.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 4**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T:$

$$
\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}={(\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)})}^{-1}=-\frac{1}{2}
$$

Note that $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}\ne 0$ everywhere inside $Δ.$ In other words, $T$ has no critical points inside $Δ.$

**Step 5**: Perform the change of variables, and evaluate the integral:

Performing the change of variables, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\frac{{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}{(x-y)^{2}}\,\text{d}x\text{d}y & ={∬}_{D}\frac{x+y}{x-y}\,\text{d}x\text{d}y \\  & ={∬}_{Δ}\frac{u}{v}\,|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & ={∬}_{Δ}\frac{u}{v}\,|-\frac{1}{2}|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{1}^{3}{\int }_{1}^{3}\frac{u}{v}\,\text{d}u\,\text{d}v \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{1}^{3}\frac{1}{v}\,\text{d}v{\int }_{1}^{3}u\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot {[\operatorname{ln}⁡v]}_{1}^{3}\cdot {[\frac{1}{2}{u}^{2}]}_{1}^{3} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot \operatorname{ln}⁡3\cdot 4 \\  & =2\operatorname{ln}⁡3.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-1dca1b12-338a-5c5f-badf-6213000ef5a1"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-1dca1b12-338a-5c5f-badf-6213000ef5a1" :answer-field/id #uuid "1dca1b12-338a-5c5f-badf-6213000ef5a1" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-930bb660-443d-5920-8d2a-07cfdc6d0a50" :answer-field/choices ["answer-930bb660-443d-5920-8d2a-07cfdc6d0a50" "answer-16926c3a-001d-572a-beb5-ac09cba7435e" "answer-943844b2-6990-576d-9141-b10699c96298" "answer-96c98676-4b18-52e8-baf0-b525847f1830" "answer-09a70e77-e143-5fe1-987f-6cf3d9622cb5"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-930bb660-443d-5920-8d2a-07cfdc6d0a50" :answer/id #uuid "930bb660-443d-5920-8d2a-07cfdc6d0a50" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "2\operatorname{ln}⁡3" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-16926c3a-001d-572a-beb5-ac09cba7435e" :answer/id #uuid "16926c3a-001d-572a-beb5-ac09cba7435e" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "2\operatorname{ln}⁡6" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-943844b2-6990-576d-9141-b10699c96298" :answer/id #uuid "943844b2-6990-576d-9141-b10699c96298" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "4\operatorname{ln}⁡2" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-96c98676-4b18-52e8-baf0-b525847f1830" :answer/id #uuid "96c98676-4b18-52e8-baf0-b525847f1830" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\operatorname{ln}⁡3" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-09a70e77-e143-5fe1-987f-6cf3d9622cb5" :answer/id #uuid "09a70e77-e143-5fe1-987f-6cf3d9622cb5" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\operatorname{ln}⁡6" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-03e70789-b720-5486-ac24-d7c0b4013554" :question/id #uuid "03e70789-b720-5486-ac24-d7c0b4013554" :question/math-academy-id "q-160937" :question/problem "Use a change of variables to evaluate the double integral 

$$
{∬}_{D}\frac{x+3y}{x}\,dxdy,
$$

where $D$ is the quadrilateral region with vertices $(1,-\frac{1}{3}),$  $(2,-\frac{2}{3}),$  $(2,-\frac{1}{3}),$ and $(1,0).$" :question/worked-solution "Let's define a transformation $T$ as follows:

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{aligned}]
$$

This transformation maps some region $Δ$ in the $uv$-plane to our region $D$ in the $xy$-plane.

To compute the required integral, we can use the change of variables formula

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dxdy={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(x(u,v),y(u,v))\,|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\text{ }dudv
$$

where $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}$ is the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T.$

To compute the required integral, we proceed as follows:

**Step 1**: Find a suitable change of variables.

The integrand

$$
f(x,y)=\frac{x+3y}{x}
$$

suggests that we use the change of variables 

$$
u=x,\,v=x+3y.
$$

This change of variables gives us the *inverse* function ${T}^{-1},$ that is

$$
{T}^{-1}:[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}u(x,y) \\ v(x,y)\end{aligned}].
$$

**Step 2**: Find $Δ,$ which is the image of $D$ under the action of ${T}^{-1}.$ 

The vertices of our domain $Δ$ in the $uv$-plane are as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{T}^{-1}(1,-\frac{1}{3}) & =(1,1+3(-\frac{1}{3})) \\  & =(1,0) \\ {T}^{-1}(2,-\frac{2}{3}) & =(2,2+3(-\frac{2}{3})) \\  & =(2,0) \\ {T}^{-1}(2,-\frac{1}{3}) & =(2,2+3(-\frac{1}{3})) \\  & =(2,1) \\ {T}^{-1}(1,0) & =(1,1+3(0)) \\  & =(1,1)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our domain in the $uv$-plane is the following rectangle:

$$
Δ=\{(u,v)\,:\,1\le u\le 2,\,0\le v\le 1\}
$$

![](images/33/33a7fa05505942d0729e5a5be2bd691a49c242937fdb9de18f6a6f97b5799424.png)

**Step 3**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 1 & 3\end{aligned}| \\  & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 4**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T:$

$$
\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}={(\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)})}^{-1}=\frac{1}{3}
$$

Note that $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}\ne 0$ everywhere inside $Δ.$ In other words, $T$ has no critical points inside $Δ.$

**Step 5**: Perform the change of variables, and evaluate the integral:

Performing the change of variables, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\frac{x+3y}{x}\,\text{d}x\text{d}y & ={∬}_{Δ}\frac{v}{u}\,|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & ={∬}_{Δ}\frac{v}{u}\,|\frac{1}{3}|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & =\frac{1}{3}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{1}^{2}\frac{v}{u}\,\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & =\frac{1}{3}{\int }_{0}^{1}v\,\text{d}v{\int }_{1}^{2}\frac{1}{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\cdot {[\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}]}_{0}^{1}\cdot [\operatorname{ln}⁡u]_{1}^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\cdot \frac{1}{2}\cdot \operatorname{ln}⁡2 \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}{6}.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-149fcd69-9998-58e5-a043-dbc9ef09dd8b"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-149fcd69-9998-58e5-a043-dbc9ef09dd8b" :answer-field/id #uuid "149fcd69-9998-58e5-a043-dbc9ef09dd8b" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-3f270f12-02ec-5549-8988-b03e5d2eae95" :answer-field/choices ["answer-fbe6534a-9156-5f3a-a3f4-adabfe81028f" "answer-e902cbe7-031f-5540-a22a-6e30754fbd91" "answer-cc1e541a-a0b5-50e1-8a46-d0f83df1d6c4" "answer-3f270f12-02ec-5549-8988-b03e5d2eae95" "answer-30fd4f57-3f0a-5ebc-aa07-bb84afb9cc7a"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-fbe6534a-9156-5f3a-a3f4-adabfe81028f" :answer/id #uuid "fbe6534a-9156-5f3a-a3f4-adabfe81028f" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "2" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-e902cbe7-031f-5540-a22a-6e30754fbd91" :answer/id #uuid "e902cbe7-031f-5540-a22a-6e30754fbd91" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "3\operatorname{ln}⁡2" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-cc1e541a-a0b5-50e1-8a46-d0f83df1d6c4" :answer/id #uuid "cc1e541a-a0b5-50e1-8a46-d0f83df1d6c4" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{1}{6}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-3f270f12-02ec-5549-8988-b03e5d2eae95" :answer/id #uuid "3f270f12-02ec-5549-8988-b03e5d2eae95" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}{6}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-30fd4f57-3f0a-5ebc-aa07-bb84afb9cc7a" :answer/id #uuid "30fd4f57-3f0a-5ebc-aa07-bb84afb9cc7a" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\operatorname{ln}⁡2" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186199451 :tutorial/content "Suppose that 

$$
\mathbf T: (u,v) \to \left(x(u,v),y(u,v)\right)
$$

is a $C^1$ transformation that has no critical points (i.e., it is invertible) inside some region $\Delta\subset \mathbb R^2,$ and that $\mathbf T(\Delta) = D,$ as shown below.

![](images/66/668b8a0dae060c7929b92c6abe3601b0ede0b8444d92f33f4a8b5627410a4447.png)

 

We've already seen how the area of a non-trivial region $D$ can be computed using the change of variables formula:

$$
\iint\limits_{D} \mathrm d x \mathrm d y = \iint\limits_{\Delta} \left| \dfrac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (u, v)} \right|  \ \mathrm d u \mathrm d v
$$

We can extend this formula to compute the integral of a function $f(x,y)$ over $D,$ as follows:

$$
\iint\limits_{D} f(x,y) \ \mathrm d x \mathrm d y = \iint\limits_{\Delta} \ f(x(u,v), y(u,v)) \:  \left| \dfrac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (u, v)} \right|  \ \mathrm d u \mathrm d v
$$

Note the similarity with the change of variables formula for the integral of a single-variable function $f(x)$ over $D = (a,b){:}$

$$
\int\limits_D f(x)\,\textrm d x = \int\limits_{\Delta} f(x(u))\,\dfrac{\textrm d x}{\textrm d u}\, \textrm d u
$$

Applying the change of variables formula is similar to when we were restricting our attention to areas in the plane. The only difference now is that we must also express the integrand $f(x,y)$ in terms of $u$ and $v.$

Let's see an example." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186198479 :activity/expected-seconds 1020.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]} {:db/id 17592186347802 :answer-field/correct Let's take a look at the number line below.

![](images/e2/e20db43f722fc4db42fc845ab20a7eef2c06437cc1d2246e0aed47dc01107aba.png)

Since $-3$ and $3$ are at the same distance from the origin, we have

$$
|-3| = |3| = 3.
$$

In general, for any real number $a,$

$$
|-a| = |a|.
$$

We can use this fact to simplify expressions containing absolute value. Let's see an example." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186055996 :tutorial/content "The absolute value operation is **distributive with respect to multiplication.** This means that the absolute value of a product equals the product of the absolute values.

To demonstrate, consider the following expression:

$$
|(-6) \cdot 2|
$$

We can evaluate this expression in two separate ways:

- The first is to find the absolute value of the product. In doing this, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}|(-6)\cdot 2| & =|-12| \\  & =12.\end{aligned}
$$

- The second is to find the product of the absolute values. In doing this, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}|(-6)\cdot 2| & =|-6|\cdot |2| \\  & =6\cdot 2 \\  & =12.\end{aligned}
$$

In general

$$
|a \cdot b| = |a|\cdot |b|.
$$

The absolute value operation is also distributive with respect to division. In general,

$$
\left|\dfrac{a}{b}\right| = \dfrac{|a|}{|b|}.
$$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186054923 :activity/expected-seconds 420.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]} {:db/id 17592186281374 :question/problem "![](images/0e/0e374f18d8b87de2fddd9a2127ee84709746c7c1b75083441afcc7b6c79402fb.png)

Which of the following could be the missing expression?" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} [:db/retract 17592186153490 :answer-field/choices 17592186153491] [:db/retract 17592186153490 :answer-field/choices 17592186153492] [:db/retract 17592186153490 :answer-field/choices 17592186153493] [:db/retract 17592186153490 :answer-field/choices 17592186153494] [:db/retract 17592186153490 :answer-field/choices 17592186153495] {:db/id 17592186157425 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-c02d4f47-274a-5db8-9775-386bac66028f"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id "question-c02d4f47-274a-5db8-9775-386bac66028f" :question/id #uuid "c02d4f47-274a-5db8-9775-386bac66028f" :question/math-academy-id "q-102684" :question/problem "Find ${f}^{″}(1,2)$ for the function $f(x,y)=y\operatorname{ln}⁡x-{y}^{2}.$" :question/worked-solution "For a function $f:{R}^{n}\to R,$ given by

$$
f:{{[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ ⋮ \\ {x}_{n}\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{x}⟶f({x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n}),
$$

the second derivative of $f$ is given by the $n\times n$ matrix

$$
{f}^{″}(x)=[\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{n}} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}^{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{n}} \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}^{2}}\end{aligned}].
$$

In our case, we have

$$
{f}^{″}(x,y)=[\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}].
$$

First, we compute the first derivative of $f(x,y),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x,y) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & \frac{∂f}{∂y}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂x}(y\operatorname{ln}⁡x-{y}^{2}) & \frac{∂}{∂y}(y\operatorname{ln}⁡x-{y}^{2})\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{y}{x} & \operatorname{ln}⁡x-2y\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we compute the second partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\frac{y}{x})=-\frac{y}{{x}^{2}}\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡x-2y)=\frac{1}{x} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\frac{y}{x})=\frac{1}{x}\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{ln}⁡x-2y)=-2\end{aligned}
$$

So, the second derivative is

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(x,y) & =[\begin{aligned}-\frac{y}{{x}^{2}} & \frac{1}{x} \\ \frac{1}{x} & -2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate this matrix at $(1,2).$ This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(1,2)=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 1 \\ 1 & -2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-3cad98c5-f0af-530e-9545-f63d666cd3ea"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id given by

$$
f:{{[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ ⋮ \\ {x}_{n}\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{x}⟶f({x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n}),
$$

the second derivative of $f$ is given by the $n\times n$ matrix

$$
{f}^{″}(x)=[\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{n}} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}^{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{n}} \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}^{2}}\end{aligned}].
$$

In our case, we have

$$
{f}^{″}(x,y)=[\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}].
$$

First, we compute the first derivative of $f(x,y),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x,y) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & \frac{∂f}{∂y}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂x}(xy-{x}^{2}{y}^{3}) & \frac{∂}{∂y}(xy-{x}^{2}{y}^{3})\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}y-2x{y}^{3} & x-3{x}^{2}{y}^{2}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we compute the second partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(y-2x{y}^{3})=-2{y}^{3}\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(x-3{x}^{2}{y}^{2})=1-6x{y}^{2} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(y-2x{y}^{3})=1-6x{y}^{2}\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(x-3{x}^{2}{y}^{2})=-6{x}^{2}y\end{aligned}
$$

So, the second derivative is

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(x,y) & =[\begin{aligned}-2{y}^{3} & 1-6x{y}^{2} \\ 1-6x{y}^{2} & -6{x}^{2}y\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate this matrix at $(1,0).$ This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(1,0)=[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}

		{\color{blue}{x}}(x + 2) + {\color{red}{3}}(x + 2) &= \[5pt]
		x^2 + 2x + 3x + 6 &= \[5pt]
		x^2 + 5x + 6
	}
$$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186064457 :activity/expected-seconds 540.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]}] "assertions" [[17592186100706 :question/problem "Express $\left(4^3\right)^2$ as a base raised to a single exponent."] [17592186100706 :question/worked-solution "To raise a power to another power, we simply multiply the exponents:

$$
\left( 3^5\right)^4 = 3^{5\cdot 4} = 3^{20}
$$

$$

["question-08715ccd-f649-5c84-af70-2145bc128aa0" :question/math-academy-id "q-162396"] ["question-08715ccd-f649-5c84-af70-2145bc128aa0" :question/problem "Find the radius of curvature for the curve $r(t)={t}^{2}\,i+({t}^{2}-t)\,j$ at $t=0.$"] ["question-08715ccd-f649-5c84-af70-2145bc128aa0" :question/worked-solution "The curvature $κ(t)$ of a plane curve $r(t)=x(t)\,i+y(t)\,j$ is given by

$$
κ(t)=\frac{|{x}^{′}(t){y}^{″}(t)-{y}^{′}(t){x}^{″}(t)|}{([{x}^{′}(t)]^{2}+[{y}^{′}(t)]^{2})^{3/2}}.
$$

The radius of curvature $R$ is defined as
$R(t)=\frac{1}{κ(t)}.$

Along our curve, we have

$$
x(t)={t}^{2},\,y(t)={t}^{2}-t.
$$

First, we calculate the derivatives of the components:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t) & =2t,\, & {y}^{′}(t) & =2t-1 \\ {x}^{″}(t) & =2,\, & {y}^{″}(t) & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting these into the formula for the curvature, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}κ(t) & =\frac{|2t\cdot 2-(2t-1)\cdot 2|}{{((2t)^{2}+(2t-1)^{2})}^{3/2}} \\  & =\frac{2}{{(8{t}^{2}-4t+1)}^{3/2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the curvature at $t=0$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}κ(0) & =\frac{2}{{(8(0)^{2}-4(0)+1)}^{3/2}} \\  & =\frac{2}{{(0-0+1)}^{3/2}} \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the radius of curvature at $t=0$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}R(0) & =\frac{1}{κ(0)}=\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-08715ccd-f649-5c84-af70-2145bc128aa0" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-e5755c53-01de-5e40-9f46-4f16d8b88aa1" :answer-field/id #uuid x(t)=(1+{t}^{2})^{2},\,y(t)=t.
$$

First, we calculate the derivatives of the components:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t) & =4t(1+{t}^{2}),\, & {y}^{′}(t) & =1 \\ {x}^{″}(t) & =12{t}^{2}+4,\, & {y}^{″}(t) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting these into the formula for the curvature, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}κ(t) & =\frac{|4t(1+{t}^{2})\cdot 0-1\cdot (12{t}^{2}+4)|}{{((4t(1+{t}^{2}))^{2}+{1}^{2})}^{3/2}} \\  & =\frac{12{t}^{2}+4}{{((4t(1+{t}^{2}))^{2}+1)}^{3/2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the curvature at $t=0$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}κ(0) & =\frac{12(0)^{2}+4}{{((4(0)(1+(0)^{2}))^{2}+1)}^{3/2}} \\  & =\frac{4}{{(0+1)}^{3/2}} \\  & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the radius of curvature at $t=0$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}R(0) & =\frac{1}{κ(0)}=\frac{1}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-cf02b7af-f8d0-5528-8cc7-2d359506a141" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-21292018-ea56-5ae6-a7f5-dac08271bdff" :answer-field/id #uuid $$

- The moment of inertia about the $y$-axis is given by

$$
{I}_{y}={∬}_{D}{x}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A.
$$

- The moment of inertia about the origin is given by

$$
{I}_{0}={∬}_{D}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A={I}_{x}+{I}_{y}.
$$

First, notice that $D$ is a type I region with representation

$$
D=\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le 4,\,\,0\le y\le \sqrt{x}\},
$$

as shown below.

![](images/dd/dd5ee021dd73317a775c0ea653212f7ee5545f8c6854e6a9daabdc93b5c3b9c0.png)

Using the formula for ${I}_{0},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{0} & ={∬}_{D}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{4}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{x}}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\cdot 3y\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{4}[{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{x}}3{x}^{2}y+3{y}^{3}\,\text{d}y]\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{4}{[\frac{3}{2}{x}^{2}{y}^{2}+\frac{3}{4}{y}^{4}]}_{y=0}^{y=\sqrt{x}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{4}\frac{3}{2}{x}^{3}+\frac{3}{4}{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={[\frac{3}{8}{x}^{4}+\frac{1}{4}{x}^{3}]}_{0}^{4} \\  & =96+16 \\  & =112.\end{aligned}
$$"] [17592186281636 :question/worked-solution "For a plane lamina $D$ with mass density function $\lambda (x,y),$ we have the following definitions:

- The moment of inertia about the $x$-axis is given by

$$
{I}_{x}={∬}_{D}{y}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A.
$$

- The moment of inertia about the $y$-axis is given by

$$
{I}_{y}={∬}_{D}{x}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A.
$$

- The moment of inertia about the origin is given by

$$
{I}_{0}={∬}_{D}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A={I}_{x}+{I}_{y}.
$$

First, notice that $D$ is a type II region with representation

$$
D=\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le y\le 3,\,\,\frac{y}{3}\le x\le 4-y\},
$$

as shown below.

![](images/47/47c897bd58a23965d9c36f683553c0817afa8bc2e37ed53a432edcd62b386e55.png)

The area of the triangular plate $D$ is 

$$
A=\frac{1}{2}\cdot 4\cdot 3=6.
$$

Since the plate has uniform density, every unit of area contains the same amount of mass. Therefore, the mass density is constant and is given by the total mass divided by the total area:

$$
\lambda (x,y)=\frac{M}{A}=\frac{M}{6}.
$$

Therefore, the moment of inertia about the $x$-axis is

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{x} & ={∬}_{D}{y}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A \\  & =\frac{M}{6}{\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{y/3}^{4-y}{y}^{2}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{M}{6}{\int }_{0}^{3}{y}^{2}[{\int }_{y/3}^{4-y}\,\text{d}x]\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{M}{6}{\int }_{0}^{3}{y}^{2}(4-y-\frac{1}{3}y)\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{M}{6}{\int }_{0}^{3}4{y}^{2}-\frac{4}{3}{y}^{3}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{M}{6}{[\frac{4}{3}{y}^{3}-\frac{1}{3}{y}^{4}]}_{0}^{3} \\  & =\frac{M}{6}(36-27) \\  & =\frac{3M}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$"] [17592186281637 :question/worked-solution "For a plane lamina $D$ with mass density function $\lambda (x,y),$ we have the following definitions:

- The moment of inertia about the $x$-axis is given by

$$
{I}_{x}={∬}_{D}{y}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A.
$$

- The moment of inertia about the $y$-axis is given by

$$
{I}_{y}={∬}_{D}{x}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A.
$$

- The moment of inertia about the origin is given by

$$

$$

First, notice that $D$ is a type I region with representation

$$
D=\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le 2,\,\,\frac{x}{2}\le y\le 3-x\},
$$

as shown below.

![](images/6c/6c2cec5e919c25623396b5ba5f052481623a868c7520aa8e3d1d3eb34f3a4a58.png)

$$
A=\frac{1}{2}\cdot 2\cdot 3=3.

Since the plate has uniform density, every unit of area contains the same amount of mass. Therefore, the mass density is constant and is given by the total mass divided by the total area:

$$

Therefore, the moment of inertia about the $y$-axis is

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{y} & ={∬}_{D}{x}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A \\  & =\frac{M}{3}{\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{x/2}^{3-x}{x}^{2}\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{M}{3}{\int }_{0}^{2}{x}^{2}[{\int }_{x/2}^{3-x}\,\text{d}y]\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{M}{3}{\int }_{0}^{2}{x}^{2}(3-x-\frac{x}{2})\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{M}{3}{\int }_{0}^{2}3{x}^{2}-\frac{3}{2}{x}^{3}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{M}{3}{[{x}^{3}-\frac{3}{8}{x}^{4}]}_{0}^{2} \\  & =\frac{M}{3}(8-6) \\  & =\frac{2M}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$"] [17592186281644 :question/worked-solution "For a plane lamina $D$ with mass density function $\lambda (r,\theta ),$ we have the following definitions:

- The moment of inertia about the $x$-axis, in polar coordinates, is given by

$$
{I}_{x}={∬}_{D}\lambda (r,\theta )\cdot {r}^{3}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

- The moment of inertia about the $y$-axis, in polar coordinates, is given by

$$
{I}_{y}={∬}_{D}\lambda (r,\theta )\cdot {r}^{3}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

- The moment of inertia about the origin, in polar coordinates, is given by

$$
{I}_{0}={∬}_{D}\lambda (r,\theta )\cdot {r}^{3}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta ={I}_{x}+{I}_{y}.
$$

First, note that the region $D$ in polar coordinates can be expressed as

$$
D=\{(r,\theta )\,:\,1\le r\le \sqrt[5]{2},\,\,\frac{\pi }{4}\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{3}\}.
$$

Also, the mass density function in polar coordinates is 

$$
\lambda (r,\theta )=15r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .
$$

Therefore, the moment of inertia about the $y$-axis is

:question/problem "$\frac{5}{36}\times 2+(5+1)^{-2}=${{field-1}}"] ["question-6433a3cf-883a-54aa-9f03-bdc753346e58" :question/worked-solution "To evaluate the given expression, we use PEMDAS.

First, we compute the expression inside the parentheses:

$$
\frac{5}{36}\times 2+(5+1)^{-2}=\frac{5}{36}\times 2+{6}^{-2}
$$

Next, notice that ${6}^{-2}=\frac{1}{{6}^{2}}=\frac{1}{36}.$ So, we obtain:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{5}{36}\times 2+{6}^{-2} & = \\ \frac{5}{36}\times 2+\frac{1}{36} & = \\ \frac{5}{36}\times \frac{2}{1}+\frac{1}{36} & = \\ \frac{5\times 2}{36\times 1}+\frac{1}{36} & = \\ \frac{10}{36}+\frac{1}{36} & = \\ \frac{10+1}{36} & = \\ \frac{11}{36}\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-6433a3cf-883a-54aa-9f03-bdc753346e58" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard] ["answer-field-3bea4dc1-0a50-536e-8358-41147aeb0b3f" :answer-field/id #uuid "3bea4dc1-0a50-536e-8358-41147aeb0b3f"] ["answer-ff108b6d-b341-5dec-bcea-441b760861b8" :answer/id #uuid "ff108b6d-b341-5dec-bcea-441b760861b8"] ["answer-ff108b6d-b341-5dec-bcea-441b760861b8" :answer/type :answer.type/math] ["answer-ff108b6d-b341-5dec-bcea-441b760861b8" :answer/value "\frac{11}{36}"] ["answer-field-3bea4dc1-0a50-536e-8358-41147aeb0b3f" :answer-field/key "field-1"] ["answer-field-3bea4dc1-0a50-536e-8358-41147aeb0b3f" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank] ["answer-field-3bea4dc1-0a50-536e-8358-41147aeb0b3f" :answer-field/correct "answer-ff108b6d-b341-5dec-bcea-441b760861b8"] ["answer-field-3bea4dc1-0a50-536e-8358-41147aeb0b3f" :answer-field/choices "answer-ff108b6d-b341-5dec-bcea-441b760861b8"] ["question-6433a3cf-883a-54aa-9f03-bdc753346e58" :question/answer-fields "answer-field-3bea4dc1-0a50-536e-8358-41147aeb0b3f"] [17592186129309 :knowledge-point/questions "question-6433a3cf-883a-54aa-9f03-bdc753346e58"] ["question-2dbc86c1-eb39-5436-87d8-eb16a5d4d270" :question/id #uuid "2dbc86c1-eb39-5436-87d8-eb16a5d4d270"] ["question-2dbc86c1-eb39-5436-87d8-eb16a5d4d270" :question/math-academy-id "q-179401"] ["question-2dbc86c1-eb39-5436-87d8-eb16a5d4d270" :question/problem "$(7-5)^{-4}+{(\frac{3}{5}-\frac{1}{2})}^{0}=${{field-1}}"] ["question-2dbc86c1-eb39-5436-87d8-eb16a5d4d270" :question/worked-solution "To evaluate the given expression, we use PEMDAS. 

First, we compute the expression inside the parentheses:

$$
\begin{aligned}(7-5)^{-4}+{(\frac{3}{5}-\frac{1}{2})}^{0} & = \\ {2}^{-4}+{(\frac{6}{10}-\frac{5}{10})}^{0} & = \\ {2}^{-4}+{(\frac{1}{10})}^{0}\end{aligned}
$$

Next, notice that ${(\frac{1}{10})}^{0}=1.$ So, we obtain:

$$
\begin{aligned}{2}^{-4}+{(\frac{1}{10})}^{0} & = \\ {2}^{-4}+1\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, notice that ${2}^{-4}=\frac{1}{{2}^{4}}=\frac{1}{16}.$ So, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{2}^{-4}+1 & = \\ \frac{1}{16}+1 & = \\ \frac{1+16}{16} & = \\ \frac{17}{16}. & \end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-2dbc86c1-eb39-5436-87d8-eb16a5d4d270" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-c9a275f8-e12f-531b-9ed6-2c3eda31cf0e" :answer-field/id #uuid "c9a275f8-e12f-531b-9ed6-2c3eda31cf0e"] ["answer-ff37ba3f-b657-5468-a046-c7a885ae86ed" :answer/id #uuid "ff37ba3f-b657-5468-a046-c7a885ae86ed"] ["answer-ff37ba3f-b657-5468-a046-c7a885ae86ed" :answer/type :answer.type/math] ["answer-ff37ba3f-b657-5468-a046-c7a885ae86ed" :answer/value "\frac{17}{16}"] ["answer-field-c9a275f8-e12f-531b-9ed6-2c3eda31cf0e" :answer-field/key "field-1"] ["answer-field-c9a275f8-e12f-531b-9ed6-2c3eda31cf0e" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank] ["answer-field-c9a275f8-e12f-531b-9ed6-2c3eda31cf0e" :answer-field/correct "answer-ff37ba3f-b657-5468-a046-c7a885ae86ed"] ["answer-field-c9a275f8-e12f-531b-9ed6-2c3eda31cf0e" :answer-field/choices "answer-ff37ba3f-b657-5468-a046-c7a885ae86ed"] ["question-2dbc86c1-eb39-5436-87d8-eb16a5d4d270" :question/answer-fields "answer-field-c9a275f8-e12f-531b-9ed6-2c3eda31cf0e"] [17592186129310 :knowledge-point/questions "question-2dbc86c1-eb39-5436-87d8-eb16a5d4d270"] ["question-5e5e796d-b724-597d-a614-e8af03095fdf" :question/id #uuid "5e5e796d-b724-597d-a614-e8af03095fdf"] ["question-5e5e796d-b724-597d-a614-e8af03095fdf" :question/math-academy-id "q-100301"] ["question-5e5e796d-b724-597d-a614-e8af03095fdf" :question/problem "Calculate ${(\frac{8}{7}-\frac{1}{16})}^{0}-11\times {(\frac{1}{2})}^{-3}.$"] ["question-5e5e796d-b724-597d-a614-e8af03095fdf" :question/worked-solution "To evaluate the given expression, we use PEMDAS.

$\frac{8}{7}-\frac{1}{16}$
is not zero. Any non-zero number raised to the power of $0$ equals $1.$ So, we have 

$$
{(\frac{8}{7}-\frac{1}{16})}^{0}=1.
$$

Next, we evaluate the negative exponent and get

$$
{(\frac{1}{2})}^{-3}={(\frac{2}{1})}^{3}={2}^{3}=8.
$$

Substituting all these values into the expression, we obtain:

$$
\begin{aligned}{(\frac{8}{7}-\frac{1}{16})}^{0}-11\times {(\frac{1}{2})}^{-3} & = \\ 1-11\times 8 & = \\ 1-88 & = \\ -87\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-5e5e796d-b724-597d-a614-e8af03095fdf" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard] ["answer-field-93d546fe-e93e-5d3c-8f24-4f640019211e" :answer-field/id #uuid "question-5e5e796d-b724-597d-a614-e8af03095fdf"] [17592186130481 :tutorial/content "As we know already, to evaluate numerical expressions with a mix of different operations, we follow the order of operations (PEMDAS).

The same rules apply to numerical expressions with zero and negative exponents. To demonstrate, let's compute the value of

$$
(-3)^0 +2^2 \div 2.
$$

To evaluate the given expression, we use PEMDAS.

Notice that $\left(-3\right)^{0}=1.$ So, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{(-3)}^{0}+{2}^{2}÷2 & = \\ 1+{2}^{2}÷2 & = \\ 1+4÷2 & = \\ 1+2 & = \\ 3 & .\end{aligned}
$$"] [17592186129335 :activity/expected-seconds 540.0] ["question-75f0d82a-dd66-5d66-8858-8e85c7e74ab7" :question/id #uuid "75f0d82a-dd66-5d66-8858-8e85c7e74ab7"] ["question-75f0d82a-dd66-5d66-8858-8e85c7e74ab7" :question/math-academy-id "q-94610"] ["question-75f0d82a-dd66-5d66-8858-8e85c7e74ab7" :question/problem "Consider the vector space ${R}_{3}[t]$ of all polynomials in the variable $t$ of degree at most $3,$ and its subset $B=\{a{t}^{3}+bt+1\,|\,a,b\in R\}.$

Which of the following statements are true?

I. $B$ is closed under polynomial addition

II. $B$ is closed under scalar multiplication

III. $B$ is a subspace of ${R}_{3}[t]$

IV. $B$ is **not** a subspace of ${R}_{3}[t]$"] ["question-75f0d82a-dd66-5d66-8858-8e85c7e74ab7" :question/worked-solution "Recall that a subset of a vector space is a subspace if it's closed under addition and scalar multiplication.

With that in mind, let's examine each statement in turn.

- Statement I is false. For example, if $f(t)=g(t)=t+1,$ then

$$
\begin{aligned}f(t)+g(t) & =(t+1)+(t+1) \\  & =2t+2,\end{aligned}
$$

which is not a polynomial from $B.$ So, $B$ is *not* closed under addition.

- Statement II is false. For example, if $f(t)=t+1$ and $k=2,$ then 

$$
\begin{aligned}kf(t) & =2(t+1)=2t+2,\end{aligned}
$$

which is not a polynomial from $B.$ So, $B$ is *not* closed under scalar multiplication.

- Statement III is false, while statement IV is true. $B$ is *not* a subspace because it's not closed under addition and scalar multiplication.

Therefore, the correct answer is "IV only.""] ["question-75f0d82a-dd66-5d66-8858-8e85c7e74ab7" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-a24ecf47-9c4a-5174-a968-bb79cd6b4d3c" - **Step 1:** Set ${\color{blue}\mathbf{v}_1}=\mathbf{a}_1.$

- **Step 2:** Find a vector $\color{blue}\mathbf{v}_2$ in $V$ that's orthogonal to $\color{blue}\mathbf{v}_1.$ This can be achieved by computing

$$

$$
\textrm{Span}\{\mathbf{a}_1,\mathbf{a}_2\} = V = \textrm{Span}\{ {\color{blue}\mathbf{v}_1}, {\color{blue}\mathbf{v}_2} \}.
$$

After applying the Gram-Schmidt process, we get the set $\mathcal{B}=\{{\color{blue}\mathbf{v}_1}, {\color{blue}\mathbf{v}_2}\},$ which is an orthogonal basis for $V.$

"question-c6e04ff1-6e26-5bfa-a6e9-85e824fdf68a"] [17592186153346 :tutorial/content "So far, we know the following:

- To find the square root of a number, we need to find another that multiplies by itself $2$ times to give the original number. For example,

$$
\sqrt{9} = \sqrt{3 \cdot 3} = \sqrt{3^2} = 3.
$$

- To find the cube root of a number, we need to find another that multiplies by itself $3$ times to give the original number. For example,

$$
\sqrt[3]{8} = \sqrt[3]{2 \cdot 2 \cdot 2} = \sqrt[3]{2^3} = 2.
$$

We can extend this to any root. In general, to find the $n$th root of a number, we needed to find another number that multiplies by itself $n$ times to give the original number. We express the $n$th root as the radical $\sqrt[n]{\phantom{0}}.$ For instance,

$$
\sqrt[{\color{blue}4}]{16} = \sqrt[{\color{blue}4}]{\underbrace{2\cdot 2\cdot 2\cdot 2}_{{\color{blue}4}\text{ times}}} = \sqrt[{\color{blue}4}]{2^4} = 2.
$$

Given a radical $\sqrt[n]{x},$ we can write an equivalent expression using the fractional exponent $x^{1/n}.$ To demonstrate, let's write an equivalent expression for $\sqrt[7]{3}.$

Comparing $\sqrt[n]{x}$ with $\sqrt[7]{3},$ we get $x = 3$ and $n = 7.$ Therefore,

$$
\sqrt[7]{3} = 3^{1/7}.
$$

The reverse is also true: the fractional exponent $x^{1/n}$ can be written as the radical $\sqrt[n]{x}.$

**Note:** Remember that the square root of a number corresponds to the case of $n=2.$ So, for example, we have

$$
\sqrt{3} = 3^{1/2}.
$$"] [17592186152321 :activity/expected-seconds 420.0] ["question-65bd6053-5f41-5a6f-ac31-815596c779fb" :question/id #uuid "65bd6053-5f41-5a6f-ac31-815596c779fb"] ["question-65bd6053-5f41-5a6f-ac31-815596c779fb" :question/math-academy-id "q-163208"] ["question-65bd6053-5f41-5a6f-ac31-815596c779fb" :question/problem "Consider the function $f(x,y)$ and the region $D$ given by

$$
f(x,y)=3y-2x,\,D=\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le y,\,0\le y\le 3\}.
$$

According to the mean value theorem for double integrals, there exists a point $(a,b)\in D$ such that the volume of the solid enclosed between the surface $z=f(x,y)$ and the $xy$-plane over the region $D$ equals the volume of the right cylinder with base $D$ and height $f(a,b).$ Find $b$ given that $a=1.$"] ["question-65bd6053-5f41-5a6f-ac31-815596c779fb" :question/worked-solution "According to the mean value theorem for double integrals, there exists a point $(a,b)\in D$ such that

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A=f(a,b)\cdot \text{Area}(D).
$$

Evaluating the integral on the left-hand side, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{D}(3y-2x)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{0}^{y}(3y-2x)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}[3xy-{x}^{2}]_{x=0}^{x=y}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}2{y}^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={[\frac{2{y}^{3}}{3}]}_{y=0}^{y=3} \\  & =18.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Area}(D) & ={∬}_{D}\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{0}^{y}\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}[x]_{x=0}^{x=y}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}y\,\text{d}y \\  & ={[\frac{{y}^{2}}{2}]}_{y=0}^{y=3} \\  & =\frac{9}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Also, we are told that $a=1.$ So, our initial equation simplifies to

$$
\begin{aligned}18 & =f(1,b)\cdot \frac{9}{2} \\ 18 & =(3b-2\cdot 1)\cdot \frac{9}{2} \\ 4 & =3b-2 \\ 6 & =3b \\ b & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that $(1,2)\in D.$ Therefore, the answer is $b=2.$"] ["question-65bd6053-5f41-5a6f-ac31-815596c779fb" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] :question/problem "Consider the function $f(x,y)$ and the region $D$ given by

$$
f(x,y)=2x+{y}^{2},\,D=\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le 2,\,0\le y\le 3\}.
$$

According to the mean value theorem for double integrals, there exists a point $(a,b)\in D$ such that the volume of the solid enclosed between the surface $z=f(x,y)$ and the $xy$-plane over the region $D$ equals the volume of the right cylinder with base $D$ and height $f(a,b).$ Find $a$ given that $b=1.$"] ["question-a130ee36-c4fa-557a-b62c-af4b4bf44ed4" :question/worked-solution "According to the mean value theorem for double integrals, there exists a point $(a,b)\in D$ such that

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A=f(a,b)\cdot \text{Area}(D).
$$

Evaluating the integral on the left-hand side, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{D}(2x+{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{3}(2x+{y}^{2})\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}[2xy+\frac{{y}^{3}}{3}]_{y=0}^{y=3}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}(6x+9)\,\text{d}x \\  & =[3{x}^{2}+9x]_{x=0}^{x=2} \\  & =(3\cdot {2}^{2}+9\cdot 2)-0 \\  & =30.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we have

$$
\text{Area}(D)=2\cdot 3=6.
$$

Also, we are told that $b=1.$ So, our initial equation simplifies to

$$
\begin{aligned}30 & =f(a,1)\cdot 6 \\ 30 & =(2a+{1}^{2})\cdot 6 \\ 30 & =12a+6 \\ 24 & =12a \\ a & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that $(2,1)\in D.$ Therefore, the answer is $a=2.$"] ["question-a130ee36-c4fa-557a-b62c-af4b4bf44ed4" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["question-a8b13a1a-6bdb-56d5-b06e-dfa9901c1db1" :question/math-academy-id "q-163149"] ["question-a8b13a1a-6bdb-56d5-b06e-dfa9901c1db1" :question/problem "Consider the function $f(x,y)$ and the region $D$ given by

$$
f(x,y)=2x+3{y}^{2},\,D=\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le 2,\,0\le y\le 2\}.
$$

According to the mean value theorem for double integrals, there exists a point $(a,b)\in D$ such that the volume of the solid enclosed between the surface $z=f(x,y)$ and the $xy$-plane over the region $D$ equals the volume of the right cylinder with base $D$ and height $f(a,b).$ Find $a$ given that $b=1.$"] ["question-a8b13a1a-6bdb-56d5-b06e-dfa9901c1db1" :question/worked-solution "According to the mean value theorem for double integrals, there exists a point $(a,b)\in D$ such that

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A=f(a,b)\cdot \text{Area}(D).
$$

Evaluating the integral on the left-hand side, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{D}(2x+3{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{2}(2x+3{y}^{2})\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}[2xy+{y}^{3}]_{y=0}^{y=2}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}(4x+8)\,\text{d}x \\  & =[2{x}^{2}+8x]_{x=0}^{x=2} \\  & =(2\cdot {2}^{2}+8\cdot 2)-0 \\  & =24.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we have

$$
\text{Area}(D)=2\cdot 2=4.
$$

Also, we are told that $b=1.$ So, our initial equation simplifies to

$$
\begin{aligned}24 & =f(a,1)\cdot 4 \\ 24 & =(2a+3\cdot {1}^{2})\cdot 4 \\ 6 & =2a+3 \\ 3 & =2a \\ a & =\frac{3}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that $(\frac{3}{2},1)\in D.$ Therefore, the answer is $a=\frac{3}{2}.$"] ["question-a8b13a1a-6bdb-56d5-b06e-dfa9901c1db1" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["question-d1845eab-f52b-5f23-bd27-faf40f79c71a" :question/math-academy-id "q-163205"] ["question-d1845eab-f52b-5f23-bd27-faf40f79c71a" :question/problem "Consider the function $f(x,y)$ and the region $D$ given by

$$
f(x,y)=2x+y,\,D=\{(x,y)\,:\,\frac{y}{2}\le x\le y,\,\,0\le y\le 6\}.
$$

According to the mean value theorem for double integrals, there exists a point $(a,b)\in D$ such that the volume of the solid enclosed between the surface $z=f(x,y)$ and the $xy$-plane over the region $D$ equals the volume of the right cylinder with base $D$ and height $f(a,b).$ Find $a$ given that $b=4.$"] ["question-d1845eab-f52b-5f23-bd27-faf40f79c71a" :question/worked-solution "According to the mean value theorem for double integrals, there exists a point $(a,b)\in D$ such that

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A=f(a,b)\cdot \text{Area}(D).
$$

Evaluating the integral on the left-hand side, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{D}(2x+y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{6}{\int }_{y/2}^{y}(2x+y)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{6}[{x}^{2}+xy]_{x=y/2}^{x=y}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{6}([{y}^{2}+{y}^{2}]-[\frac{{y}^{2}}{4}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{2}])\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{6}\frac{5{y}^{2}}{4}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={[\frac{5{y}^{3}}{12}]}_{y=0}^{y=6} \\  & =90.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Area}(D) & ={∬}_{D}\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{6}{\int }_{y/2}^{y}\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{6}[x]_{x=y/2}^{x=y}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{6}\frac{y}{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={[\frac{{y}^{2}}{4}]}_{y=0}^{y=6} \\  & =9.\end{aligned}
$$

Also, we are told that $b=4.$ So, our initial equation simplifies to

$$
\begin{aligned}90 & =f(a,4)\cdot 9 \\ 90 & =(2a+4)\cdot 9 \\ 10 & =2a+4 \\ 6 & =2a \\ a & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that $(3,4)\in D.$ Therefore, the answer is $a=3.$"] ["question-d1845eab-f52b-5f23-bd27-faf40f79c71a" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate]
