the average value of the function $f(x,y)={y}^{2}$ on the disk of radius $2$ centered at the origin."] ["question-3b9226c2-67e0-5858-9c64-ae46c4147a95" :question/worked-solution "First, notice that 

$$
\text{Area}(D)=\pi \cdot {2}^{2}=4\pi .
$$

The average value of the function over a region $D$ is given by

$$
{f}_{\text{ave}}=\frac{1}{\text{Area}(D)}\,{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A.
$$

We will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .
$$

In polar coordinates $(r,\theta ),$ the region can be expressed as 

$$
Δ=\{(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le 2,\,0\le \theta <2\pi \}.
$$

Using the change of variables formula, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}{y}^{2}\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2}\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{2}{r}^{3}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{sin}^{2}⁡\theta {\int }_{0}^{2}{r}^{3}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{sin}^{2}⁡\theta \,{[\frac{{r}^{4}}{4}]}_{0}^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{sin}^{2}⁡\theta (4-0)\text{d}\theta  \\  & =4{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{sin}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =4{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\frac{1}{2}(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta )\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =2{[\theta -\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta ]}_{0}^{2\pi } \\  & =2[(2\pi -0)-\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{sin}⁡4\pi -\operatorname{sin}⁡0)] \\  & =2\cdot 2\pi  \\  & =4\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
{f}_{\text{ave}}=\frac{1}{4\pi }\cdot 4\pi =1.
$$"] ["question-3b9226c2-67e0-5858-9c64-ae46c4147a95" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-2a10b6cc-8155-5c1e-bf70-aecfcd94d2ca" :answer-field/id #uuid :question/worked-solution "First, notice that 

$$
\text{Area}(D)=\pi \cdot {(\frac{1}{2})}^{2}=\frac{\pi }{4}.
$$

The average value of the function over a region $D$ is given by

$$
{f}_{\text{ave}}=\frac{1}{\text{Area}(D)}\,{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A.
$$

We will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .
$$

In polar coordinates $(r,\theta ),$ the region can be expressed as 

$$
Δ=\{(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le \frac{1}{2},\,0\le \theta <2\pi \}.
$$

Using the change of variables formula, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}{e}^{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}{e}^{(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2}}\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={∬}_{Δ}{e}^{{r}^{2}}\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\,{[\frac{{e}^{{r}^{2}}}{2}]}_{0}^{1/2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(\frac{{e}^{1/4}}{2}-\frac{1}{2})\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{\sqrt[4]{e}-1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{\sqrt[4]{e}-1}{2}[\theta ]_{0}^{2\pi } \\  & =\frac{\sqrt[4]{e}-1}{2}(2\pi -0) \\  & =(\sqrt[4]{e}-1)\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
{f}_{\text{ave}}=\frac{4}{\pi }\cdot (\sqrt[4]{e}-1)\pi =4(\sqrt[4]{e}-1).
$$"] ["question-b2ff4fa5-a334-50b5-9869-f8e569ec5011" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-d1136c19-2541-5007-b027-75b59e3253ba" :answer-field/id #uuid Find the average value of the function $f(x,y)=5y({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})$ on the semicircle shown above."] ["question-b0a81f04-6f59-512d-aa20-c54e3b26a51d" :question/worked-solution "First, notice that 

$$
\text{Area}(D)=\frac{1}{2}\cdot \pi \cdot {1}^{2}=\frac{\pi }{2}.
$$

The average value of the function over a region $D$ is given by

$$
{f}_{\text{ave}}=\frac{1}{\text{Area}(D)}\,{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A.
$$

We will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .
$$

Notice that the region $D$ represents a portion of the disk of radius $1$ centered at 
$(1,0).$

Cartesian and polar coordinates are connected by the following equations:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \end{aligned}
$$

With that is mind, let's now write the $y=-\sqrt{2x-{x}^{2}}$ in polar coordinates:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =-\sqrt{2x-{x}^{2}} \\ {y}^{2} & =2x-{x}^{2} \\ {x}^{2}+{y}^{2} & =2x \\ (r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2} & =2r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ {r}^{2}({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta ) & =2r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ {r}^{2} & =2r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ {r}^{2}-2r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =0 \\ r(r-2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

 

Since $r$ cannot be identical to zero on the entire semicircle, we must have $r=2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .$

Therefore, in polar coordinates $(r,\theta ),$ the region can be expressed as 

$$
Δ=\{(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le 2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,-\frac{\pi }{2}\le \theta \le 0\}.
$$

Therefore, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}5y({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}5r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ((r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2})\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{0}{\int }_{0}^{2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }5{r}^{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{0}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta {\int }_{0}^{2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }5{r}^{4}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{0}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta [{r}^{5}]_{0}^{2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{0}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ((2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{5}-0)\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =32{\int }_{-\pi /2}^{0}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta {cos}^{5}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =32{[-\frac{1}{6}{cos}^{6}⁡\theta ]}_{-\pi /2}^{0} \\  & =-\frac{16}{3}[{cos}^{6}⁡(0)-{cos}^{6}⁡(-\frac{\pi }{2})] \\  & =-\frac{16}{3}(1-0) \\  & =-\frac{16}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
{f}_{\text{ave}}=\frac{1}{(\frac{\pi }{2})}\cdot (-\frac{16}{3})=-\frac{32}{3\pi }.
$$"] ["question-b0a81f04-6f59-512d-aa20-c54e3b26a51d" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard] ["answer-field-7e8c2182-159c-53aa-a9ec-6a0270a24944" :answer-field/id #uuid $$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .

In polar coordinates $(r,\theta ),$ the region can be expressed as

$$

$$

$$
\int_a^b f(x)\, \textrm d x = f(c) \cdot (b-a),
$$

which can be visualized as shown below.

![](images/0a/0afb9b15787eb89f73f322290bdbe2288027c54924d274c438773ce151a17291.png)

 

We have a similar theorem for functions with two variables. The so-called **mean value theorem for double integrals** states:

*If the function $f(x,y)$ is continuous on a closed and bounded region $D,$ then there exists a point $(a,b) \in D$ such that*

$$
\iint\limits_D f(x,y) \: \textrm{d}A = f(a,b) \cdot \textrm{Area}(D).
$$

This has a nice geometrical interpretation when $f$ is non-negative on $D.$ In this case, the theorem tells us that there exists a point $(a,b) \in D$ such that the volume of the solid enclosed between the surface $z=f(x,y)$ and the $xy$-plane over the region $D$ equals the volume of the right cylinder with base $D$ and height $f(a,b).$ 

The diagram below shows the case when $D$ is rectangular, and the corresponding cylinder is a rectangular solid.

![](images/8e/8ed477207ee61fbdaf963ed8a127e3f1d4cf76707d2eeb4b450fd49f78e15b7e.png)

 

In general, the point $(a,b)$ mentioned in the theorem is not unique. Let's see an example."] [17592186168151 :tutorial/content "Consider the continuous function 

$$
f(x,y) = x+3y^2+2
$$

and the region $D$ given by

$$
D = \big\{ (x,y) \: : \: 0 \leq x \leq 2, \: 0 \leq y \leq 2 \big\}.
$$

According to the mean value theorem for double integrals, there exists a point $(a,b) \in D$ such that

$$
\iint\limits_D f(x,y) \: \textrm{d}A = f(a,b) \cdot \textrm{Area}(D).
$$

Evaluating the integral on the left-hand side, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{D}(x+3{y}^{2}+2)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{2}(x+3{y}^{2}+2)\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{[xy+{y}^{3}+2y]}_{y=0}^{y=2}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}(2x+12)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={[{x}^{2}+12x]}_{x=0}^{x=2} \\  & =28.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we have

$$
\textrm{Area}(D) = 2 \cdot 2 = 4.
$$

So, our mean-value equation simplifies to

$$
\begin{aligned}28 & =f(a,b)\cdot 4 \\ 7 & =f(a,b) \\ 7 & =a+3{b}^{2}+2 \\ a & =5-3{b}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

This equation describes part of a parabola in the $xy$-plane, as shown below.

![](images/46/46873c4ecb290380488e589082fc0759324d3540494f5b83e2d64db5d9cdf62a.png)

  

To find a particular point that satisfies the mean value theorem, we can set, for example, $b=1 \in [0,2]$ and obtain $a=2.$ So, the point $(2,1)$ satisfies the mean value theorem for double integrals. Consequently, the two solids below must have the same volume.

![](images/de/ded8743284f207bff35eba24617fd4245a69d439ed151d09eed564813f9d72fb.png)

The *distance* between the number $-3$ and $0$ is known as the **absolute value** of $-3.$ We write it as

$$
|-3| = {\color{red}3}.
$$

Similarly, $|\,2\,|$, the absolute value of the number $2$, is the distance between $2$ and $0$:

![](images/f4/f44fcd05fb0932083d48c8b11892247d8de8fbc46ccf7186fb12843702181aea.png)

We write $|\,2\,| = {\color{red}2}.$

So, the absolute value simply 

- *removes the minus sign*, if the number is negative, or

- does nothing, if the number is non-negative.

Sometimes, we can be asked to evaluate an expression involving the absolute value function, like $|x +1| + 5$ when $x=-3.$ In this case, we evaluate the expression inside the absolute value before simplifying the rest of the expression: 

$$
\begin{aligned}|x+1|+5 & = \\ |(-3)+1|+5 & = \\ |-2|+5 & = \\ 2+5 & = \\ 7 & \end{aligned}
$$"] [17592186054936 :activity/expected-seconds 420.0] [17592186157080 :question/problem "Given the orthogonal basis $\mathcal{B}$ of $\mathbb{R}^3$ and the vector $\mathbf{x}$ below, find the value of $x_2,$ the second component of $[\mathbf{x}]_{\mathcal{B}}.$

$$"] ["question-8702bab9-12cd-5dfe-a35e-1fe882de5059" :question/id #uuid "8702bab9-12cd-5dfe-a35e-1fe882de5059"] ["question-8702bab9-12cd-5dfe-a35e-1fe882de5059" :question/math-academy-id "q-81138"] ["question-8702bab9-12cd-5dfe-a35e-1fe882de5059" :question/problem "Given the orthogonal basis $B$ of ${R}^{3}$ and the vector $x$ below, find the value of $20{x}_{2}$, where ${x}_{2}$ is the second component of $[x]_{B}.$

$$

Therefore, 

$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}F(3,-1) & =P(X\le 3,Y\le -1).\end{aligned}

| $f$ | $Y=-1$ | $Y=0$ | $Y=1$ |

| $X=3$ | $0.05$ | $0.05$ | $0.1$ |

$$
\begin{aligned}F(3,-1) & ={\sum }_{x\le 3}{\sum }_{y\le -1}f(x,y) \\  & =f(1,-1)+f(2,-1)+f(3,-1) \\  & =0.1+0.05+0.05 \\  & =0.2.\end{aligned}

$$

| $f$ | $Y=2$ | $Y=4$ | $Y=6$ |

$$

$$

Find an expression for the corresponding joint CDF when $x>3,y<1.$"] ["question-9db88b4b-2611-5ba3-82d8-88e768790963" :question/worked-solution "If $X$ and $Y$ are discrete random variables with the joint probability mass function $f(x,y),$ then the corresponding joint CDF is given by

$$
F(x,y)=P(X\le x,Y\le y)={\sum }_{{x}_{i}\le x}{\sum }_{{y}_{i}\le y}f({x}_{i},{y}_{i}).
$$

Note the following:

- We can think of each point where $f(x,y)\ne 0$ as a point mass in the plane, where the "probability mass" at each point equals the probability associated with that point.

- The joint CDF $F(x,y)=P(X\le x,Y\le y)$ is the total "probability mass" that lies in the infinite rectangular region that has its top-right corner at $(x,y)$ and whose sides are parallel to the coordinate axis.

Given the supports of $X$ and $Y,$ the joint support $S$ is a subset of

$$
{S}_{X}\times {S}_{Y}=\{1,3\}\times \{1,2,3,4\}.
$$

Let's sketch the points in ${S}_{X}\times {S}_{Y},$ which contains the joint support. Let's also consider a point $(x,y)$ where $x>3$ and $y<1,$ and a region $Δ$ that lies below and to the left of this point.

![](images/2e/2ef3347831324b55e1a8ddaff2b0eb6af7fb7fc171867906e70c4b51f0051b05.png)

Since every value in the support of $Y$ is at least $1$ and $y<1,$ no possible value of $Y$ satisfies $Y\le y.$ Therefore, there are no points in the joint support that lie in the region $Δ.$

Hence,

$$
F(x,y)=P(X\le x,Y\le y)=0.
$$"] ["question-9db88b4b-2611-5ba3-82d8-88e768790963" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-bff05c4f-8ecf-52a9-80bb-3008a1ac8466" :answer-field/id #uuid $$

$$

Note the following:

- We can think of each point where $f(x,y)\ne 0$ as a point mass in the plane, where the "probability mass" at each point equals the probability associated with that point.

- The joint CDF $F(x,y)=P(X\le x,Y\le y)$ is the total "probability mass" that lies in the infinite rectangular region that has its top-right corner at $(x,y)$ and whose sides are parallel to the coordinate axis.

Given the supports of $X$ and $Y,$ the joint support $S$ is a subset of

$$
{S}_{X}\times {S}_{Y}=\{0,1,2,4\}\times \{0,1,2\}.
$$

Let's sketch the points in ${S}_{X}\times {S}_{Y},$ which contains the joint support. Let's also consider a point $(x,y)$ where $x>4$ and $y<0,$ and a region $Δ$ that lies below and to the left of this point.

Let the joint CDF of $X$ and $Y$ be $F(x,y),$ where the supports of $X$ and $Y$, respectively, are

$$
{S}_{X}=\{0,1\},\,{S}_{Y}=\{1,2,3,4,5,6\}.
$$

Find an expression for the corresponding joint CDF when $x>1,y>6.$"] ["question-5555465c-a779-5eab-9f3a-3128b4e5cfe0" :question/worked-solution "If $X$ and $Y$ are discrete random variables with the joint probability mass function $f(x,y),$ then the corresponding joint CDF is given by

$$
F(x,y)=P(X\le x,Y\le y)={\sum }_{{x}_{i}\le x}{\sum }_{{y}_{i}\le y}f({x}_{i},{y}_{i}).
$$

Note the following:

- We can think of each point where $f(x,y)\ne 0$ as a point mass in the plane, where the "probability mass" at each point equals the probability associated with that point.

- The joint CDF $F(x,y)=P(X\le x,Y\le y)$ is the total "probability mass" that lies in the infinite rectangular region that has its top-right corner at $(x,y)$ and whose sides are parallel to the coordinate axis.

Given the supports of $X$ and $Y,$ the joint support $S$ is a subset of

$$
{S}_{X}\times {S}_{Y}=\{0,1\}\times \{1,2,3,4,5,6\}.
$$

Let's sketch the points in ${S}_{X}\times {S}_{Y},$ which contains the joint support. Let's also consider a point $(x,y)$ where $x>1$ and $y>6,$ and a region $Δ$ that lies below and to the left of this point.

![](images/64/644db930cdb0d683a0bcae61b2596dbaeaa4c46df45d8347053c742d2ded3af9.png)

Since every value in the support of $X$ is at most $1$ and $x>1,$ every possible value of $X$ satisfies $X\le x.$ Similarly, every value in the support of $Y$ is at most $6$ and $y>6,$ so every possible value of $Y$ satisfies $Y\le y.$

Therefore, the region $Δ$ contains the entire joint support, and

$$
F(x,y)=P(X\le x,Y\le y)=1.
$$"] ["question-5555465c-a779-5eab-9f3a-3128b4e5cfe0" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-c47eb18a-bfe5-5e49-bb9e-a97fe694f936" :answer-field/id #uuid $$

Note the following:

- We can think of each point where $f(x,y)\ne 0$ as a point mass in the plane, where the "probability mass" at each point equals the probability associated with that point.

- The joint CDF $F(x,y)=P(X\le x,Y\le y)$ is the total "probability mass" that lies in the infinite rectangular region that has its top-right corner at $(x,y)$ and whose sides are parallel to the coordinate axis.

Given the supports of $X$ and $Y,$ the joint support $S$ is a subset of

$$
{S}_{X}\times {S}_{Y}=\{2,3,4\}\times \{2,3,4\}.
$$

Let's sketch the points in ${S}_{X}\times {S}_{Y},$ which contains the joint support. Let's also consider a point $(x,y)$ where $2<x<4$ and $y<2,$ and a region $Δ$ that lies below and to the left of this point.

:question/problem "Suppose $X$ and $Y$ are discrete random variables. Let the joint CDF of $X$ and $Y$ be $F(x,y),$ where

$$
F(1,1)=0.6,\,F(1,0)=0.5,\,F(1,-1)=0.2,
$$

and the supports of $X$ and $Y$, respectively, are

$$
{S}_{X}=\{-2,-1,0,1,2\},\,{S}_{Y}=\{-2,-1,0,1,2\}.
$$

Find $P(X\le 1,-1<Y\le 1).$"] ["question-af981bc5-9b24-55d4-b993-5b515801ef39" :question/worked-solution "Note the following:

- For a given joint PMF $f(x,y),$ we can think of each point where $f(x,y)\ne 0$ as a point mass in the plane, where the "probability mass" at each point equals the probability associated with that point.

- The joint CDF $F(x,y)=P(X\le x,Y\le y)$ is the total "probability mass" that lies in the infinite rectangular region that has its top-right corner at $(x,y)$ and whose sides are parallel to the coordinate axis.

Given the supports of $X$ and $Y,$ the joint support $S$ is a subset of

$$
{S}_{X}\times {S}_{Y}=\{-2,-1,0,1,2\}\times \{-2,-1,0,1,2\}.
$$

Let's sketch the points in ${S}_{X}\times {S}_{Y},$ which contains the joint support.

![](images/dd/dd49cc4b7cb5cc80bb325819c5c8f3c31f8bc3ed762139c2c3b9567a24db2324.png)

Let's sketch the region corresponding to the probability we wish to find.

![](images/34/344fec686907843b4b9375db138592f93be9d0232500fb35dceb90086db503cc.png)

Geometrically, this region can be obtained by taking all points in the infinite rectangle that has its top-right corner at $(1,1)$ (the blue region below) and *subtracting* all points in the infinite rectangle that has its top-right corner at $(1,-1)$ (the red region below).

![](images/6e/6e3a7389008d67f4096fdaa6a98c0e3e2bdeda64ec1e47b93a6d3ba66a54b18d.png)

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X\le 1,-1<Y\le 1) & =\overset{\text{top-right corner at }(1,1)}{\overset{⏞}{P(X\le 1,Y\le 1)}}-\overset{\text{top-right corner at }(1,-1)}{\overset{⏞}{P(X\le 1,Y\le -1)}} \\  & =F(1,1)-F(1,-1) \\  & =0.6-0.2 \\  & =0.4.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-af981bc5-9b24-55d4-b993-5b515801ef39" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-4f967f58-22eb-508f-8d10-16ff3515e346" :answer-field/id #uuid ["question-1374041d-2f69-55e3-9b42-ce863bb1bab0" :question/math-academy-id "q-146615"] ["question-1374041d-2f69-55e3-9b42-ce863bb1bab0" :question/problem "Suppose $X$ and $Y$ are discrete random variables. Let the joint CDF of $X$ and $Y$ be $F(x,y),$ where

$$
F(4,1)=0.77,\,F(4,-1)=0.15,\,F(1,1)=0.19,\,F(1,-1)=0.09,
$$

and the supports of $X$ and $Y$, respectively, are

$$
{S}_{X}=\{0,1,2,3,4,5\},\,{S}_{Y}=\{-2,-1,0,1,2\}.
$$

Find $P(1<X\le 4,-1<Y\le 1).$"] ["question-1374041d-2f69-55e3-9b42-ce863bb1bab0" :question/worked-solution "Note the following:

- For a given joint PMF $f(x,y),$ we can think of each point where $f(x,y)\ne 0$ as a point mass in the plane, where the "probability mass" at each point equals the probability associated with that point.

- The joint CDF $F(x,y)=P(X\le x,Y\le y)$ is the total "probability mass" that lies in the infinite rectangular region that has its top-right corner at $(x,y)$ and whose sides are parallel to the coordinate axis.

Given the supports of $X$ and $Y,$ the joint support $S$ is a subset of

$$
{S}_{X}\times {S}_{Y}=\{0,1,2,3,4,5\}\times \{-2,-1,0,1,2\}.
$$

Let's sketch the points in ${S}_{X}\times {S}_{Y},$ which contains the joint support.

![](images/01/01e04dfdac5f4abc16bd856dcfbe1b7361010cce2e7779658a33f293c1c52ae4.png)

Let's sketch the region corresponding to the probability we wish to find.

![](images/2d/2d2525118ca3b62c0829c0308fab168d0b806dfa13302c007a63cd354314d63f.png)

Geometrically, this region can be obtained as follows:

1\. Take the infinite rectangle that has its top-right corner at $(4,1).$

2\. Subtract the infinite rectangles that have their top-right corners at $(4,-1)$ and $(1,1).$

3\. Finally, we need to add back the infinite rectangle that has its top-right corner at $(1,-1).$ This is because we subtracted this region twice in step 2.

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}P(1<X\le 4,-1<Y\le 1) & =\overset{\text{top-right corner at }(4,1)}{\overset{⏞}{P(X\le 4,Y\le 1)}} \\  & \,-\overset{\text{top-right corner at }(4,-1)}{\overset{⏞}{P(X\le 4,Y\le -1)}}-\overset{\text{top-right corner at }(1,1)}{\overset{⏞}{P(X\le 1,Y\le 1)}} \\  & \,+\overset{\text{top-right corner at }(1,-1)}{\overset{⏞}{P(X\le 1,Y\le -1)}} \\  & =F(4,1)-F(4,-1)-F(1,1)+F(1,-1) \\  & =0.77-0.15-0.19+0.09 \\  & =0.52.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-1374041d-2f69-55e3-9b42-ce863bb1bab0" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-0973e0ae-8949-52fe-9d14-7a1a4925ba53" :answer-field/id #uuid Given the supports of $X$ and $Y,$ the joint support $S$ is a subset of

$$
{S}_{X}\times {S}_{Y}=\{2,4,6,8,10,12\}\times \{3,6,9,12\}.
$$

Let's sketch the points in ${S}_{X}\times {S}_{Y},$ which contains the joint support.

![](images/04/045903aeef84fbd38d09e97f203d9169f0c1f10b662e343b82fc8113dbd1ecc3.png)

$$

- The joint CDF $F(x,y)=P(X\le x,Y\le y)$ is the total "probability mass" that lies in the infinite rectangular region that has its top-right corner at $(x,y)$ and whose sides are parallel to the coordinate axis.

Given the supports of $X$ and $Y,$ the joint support $S$ is a subset of

$$
{S}_{X}\times {S}_{Y}=\{2,4,6\}\times \{0,1,2,3,4\}.
$$

Let's sketch the points in ${S}_{X}\times {S}_{Y},$ which contains the joint support.

![](images/2b/2b159f4ba1873270f42b7afd2fdc4b969672c7d3cb7e694d519ab82dab33b283.png)

![](images/eb/ebcfd8e0b553cab38a76eac77aab45186db92b3fe47a1fbb87a8623db4c29389.png)

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X\le 4,1<Y\le 3) & =\overset{\text{top-right corner at }(4,3)}{\overset{⏞}{P(X\le 4,Y\le 3)}}-\overset{\text{top-right corner at }(4,1)}{\overset{⏞}{P(X\le 4,Y\le 1)}} \\  & =F(4,3)-F(4,1) \\  & =0.8-0.3 \\  & =0.5.\end{aligned}

variables. Let the joint CDF of $X$ and $Y$ be $F(x,y),$ where

$$
F(12,6)=0.7,\,F(9,6)=0.5,\,F(6,6)=0.4,
$$

and the supports of $X$ and $Y$, respectively, are

$$
{S}_{X}=\{3,6,9,12\},\,{S}_{Y}=\{2,6,10\}.
$$

Find $P(X>6,Y\le 8).$"] ["question-01cad121-bd37-5572-936b-c4e7143fa3ed" :question/worked-solution "Note the following:

- For a given joint PMF $f(x,y),$ we can think of each point where $f(x,y)\ne 0$ as a point mass in the plane, where the "probability mass" at each point equals the probability associated with that point.

- The joint CDF $F(x,y)=P(X\le x,Y\le y)$ is the total "probability mass" that lies in the infinite rectangular region that has its top-right corner at $(x,y)$ and whose sides are parallel to the coordinate axis.

Given the supports of $X$ and $Y,$ the joint support $S$ is a subset of

$$
{S}_{X}\times {S}_{Y}=\{3,6,9,12\}\times \{2,6,10\}.
$$

Let's plot the points in ${S}_{X}\times {S}_{Y},$ which contains the joint support, and sketch the region corresponding to the probability we wish to find.

![](images/00/0036b6bd64900e2c6a0319f16788b2d563a8415256e2f21ba561b1fb41afdf34.png)

Notice that this region encompasses the same possible support points as the infinite rectangle with its top-right corner at $(12,6)$ and top-left corner at $(6,6),$ where the top and right boundaries are included, and the left boundary is excluded.

![](images/43/4394f404e54b8e585becb601f688eece3d4769efe2a124cb53b11d3432a9996b.png)

Geometrically, this region can be obtained by taking all points in the infinite rectangle that has its top-right corner at $(12,6)$ (the blue region below) and *subtracting* all points in the infinite rectangle that has its top-right corner at $(6,6)$ (the red region below).

![](images/5e/5ed86031d5762e3a2fe440fba52775fc6833243664fa18ee85c3449b50ff6cee.png)

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X>6,Y\le 8) & =\overset{\text{top-right corner at }(12,6)}{\overset{⏞}{P(X\le 12,Y\le 6)}}-\overset{\text{top-right corner at }(6,6)}{\overset{⏞}{P(X\le 6,Y\le 6)}} \\  & =F(12,6)-F(6,6) \\  & =0.7-0.4 \\  & =0.3.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-01cad121-bd37-5572-936b-c4e7143fa3ed" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-c7ab1ae6-237e-56d8-8f03-0612304e4446" :answer-field/id #uuid Given the supports of $X$ and $Y,$ the joint support $S$ is a subset of

$$
{S}_{X}\times {S}_{Y}=\{1,2,3,4,5\}\times \{-2,-1,0,1,2\}.
$$

Let's plot the points in ${S}_{X}\times {S}_{Y},$ which contains the joint support, and sketch the region corresponding to the probability we wish to find.

![](images/1c/1c28f3e2f820511a30aa64ccd3affacaa6d72e69da9c596827429b244bf1129a.png)

Geometrically, this region can be obtained by taking all points in the infinite rectangle that has its top-right corner at $(5,1)$ (the blue region below) and *subtracting* all points in the infinite rectangle that has its top-right corner at $(3,1)$ (the red region below).

![](images/ae/ae993ae6e8c0d71a42ca0e11ed5b30a8d762b3fab12771247eca262f0131c4f5.png)

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X>3,Y<2) & =\overset{\text{top-right corner at }(5,1)}{\overset{⏞}{P(X\le 5,Y\le 1)}}-\overset{\text{top-right corner at }(3,1)}{\overset{⏞}{P(X\le 3,Y\le 1)}} \\  & =F(5,1)-F(3,1) \\  & =0.67-0.43 \\  & =0.24.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-fd922824-164f-5af2-954c-b939958ff429" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-7b5302b1-965f-57a3-8e52-58216fd37b2b" :answer-field/id #uuid ["question-9ab8b5f0-f462-5316-91ff-26b04644c742" :question/math-academy-id "q-146848"] ["question-9ab8b5f0-f462-5316-91ff-26b04644c742" :question/problem "Suppose $X$ and $Y$ are discrete random variables. Let the joint CDF of $X$ and $Y$ be $F(x,y),$ where

$$
F(10,9)=0.55,\,F(10,3)=0.15,\,F(4,9)=0.1,\,F(4,3)=0.05,
$$

and the supports of $X$ and $Y$, respectively, are

$$
{S}_{X}=\{2,4,6,8,10,12\},\,{S}_{Y}=\{3,6,9,12\}.
$$

Find $P(5<X<11,4<Y<10).$"] ["question-9ab8b5f0-f462-5316-91ff-26b04644c742" :question/worked-solution "Note the following:

- For a given joint PMF $f(x,y),$ we can think of each point where $f(x,y)\ne 0$ as a point mass in the plane, where the "probability mass" at each point equals the probability associated with that point.

- The joint CDF $F(x,y)=P(X\le x,Y\le y)$ is the total "probability mass" that lies in the infinite rectangular region that has its top-right corner at $(x,y)$ and whose sides are parallel to the coordinate axis.

Given the supports of $X$ and $Y,$ the joint support $S$ is a subset of

$$
{S}_{X}\times {S}_{Y}=\{2,4,6,8,10,12\}\times \{3,6,9,12\}.
$$

Let's plot the points in ${S}_{X}\times {S}_{Y},$ which contains the joint support, and sketch the region corresponding to the probability we wish to find.

![](images/f4/f43c5ae8d27872c4aebe235c507600b7bf1806e22b52dd3b3ff2261509ac9925.png)

Notice that this region encompasses the same possible support points as the rectangular region with its top-right corner at $(10,9)$ and bottom-left corner at $(4,3)$ below, where the top and right boundaries are inclusive and the bottom and left boundaries are exclusive.

![](images/60/60bf5a958b682d513010c3eff9a8084072be62e286c0b0dfacb09960a3283e38.png)

Geometrically, this region can be obtained as follows:

1\. Take the infinite rectangle that has its top-right corner at $(10,9).$

2\. Subtract the infinite rectangles that have their top-right corners at $(10,3)$ and $(4,9).$

3\. Finally, we need to add back the infinite rectangle that has its top-right corner at $(4,3).$ This is because we subtracted this region twice in step 2.

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}P(5<X<11,4<Y<10) & =\overset{\text{top-right corner at }(10,9)}{\overset{⏞}{P(X\le 10,Y\le 9)}} \\  & \,-\overset{\text{top-right corner at }(10,3)}{\overset{⏞}{P(X\le 10,Y\le 3)}}-\overset{\text{top-right corner at }(4,9)}{\overset{⏞}{P(X\le 4,Y\le 9)}} \\  & \,+\overset{\text{top-right corner at }(4,3)}{\overset{⏞}{P(X\le 4,Y\le 3)}} \\  & =F(10,9)-F(10,3)-F(4,9)+F(4,3) \\  & =0.55-0.15-0.1+0.05 \\  & =0.35.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-9ab8b5f0-f462-5316-91ff-26b04644c742" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard] ["answer-field-23fa940f-fe5f-5cda-bceb-aaf37edf3942" :answer-field/id #uuid Geometrically, this region can be obtained as follows:

1\. Take the infinite rectangle that has its top-right corner at $(1,1).$

2\. Subtract the infinite rectangles that have their top-right corners at $(1,-2)$ and $(-2,1).$

3\. Finally, we need to add back the infinite rectangle that has its top-right corner at $(-2,-2).$ This is because we subtracted this region twice in step 2.

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}P(-1.5\le X\le 1.5,-1.5\le Y\le 1.5) & =\overset{\text{top-right corner at }(1,1)}{\overset{⏞}{P(X\le 1,Y\le 1)}} \\  & \,-\overset{\text{top-right corner at }(1,-2)}{\overset{⏞}{P(X\le 1,Y\le -2)}}-\overset{\text{top-right corner at }(-2,1)}{\overset{⏞}{P(X\le -2,Y\le 1)}} \\  & \,+\overset{\text{top-right corner at }(-2,-2)}{\overset{⏞}{P(X\le -2,Y\le -2)}} \\  & =F(1,1)-F(1,-2)-F(-2,1)+F(-2,-2) \\  & =0.7-0.3-0.4+0.1 \\  & =0.1.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-d10653a4-2ac5-5be4-9b7e-7dbc6ddafa84" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard] ["answer-field-04cedd67-eefd-5664-9e79-71d0a4cd5a23" :answer-field/id #uuid ["question-8dece31e-c114-5d98-b9c8-904ef5ba8d5d" :question/math-academy-id "q-146851"] ["question-8dece31e-c114-5d98-b9c8-904ef5ba8d5d" :question/problem "Suppose $X$ and $Y$ are discrete random variables. Let the joint CDF of $X$ and $Y$ be $F(x,y),$ where

$$
F(5,3)=0.6,\,F(5,1)=0.23,\,F(2,3)=0.32,\,F(2,1)=0.05,
$$

and the supports of $X$ and $Y$, respectively, are

$$
{S}_{X}=\{1,2,3,4,5,6\},\,{S}_{Y}=\{1,2,3,4\}.
$$

Find $P(2<X\le 5,2\le Y<4).$"] ["question-8dece31e-c114-5d98-b9c8-904ef5ba8d5d" :question/worked-solution "Note the following:

- For a given joint PMF $f(x,y),$ we can think of each point where $f(x,y)\ne 0$ as a point mass in the plane, where the "probability mass" at each point equals the probability associated with that point.

- The joint CDF $F(x,y)=P(X\le x,Y\le y)$ is the total "probability mass" that lies in the infinite rectangular region that has its top-right corner at $(x,y)$ and whose sides are parallel to the coordinate axis.

Given the supports of $X$ and $Y,$ the joint support $S$ is a subset of

$$
{S}_{X}\times {S}_{Y}=\{1,2,3,4,5,6\}\times \{1,2,3,4\}.
$$

Let's plot the points in ${S}_{X}\times {S}_{Y},$ which contains the joint support, and sketch the region corresponding to the probability we wish to find.

![](images/2d/2dd2929b39c9d0357516ebea9f1f31ed2b5f64c6154184ec904996c51162c144.png)

Notice that this region encompasses the same possible support points as the rectangular region with its top-right corner at $(5,3)$ and bottom-left corner at $(2,1)$ below, where the top and right boundaries are inclusive and the bottom and left boundaries are exclusive.

![](images/db/db601c0b0d2931a61d2218e196ea7485fc8d258cb77c604dc44661687de43beb.png)

Geometrically, this region can be obtained as follows:

1\. Take the infinite rectangle that has its top-right corner at $(5,3).$

2\. Subtract the infinite rectangles that have their top-right corners at $(5,1)$ and $(2,3).$

3\. Finally, we need to add back the infinite rectangle that has its top-right corner at $(2,1).$ This is because we subtracted this region twice in step 2.

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}P(2<X\le 5,2\le Y<4) & =\overset{\text{top-right corner at }(5,3)}{\overset{⏞}{P(X\le 5,Y\le 3)}} \\  & \,-\overset{\text{top-right corner at }(5,1)}{\overset{⏞}{P(X\le 5,Y\le 1)}}-\overset{\text{top-right corner at }(2,3)}{\overset{⏞}{P(X\le 2,Y\le 3)}} \\  & \,+\overset{\text{top-right corner at }(2,1)}{\overset{⏞}{P(X\le 2,Y\le 1)}} \\  & =F(5,3)-F(5,1)-F(2,3)+F(2,1) \\  & =0.6-0.23-0.32+0.05 \\  & =0.1.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-8dece31e-c114-5d98-b9c8-904ef5ba8d5d" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard] ["answer-field-ad0272b4-dd5a-544a-a7d4-a49f4c49e16a" :answer-field/id #uuid "question-8dece31e-c114-5d98-b9c8-904ef5ba8d5d"] [17592186163341 :tutorial/content "The **joint cumulative distribution function** (or joint CDF) of two discrete random variables $X,$ and $Y$ is defined as

$$
F(x,y) = P( X \leq x, Y \leq y)  = \sum\limits_{x_i \leq x} \sum\limits_{y_i \leq y} f(x_i, y_i).
$$

The sets $S_X$ and $S_Y,$ on which the variables $X$ and $Y$ are defined, are the **supports** of $X$ and $Y,$ respectively.

We can see from this definition that the joint CDF is analogous to the cumulative distribution function of a single random variable.

Consider the joint PMF for the discrete random variables $X$ and $Y,$ shown below.

| $f$ | $Y=0$ | $Y=1$ | $Y=2$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $X=0$ | $0.1$ | $0.2$ | $0.1$ |
| $X=1$ | $0.3$ | $0.2$ | $0.1$ |

Here, the supports of $X$ and $Y$ are $S_X = \{ 0, 1 \}$ and $S_Y = \{ 0, 1, 2 \},$ respectively. 

As an example, let's compute $F(1,1).$ By definition, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F(1,1) & =P(X\le 1,Y\le 1).\end{aligned}
$$

We start by highlighting all cells in the table that correspond to $X \leq 1, Y \leq 1.$

| $f$ | $Y=0$ | $Y=1$ | $Y=2$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $X=0$ | $0.1$ | $0.2$ | $0.1$ |
| $X=1$ | $0.3$ | $0.2$ | $0.1$ |

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(1,1) & =f(0,0)+f(0,1)+f(1,0)+f(1,1) \\  & =0.1+0.2+0.3+0.2 \\  & =0.8.\end{aligned}
$$"] [17592186163360 :tutorial/content "Consider the joint PMF for the discrete random variables $X$ and $Y,$ shown below.

| $f$ | $Y=0$ | $Y=1$ | $Y=2$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $X=1$ | $0.1$ | $0.2$ | $0.1$ |
| $X=2$ | $0.3$ | $0.2$ | $0.1$ |

We can think of each point where $f(x,y)\neq 0$ as a point mass in the plane, where the "probability mass" at each point equals the probability associated with that point.

![](images/c6/c6d8e4012a0a16f865bf229549512ff772e103d3fcd7667738cf7250d7267e84.png)

 

Now, the joint CDF is given by

$$
F(x,y) = \sum\limits_{x_i \leq x} \sum\limits_{y_i \leq y} f(x_i, y_i).
$$

Geometrically, then, the joint CDF gives the total "probability mass" that lies inside the infinite rectangular region that has its top-right corner at $(x,y)$ and whose sides are parallel to the coordinate axes.

For example, consider the point $(2,1.5)$ and the infinite rectangular region that has its top-right corner at this point, shown below.

![](images/46/46837da3e8f8f44831da4e6b464e9f8562f322b17f584df3fc87912d1c09d4c4.png)

The value of $F(2,1.5)$ equals the total "probability mass" contained within this rectangle. That is,

$$
F(2,1.5) = f(1,0) + f(2,0) + f(1,1) + f(2,1).
$$

It's worth highlighting a few important cases:

- If our rectangular region doesn't include any points where the probability is nonzero, then we must have $F(x,y) = 0.$

![](images/bb/bb5faa2b42c9ece2fe80cff4dd27a8b720cb363f5319c3cb5f5dd065f818c403.png)

- If our rectangular region includes *all* points where the probability is nonzero, then we must have $F(x,y) = 1.$

![](images/81/811b15e3cea46e0a4a546e68217a2994a7b2a7b80d6bc444bc6fbaa2ebaed355.png)

Finally, we note the following properties of the joint CDF:

- $0 \leq F(x,y) \leq 1$

- The marginal CDF of $X$ is given by $F_X(x) = F(x, \infty).$

- The marginal CDF of $Y$ is given by $F_Y(y) = F( \infty, y).$

- $F(\infty, \infty) = 1$

- $F(-\infty,y) = F(x, -\infty) = 0$

- If $X$ and $Y$ are independent random variables, then $F(x,y) = F_X(x) \cdot F_Y(y).$"] [17592186162165 :activity/expected-seconds 900.0] [17592186063984 :question/problem "Simplify $-3t^3\left(3t^2+2t\right).$"] [17592186063984 :question/worked-solution "We multiply each term inside the parentheses by the term outside the parentheses, simplify using the rules of exponents, and then we add the results together:

"question-656e0655-2fab-5e41-bca0-28f4bd148f34"] [17592186120530 :question/problem "Let ${v}_{1},{v}_{2},{v}_{3}$ be linearly independent vectors, and suppose that the vector $w$ can be written as a linear combination of ${v}_{1},{v}_{2},{v}_{3}.$ Which of the following statements are true?

I. ${v}_{1},{v}_{2},{v}_{3}$ form a basis of $\text{Span}\{{v}_{1},{v}_{2},{v}_{3}\}$

II. $\text{dim}(\text{Span}\{{v}_{1},{v}_{2},{v}_{3}\})=3$

III. $\text{dim}(\text{Span}\{{v}_{1},{v}_{2},{v}_{3},w\})=4$"] [17592186120530 :question/worked-solution "Recall that a basis of a vector space $V$ is a set of linearly independent vectors that span $V.$ The dimension of $V$ is the number of vectors in any basis of $V$ (if such a basis exists). 

With that in mind, let's consider each of the statements.

- Statement I is true. Indeed, $\text{Span}\{{v}_{1},{v}_{2},{v}_{3}\}$ is spanned by ${v}_{1},{v}_{2},{v}_{3}$, and we are told that ${v}_{1},{v}_{2},{v}_{3}$ are linearly independent vectors. So, ${v}_{1},{v}_{2},{v}_{3}$ is a basis of the span.

- Statement II is true. Since ${v}_{1},{v}_{2},{v}_{3}$ is a basis of the given span and this basis contains $3$ vectors, we have $\text{dim}(\text{Span}\{{v}_{1},{v}_{2},{v}_{3}\})=3.$

- Statement III is false. We are told that $w$ can be written as a linear combination of ${v}_{1},{v}_{2},{v}_{3}.$ This means that $\text{Span}\{{v}_{1},{v}_{2},{v}_{3},w\}$ is completely spanned by the vectors ${v}_{1},{v}_{2},{v}_{3}$ only. So, $\text{dim}(\text{Span}\{{v}_{1},{v}_{2},{v}_{3},w\})=3$ (not $4$).

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and II only.""] [17592186120530 :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] [17592186119294 :answer-field/correct 17592186119295] [17592186198235 :question/worked-solution "Let's define a transformation $\mathbf{T}$ as follows:

![](images/e9/e9a07b75be73621bb23edb6f4da67999c5f5ce07b8776f549cf12464e74fa702.svg)

This transformation maps some region $\Delta$ in the $uv$-plane to our region $D$ in the $xy$-plane.

To compute the required integral, we can use the change of variables formula

$$
\iint\limits_{D} f(x,y) \, \mathrm d x \, \mathrm d y = \iint\limits_{\Delta} \ f(x(u,v), y(u,v))  \left| \dfrac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (u, v)} \right|  \mathrm d u \, \mathrm d v
$$

where $\dfrac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (u, v)}$ is the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $\mathbf{T}.$

Note that the change of variables

$$
u = 4x + 2y, \qquad v = y - x
$$

 

gives us the *inverse* function $\mathbf T^{-1},$ that is

![](images/a1/a1228e77194b92d8b2c527845273ae9f70d9b90d4c3091f5ed9dd9f8c430776c.svg)

To compute the required integral, we proceed as follows:

**Step 1**: Find $\Delta,$ which is the image of $D$ under the action of $\mathbf{T}^{-1}.$ 

Our domain in the $uv$-plane is

$$
\begin{aligned}Δ & =\{(u,v)\,:\,-2\le u\le 2,\,0\le v\le 3\}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $\mathbf T^{-1}.$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to $\mathbf T^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}4 & 2 \\ -1 & \text{ }\text{ }1\end{aligned}| \\  & =6.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $\mathbf T.$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to $\mathbf T$ is

$$
\dfrac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (u, v)} = \left( \dfrac{\partial (u, v)}{\partial (x, y)} \right)^{-1} = \dfrac{1}{6}.
$$

Note that $\dfrac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (u, v)} \neq 0$ everywhere inside $\Delta.$ In other words, $\mathbf T$ has no critical points inside $\Delta.$

**Step 4**: Perform the change of variables.

In this case, we first need to solve the transformation equations

$$
u = 4x+2y, \qquad v = y-x
$$

 
for $x$ and $y$, which gives

$$
x = \dfrac{u-2v}6, \qquad y =\dfrac{u+4v}6.
$$

 

Performing the change of variables, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3(x+y))\,dx\,dy & ={∬}_{Δ}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3(\frac{u-2v}{6}+\frac{u+4v}{6}))|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\text{d}u\,\text{d}v \\  & ={∬}_{Δ}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3(\frac{2u+2v}{6}))|\frac{1}{6}|\text{d}u\,\text{d}v \\  & =\frac{1}{6}{\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{-2}^{2}sin\,(u+v)\,du\,dv.\end{aligned}
$$"] [17592186198015 :question/worked-solution "Let's define a transformation $\mathbf{T}$ as follows:

$$

$$"] [17592186198016 :question/worked-solution "Let's define a transformation $\mathbf{T}$ as follows:

\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}(2x+y){y}^{2}\,\text{d}x\text{d}y & ={∬}_{Δ}u{v}^{2}\,|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & ={∬}_{Δ}u{v}^{2}\,|\frac{1}{2}|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{3}^{5}u{v}^{2}\,\text{d}u\,\text{d}v \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{3}{v}^{2}\,\text{d}v{\int }_{3}^{5}u\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot {[\frac{1}{3}{v}^{3}]}_{0}^{3}\cdot {[\frac{1}{2}{u}^{2}]}_{3}^{5}\,\text{d}v \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 9\cdot 8 \\  & =36.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-d52198ba-3323-5776-a083-de931434cfe0" :question/id #uuid "d52198ba-3323-5776-a083-de931434cfe0"] ["question-d52198ba-3323-5776-a083-de931434cfe0" :question/math-academy-id "q-82798"] ["question-d52198ba-3323-5776-a083-de931434cfe0" :question/problem "Consider the region $D$ in the $xy$-plane, given by

$$
D=\{(x,y)\,:\,1\le 2y-x\le 2,\,0\le y-x\le 1\}.
$$

By performing the change of variables $u=2y-x$ and $v=y-x,$ the integral

$$
{∬}_{D}{x}^{2}\,dx\,dy
$$

can be written in terms of $u$ and $v$ as"] ["question-d52198ba-3323-5776-a083-de931434cfe0" :question/worked-solution "Let's define a transformation $T$ as follows:

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{aligned}]
$$

This transformation maps some region $Δ$ in the $uv$-plane to our region $D$ in the $xy$-plane.

To compute the required integral, we can use the change of variables formula

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dx\,dy={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(x(u,v),y(u,v))|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|du\,dv
$$

where $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}$ is the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T.$

Note that the change of variables

$$
u=2y-x,\,v=y-x
$$

 

gives us the *inverse* function ${T}^{-1},$ that is

$$
{T}^{-1}:[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}u(x,y) \\ v(x,y)\end{aligned}].
$$

To compute the required integral, we proceed as follows:

**Step 1**: Find $Δ,$ which is the image of $D$ under the action of ${T}^{-1}.$ 

Our domain in the $uv$-plane is

$$
\begin{aligned}Δ & =\{(u,v)\,:\,1\le u\le 2,\,0\le v\le 1\}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}-1 & 2 \\ -1 & \text{ }\text{ }1\end{aligned}| \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T$ is

$$
\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}={(\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)})}^{-1}=1.
$$

Note that $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}\ne 0$ everywhere inside $Δ.$ In other words, $T$ has no critical points inside $Δ.$

**Step 4**: Perform the change of variables:

In this case, we first need to solve the transformation equations

$$
u=2y-x,\,v=y-x
$$

 
for $x$ and $y$, which gives

$$
x=u-2v,\,y=u-v.
$$

 

Performing the change of variables, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}{x}^{2}\,dx\,dy & ={∬}_{Δ}{(u-2v)}^{2}|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\text{d}u\,\text{d}v \\  & ={∬}_{Δ}{(u-2v)}^{2}\cdot 1\,\text{d}u\,\text{d}v \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{1}^{2}{(u-2v)}^{2}\text{d}u\,\text{d}v.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-d52198ba-3323-5776-a083-de931434cfe0" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-912cb459-ddba-5110-ba83-e5c7cb9c0fab" :answer-field/id #uuid given by

$$
D=\{(x,y)\,:\,-1\le x\le 0,\,\,1-(x+1)^{2}\le y\le 2-(x+1)^{2}\}.
$$

By performing the change of variables $u=x+1$ and $v=y+(x+1)^{2},$ the integral

$$
{∬}_{D}(x-y+1)\,dx\,dy
$$

can be written in terms of $u$ and $v$ as"] ["question-e0897fe5-68e3-5373-b337-c33b7a65cd54" :question/worked-solution "Let's define a transformation $T$ as follows:

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{aligned}]
$$

This transformation maps some region $Δ$ in the $uv$-plane to our region $D$ in the $xy$-plane.

To compute the required integral, we can use the change of variables formula

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,dx\,dy={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(x(u,v),y(u,v))|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|du\,dv
$$

where $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}$ is the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T.$

Note that the change of variables

$$
u=x+1,\,v=y+(x+1)^{2}
$$

 

gives us the *inverse* function ${T}^{-1},$ that is

$$
{T}^{-1}:[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}u(x,y) \\ v(x,y)\end{aligned}].
$$

To compute the required integral, we proceed as follows::

**Step 1**: Find $Δ,$ which is the image of $D$ under the action of ${T}^{-1}.$ 

Our domain in the $uv$-plane is

$$
\begin{aligned}Δ & =\{(u,v)\,:\,0\le u\le 1,\,1\le v\le 2\}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 2(x+1) & \text{ }\text{ }1\end{aligned}| \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T$ is

$$
\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}={(\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)})}^{-1}=1.
$$

Note that $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}\ne 0$ everywhere inside $Δ.$ In other words, $T$ has no critical points inside $Δ.$

**Step 4**: Perform the change of variables:

In this case, we first need to solve the transformation equations

$$
u=x+1,\,v=y+(x+1)^{2}
$$

 
for $x$ and $y$, which gives

$$
x=u-1,\,y=v-{u}^{2}.
$$

 

Performing the change of variables, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}(x-y+1)\,dx\,dy & ={∬}_{Δ}[(u-1)-(v-{u}^{2})+1]|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\text{d}u\,\text{d}v \\  & ={∬}_{Δ}({u}^{2}+u-v)\,|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\text{d}u\,\text{d}v \\  & ={∬}_{Δ}({u}^{2}+u-v)\cdot |1|\text{d}u\,\text{d}v \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}({u}^{2}+u-v)\,\text{d}u\,\text{d}v.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-e0897fe5-68e3-5373-b337-c33b7a65cd54" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-8ab7f9c1-3d45-58a6-bbb6-a63febcef757" :answer-field/id #uuid $v={e}^{y},$ evaluate the double integral

$$
{∬}_{D}y\,dx\,dy,
$$

where $D=\{(x,y)\,:\,1\le {e}^{x}\le 2,\,1\le {e}^{y}\le 4\}.$"] ["question-5de90e63-3afe-527a-b599-3cdcd703aa52" :question/worked-solution "Let's define a transformation $T$ as follows:

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{aligned}]
$$

This transformation maps some region $Δ$ in the $uv$-plane to our region $D$ in the $xy$-plane.

To compute the required integral, we can use the change of variables formula

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,dx\,dy={∬}_{Δ}f(x(u,v),y(u,v))|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|du\,dv
$$

where $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}$ is the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T.$

Note that the change of variables

$$
u={e}^{x},\,v={e}^{y}
$$

 

gives us the *inverse* function ${T}^{-1},$ that is

$$
{T}^{-1}:[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}u(x,y) \\ v(x,y)\end{aligned}].
$$

To compute the required integral, we proceed as follows:

**Step 1**: Find $Δ,$ which is the image of $D$ under the action of ${T}^{-1}.$ 

Our domain in the $uv$-plane is

$$
\begin{aligned}Δ & =\{(u,v)\,:\,1\le u\le 2,\,1\le v\le 4\}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}{e}^{x} & 0 \\ 0 & \text{ }\text{ }{e}^{y}\end{aligned}| \\  & ={e}^{x+y}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T$ is

$$
\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}={(\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)})}^{-1}=\frac{1}{{e}^{x+y}}=\frac{1}{uv}.
$$

Note that $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}\ne 0$ everywhere inside $Δ.$ In other words, $T$ has no critical points inside $Δ.$

**Step 4**: Perform the change of variables:

Performing the change of variables, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}y\,dx\,dy & ={∬}_{Δ}\operatorname{ln}⁡v\,|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\text{d}u\,\text{d}v \\  & ={∬}_{Δ}\operatorname{ln}⁡v\cdot |\frac{1}{uv}|\,\text{d}u\,\text{d}v \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}\frac{1}{u}[{\int }_{1}^{4}\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡v}{v}\,dv]du \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}\frac{1}{u}{[\frac{{ln}^{2}⁡v}{2}]}_{1}^{4}du \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{1}^{2}\frac{1}{u}[{ln}^{2}⁡4-{ln}^{2}⁡1]\,du \\  & =\frac{{ln}^{2}⁡4}{2}{\int }_{1}^{2}\frac{1}{u}\,du \\  & =2{ln}^{2}⁡2[\operatorname{ln}⁡u]_{1}^{2} \\  & =2{ln}^{2}⁡2(\operatorname{ln}⁡2-\operatorname{ln}⁡1) \\  & =2{ln}^{3}⁡2.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-5de90e63-3afe-527a-b599-3cdcd703aa52" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-f081c215-96de-53ac-b301-926b90ac00ff" :answer-field/id #uuid ["question-ea750ce2-b7b3-5ba2-80fa-7d5a87470671" :question/math-academy-id "q-160850"] ["question-ea750ce2-b7b3-5ba2-80fa-7d5a87470671" :question/problem "Using the change of variables $u=x+y$ and $v=x-y,$ evaluate the double integral

$$
{∬}_{D}(x+y)(x-y)^{3/2}\,dx\,dy,
$$

where $D=\{(x,y)\,:\,1\le x+y\le 3,\,0\le x-y\le 1\}.$"] ["question-ea750ce2-b7b3-5ba2-80fa-7d5a87470671" :question/worked-solution "Let's define a transformation $T$ as follows:

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{aligned}]
$$

This transformation maps some region $Δ$ in the $uv$-plane to our region $D$ in the $xy$-plane.

To compute the required integral, we can use the change of variables formula

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,dx\,dy={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(x(u,v),y(u,v))|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|du\,dv
$$

where $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}$ is the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T.$

Note that the change of variables

$$
u=x+y,\,v=x-y
$$

 

gives us the *inverse* function ${T}^{-1},$ that is

$$
{T}^{-1}:[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}u(x,y) \\ v(x,y)\end{aligned}].
$$

To compute the required integral, we proceed as follows:

**Step 1**: Find $Δ,$ which is the image of $D$ under the action of ${T}^{-1}.$ 

Our domain in the $uv$-plane is

$$
\begin{aligned}Δ & =\{(u,v)\,:\,1\le u\le 3,\,0\le v\le 1\}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 1 & \text{ }\text{ }-1\end{aligned}| \\  & =-2.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T$ is

$$
\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}={(\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)})}^{-1}=-\frac{1}{2}.
$$

Note that $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}\ne 0$ everywhere inside $Δ.$ In other words, $T$ has no critical points inside $Δ.$

**Step 4**: Perform the change of variables:

Performing the change of variables, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}(x+y)(x-y)^{3/2}\,dx\,dy & ={∬}_{Δ}u{v}^{3/2}|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\text{d}u\,\text{d}v \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{1}^{3}u{v}^{3/2}|-\frac{1}{2}|du\,dv \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}{v}^{3/2}[{\int }_{1}^{3}u\,du]dv \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}{v}^{3/2}{[\frac{{u}^{2}}{2}]}_{1}^{3}\,dv \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}{v}^{3/2}[\frac{9}{2}-\frac{1}{2}]dv \\  & =2{\int }_{0}^{1}{v}^{3/2}\,dv \\  & =2{[\frac{2}{5}\,{v}^{5/2}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{4}{5}[1-0] \\  & =\frac{4}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-ea750ce2-b7b3-5ba2-80fa-7d5a87470671" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-6b345d81-65d6-5a3f-9150-c97ad1b7b016" :answer-field/id #uuid where $D=\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le x+y\le 2,\,2\le x-y\le 4\}.$"] ["question-fee52d9d-67c4-5104-9f57-4122f892110d" :question/worked-solution "Let's define a transformation $T$ as follows:

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{aligned}]
$$

This transformation maps some region $Δ$ in the $uv$-plane to our region $D$ in the $xy$-plane.

To compute the required integral, we can use the change of variables formula

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,dx\,dy={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(x(u,v),y(u,v))|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|du\,dv
$$

where $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}$ is the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T.$

Note that the change of variables

$$
u=x+y,\,v=x-y
$$

 

gives us the *inverse* function ${T}^{-1},$ that is

$$
{T}^{-1}:[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}u(x,y) \\ v(x,y)\end{aligned}].
$$

To compute the required integral, we proceed as follows:

**Step 1**: Find $Δ,$ which is the image of $D$ under the action of ${T}^{-1}.$ 

Our domain in the $uv$-plane is

$$
\begin{aligned}Δ & =\{(u,v)\,:\,0\le u\le 2,\,2\le v\le 4\}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 1 & \text{ }\text{ }-1\end{aligned}| \\  & =-2.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T$ is

$$
\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}={(\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)})}^{-1}=-\frac{1}{2}.
$$

Note that $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}\ne 0$ everywhere inside $Δ.$ In other words, $T$ has no critical points inside $Δ.$

**Step 4**: Perform the change of variables:

Performing the change of variables, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}({x}^{2}-{y}^{2})\,dx\,dy & ={∬}_{Δ}(x+y)(x-y)|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\text{d}u\,\text{d}v \\  & ={∬}_{Δ}uv\cdot |-\frac{1}{2}|\text{d}u\,\text{d}v \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{∬}_{Δ}uv\,\text{d}u\,\text{d}v \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{2}u[{\int }_{2}^{4}v\,dv]du \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{2}u{[\frac{{v}^{2}}{2}]}_{2}^{4}\,du \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{2}u(\frac{{4}^{2}}{2}-\frac{{2}^{2}}{2})\,du \\  & =3{\int }_{0}^{2}u\,du \\  & =3[\frac{{u}^{2}}{2}]_{0}^{2} \\  & =3\cdot 2 \\  & =6.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-fee52d9d-67c4-5104-9f57-4122f892110d" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-7505a4fd-3c5e-5a38-a1f7-3891a3c2965c" :answer-field/id #uuid ["question-f47eca8f-5f35-574c-b95e-5dc9a27cb04d" :question/math-academy-id "q-160916"] ["question-f47eca8f-5f35-574c-b95e-5dc9a27cb04d" :question/problem "Use a change of variables to evaluate the double integral 

$$
{∬}_{D}\operatorname{cos}⁡(y-x)\operatorname{sin}⁡(x+y)\,dxdy,
$$

where $D=\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le y-x\le \frac{\pi }{2},\,0\le x+y\le \pi \}.$"] ["question-f47eca8f-5f35-574c-b95e-5dc9a27cb04d" :question/worked-solution "Let's define a transformation $T$ as follows:

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{aligned}]
$$

This transformation maps some region $Δ$ in the $uv$-plane to our region $D$ in the $xy$-plane.

To compute the required integral, we can use the change of variables formula

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dxdy={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(x(u,v),y(u,v))\,|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\text{ }dudv
$$

where $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}$ is the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T.$

To compute the required integral, we proceed as follows:

**Step 1**: Find a suitable change of variables.

The inequalities that define the region $D,$

$$
0\le y-x\le \frac{\pi }{2},\,0\le x+y\le \pi ,
$$

suggest that we use the change of variables 

$$
u=y-x\,\text{and}\,v=x+y.
$$

This change of variables gives us the *inverse* function ${T}^{-1},$ that is

$$
{T}^{-1}:[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}u(x,y) \\ v(x,y)\end{aligned}].
$$

**Step 2**: Find $Δ,$ which is the image of $D$ under the action of ${T}^{-1}.$ 

Our domain in the $uv$-plane is

$$
\begin{aligned}Δ & =\{(u,v)\,:\,0\le u\le \frac{\pi }{2},\,0\le v\le \pi \}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 \\ \text{ }\text{ }\text{ }1 & 1\end{aligned}| \\  & =-2.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 4**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T:$

$$
\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}={(\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)})}^{-1}=-\frac{1}{2}
$$

Note that $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}\ne 0$ everywhere inside $Δ.$ In other words, $T$ has no critical points inside $Δ.$

**Step 5**: Perform the change of variables, and evaluate the integral:

Performing the change of variables, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\operatorname{cos}⁡(y-x)\operatorname{sin}⁡(x+y)\,\text{d}x\text{d}y & ={∬}_{Δ}\operatorname{cos}⁡u\operatorname{sin}⁡v\,|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & ={∬}_{Δ}\operatorname{cos}⁡u\operatorname{sin}⁡v|-\frac{1}{2}|\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{cos}⁡u[{\int }_{0}^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡v\,dv]du \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{cos}⁡u\cdot [-\operatorname{cos}⁡v]_{0}^{\pi }\,du \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{cos}⁡u\cdot 2\,du \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{cos}⁡u\,du \\  & =[\operatorname{sin}⁡u]_{0}^{\pi /2} \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-f47eca8f-5f35-574c-b95e-5dc9a27cb04d" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-ba1ace49-0ce8-5f3b-a500-296b7a164c42" :answer-field/id #uuid :question/problem "Use a change of variables to evaluate the double integral 

$$
{∬}_{D}\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡(y-2x)}{y-2x}\,dxdy,
$$

where $D=\{(x,y)\,:\,1\le y-2x\le 4,\,0\le y\le 2\}.$"] ["question-7fe6b99e-c147-51fb-b13e-2b0491dcfd3c" :question/worked-solution "Let's define a transformation $T$ as follows:

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{aligned}]
$$

This transformation maps some region $Δ$ in the $uv$-plane to our region $D$ in the $xy$-plane.

To compute the required integral, we can use the change of variables formula

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dxdy={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(x(u,v),y(u,v))\,|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\text{ }dudv
$$

where $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}$ is the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T.$

To compute the required integral, we proceed as follows:

**Step 1**: Find a suitable change of variables.

The inequalities that define the region $D,$

$$
1\le y-2x\le 4,\,0\le y\le 2,
$$

suggest that we use the change of variables 

$$
u=y-2x\,\text{and}\,v=y.
$$

This change of variables gives us the *inverse* function ${T}^{-1},$ that is

$$
{T}^{-1}:[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}u(x,y) \\ v(x,y)\end{aligned}].
$$

**Step 2**: Find $Δ,$ which is the image of $D$ under the action of ${T}^{-1}.$ 

Our domain in the $uv$-plane is

$$
\begin{aligned}Δ & =\{(u,v)\,:\,1\le u\le 4,\,0\le v\le 2\}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}-2 & \text{ }\text{ }1 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}| \\  & =-2.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 4**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T:$

$$
\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}={(\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)})}^{-1}=-\frac{1}{2}.
$$

Note that $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}\ne 0$ everywhere inside $Δ.$ In other words, $T$ has no critical points inside $Δ.$

**Step 5**: Perform the change of variables, and evaluate the integral:

Performing the change of variables, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡(y-2x)}{y-2x}\,\text{d}x\text{d}y & ={∬}_{Δ}\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡u}{u}\,|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & ={∬}_{Δ}\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡u}{u}\,|-\frac{1}{2}|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{2}[{\int }_{1}^{4}\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡u}{u}\,du]dv \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{2}{[\frac{{ln}^{2}⁡u}{2}]}_{1}^{4}dv \\  & =\frac{1}{4}{\int }_{0}^{2}({ln}^{2}⁡4-{ln}^{2}⁡1)\,dv \\  & =\frac{1}{4}{ln}^{2}⁡4{\int }_{0}^{2}dv \\  & =\frac{1}{4}(2\operatorname{ln}⁡2)^{2}\cdot [v]_{0}^{2} \\  & ={ln}^{2}⁡2\cdot (2-0) \\  & =2{ln}^{2}⁡2.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-7fe6b99e-c147-51fb-b13e-2b0491dcfd3c" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-a913f95c-4f3f-51d9-a609-d167776b85b5" :answer-field/id #uuid where $D=\{(x,y)\,:\,1\le x+y\le 3,\,0\le x-y\le 2\}.$"] ["question-ebe24ae4-1aba-5953-99d8-8533d35f69cf" :question/worked-solution "Let's define a transformation $T$ as follows:

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{aligned}]

where $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}$ is the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T.$

To compute the required integral, we proceed as follows:

**Step 1**: Find a suitable change of variables.

The inequalities that define the region $D,$

$$
1\le x+y\le 3,\,0\le x-y\le 2,
$$

suggest that we use the change of variables 

$$
u=x+y\,\text{and}\,v=x-y.
$$

This change of variables gives us the *inverse* function ${T}^{-1},$ that is

$$
{T}^{-1}:[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}u(x,y) \\ v(x,y)\end{aligned}].

**Step 2**: Find $Δ,$ which is the image of $D$ under the action of ${T}^{-1}.$ 

Our domain in the $uv$-plane is

**Step 3**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}1 & \text{ }\text{ }\text{ }1 \\ 1 & -1\end{aligned}| \\  & =-2.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 4**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T:$

$$
\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}={(\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)})}^{-1}=-\frac{1}{2}
$$

Note that $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}\ne 0$ everywhere inside $Δ.$ In other words, $T$ has no critical points inside $Δ.$

**Step 5**: Perform the change of variables, and evaluate the integral:

$$

where $D=\{(x,y)\,:\,|y-x|\le \frac{\pi }{2},\,0\le y\le \frac{\pi }{2}\}.$"] ["question-c8466ab0-fd66-5adb-8220-fa89c46bae69" :question/worked-solution "Let's define a transformation $T$ as follows:

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{aligned}]
$$

This transformation maps some region $Δ$ in the $uv$-plane to our region $D$ in the $xy$-plane.

To compute the required integral, we can use the change of variables formula

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dxdy={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(x(u,v),y(u,v))\,|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\text{ }dudv
$$

where $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}$ is the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T.$

To compute the required integral, we proceed as follows:

**Step 1**: Find a suitable change of variables.

The inequalities that define the region $D,$

$$
\frac{\pi }{2}\le y-x\le \frac{\pi }{2},\,0\le y\le \frac{\pi }{2},
$$

suggest that we use the change of variables 

$$
u=y-x\,\text{and}\,v=y.
$$

This change of variables gives us the *inverse* function ${T}^{-1},$ that is

$$
{T}^{-1}:[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}u(x,y) \\ v(x,y)\end{aligned}].
$$

**Step 2**: Find $Δ,$ which is the image of $D$ under the action of ${T}^{-1}.$ 

Our domain in the $uv$-plane is

$$
\begin{aligned}Δ & =\{(u,v)\,:\,-\frac{\pi }{2}\le u\le \frac{\pi }{2},\,0\le v\le \frac{\pi }{2}\}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}-1 & \text{ }\text{ }1 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}| \\  & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 4**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T:$

$$
\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}={(\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)})}^{-1}=-1.
$$

Note that $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}\ne 0$ everywhere inside $Δ.$ In other words, $T$ has no critical points inside $Δ.$

**Step 5**: Perform the change of variables, and evaluate the integral:

Performing the change of variables, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}y{cos}^{2}⁡(y-x)\,\text{d}x\text{d}y & ={∬}_{Δ}v{cos}^{2}⁡u\,|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & ={∬}_{Δ}v{cos}^{2}⁡u\cdot |-1|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}v[{\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}{cos}^{2}⁡u\,du]dv \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}v[{\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡2u+1)du]dv \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}v[\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡2u}{2}+u]_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}\,dv \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\pi v\,dv \\  & =\frac{\pi }{2}[\frac{{v}^{2}}{2}]_{0}^{\pi /2} \\  & =\frac{\pi }{2}\cdot \frac{{\pi }^{2}}{8} \\  & =\frac{{\pi }^{3}}{16}.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-c8466ab0-fd66-5adb-8220-fa89c46bae69" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-be68da14-ad39-5dd8-8b81-96f9bc5c3b1f" :answer-field/id #uuid where $D=\{(x,y)\,:\,1\le x\le 5,\,0\le x+2y\le 1\}.$"] [17592186199007 :question/worked-solution "Let's define a transformation $T$ as follows:

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{aligned}]
$$

This transformation maps some region $Δ$ in the $uv$-plane to our region $D$ in the $xy$-plane.

To compute the required integral, we can use the change of variables formula

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dxdy={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(x(u,v),y(u,v))\,|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\text{ }dudv
$$

where $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}$ is the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T.$

To compute the required integral, we proceed as follows:

**Step 1**: Find a suitable change of variables.

The inequalities that define the region $D,$

$$
1\le x\le 5,\,0\le x+2y\le 1,
$$

suggest that we use the change of variables 

$$
u=x\,\text{and}\,v=x+2y.
$$

This change of variables gives us the *inverse* function ${T}^{-1},$ that is

$$
{T}^{-1}:[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}u(x,y) \\ v(x,y)\end{aligned}].
$$

**Step 2**: Find $Δ,$ which is the image of $D$ under the action of ${T}^{-1}.$ 

Our domain in the $uv$-plane is

$$
\begin{aligned}Δ & =\{(u,v)\,:\,1\le u\le 5,\,0\le v\le 1\}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}1 & \text{ }\text{ }0 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}| \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 4**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T:$

$$
\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}={(\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)})}^{-1}=\frac{1}{2}.
$$

Note that $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}\ne 0$ everywhere inside $Δ.$ In other words, $T$ has no critical points inside $Δ.$

**Step 5**: Perform the change of variables, and evaluate the integral:

Performing the change of variables, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}(x+2y){e}^{(x+2y)^{2}}\,\text{d}x\text{d}y & ={∬}_{Δ}v{e}^{{v}^{2}}\,|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & ={∬}_{Δ}v{e}^{{v}^{2}}\,|\frac{1}{2}|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{1}^{5}[{\int }_{0}^{1}v{e}^{{v}^{2}}\,dv]du \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{1}^{5}{[\frac{{e}^{{v}^{2}}}{2}]}_{0}^{1}du \\  & =\frac{1}{4}{\int }_{1}^{5}(e-1)\,du \\  & =\frac{1}{4}(e-1)[u]_{1}^{5} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}(e-1)(5-1) \\  & =e-1.\end{aligned}
$$"] [17592186199007 :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-a5e7b49a-7376-5f77-b4cd-07e49c94ad93" :answer/id #uuid "a5e7b49a-7376-5f77-b4cd-07e49c94ad93"] ["answer-a5e7b49a-7376-5f77-b4cd-07e49c94ad93" :answer/type :answer.type/math] ["answer-a5e7b49a-7376-5f77-b4cd-07e49c94ad93" :answer/value "\frac{e-2}{2}"] ["answer-69ed5ffb-e837-50a7-83fa-9b0d9378cfad" :answer/id #uuid "69ed5ffb-e837-50a7-83fa-9b0d9378cfad"] ["answer-69ed5ffb-e837-50a7-83fa-9b0d9378cfad" :answer/type :answer.type/math] ["answer-69ed5ffb-e837-50a7-83fa-9b0d9378cfad" :answer/value "\frac{{e}^{2}-e}{4}"] ["answer-4cfe915e-292f-5afc-a987-feaf8645491b" :answer/id #uuid "4cfe915e-292f-5afc-a987-feaf8645491b"] ["answer-4cfe915e-292f-5afc-a987-feaf8645491b" :answer/type :answer.type/math] ["answer-4cfe915e-292f-5afc-a987-feaf8645491b" :answer/value "e-1"] ["answer-50bbbf00-20cb-560c-a0ab-ee8b2c1c6005" :answer/id #uuid "50bbbf00-20cb-560c-a0ab-ee8b2c1c6005"] ["answer-50bbbf00-20cb-560c-a0ab-ee8b2c1c6005" :answer/type :answer.type/math] ["answer-50bbbf00-20cb-560c-a0ab-ee8b2c1c6005" :answer/value "{e}^{2}-1"] [17592186197912 :answer-field/correct "answer-4cfe915e-292f-5afc-a987-feaf8645491b"] [17592186197912 :answer-field/choices "answer-a5e7b49a-7376-5f77-b4cd-07e49c94ad93"] [17592186197912 :answer-field/choices "answer-69ed5ffb-e837-50a7-83fa-9b0d9378cfad"] [17592186197912 :answer-field/choices "answer-4cfe915e-292f-5afc-a987-feaf8645491b"] [17592186197912 :answer-field/choices "answer-50bbbf00-20cb-560c-a0ab-ee8b2c1c6005"] ["question-d3e35845-58c1-5603-a038-b92edbbc2e02" :question/id #uuid "d3e35845-58c1-5603-a038-b92edbbc2e02"] ["question-d3e35845-58c1-5603-a038-b92edbbc2e02" :question/math-academy-id "q-160906"] ["question-d3e35845-58c1-5603-a038-b92edbbc2e02" :question/problem "Use a change of variables to evaluate the double integral 

$$
{∬}_{D}2x\operatorname{cos}⁡(x+2y)\,dxdy,
$$

where $D$ is the quadrilateral region with vertices $(1,-\frac{1}{2}),$ $(\frac{3}{2},-\frac{3}{4}),$ $(\frac{3}{2},\frac{\pi -3}{4}),$ and $(1,\frac{\pi -2}{4}).$"] ["question-d3e35845-58c1-5603-a038-b92edbbc2e02" :question/worked-solution "Let's define a transformation $T$ as follows:

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{aligned}]
$$

This transformation maps some region $Δ$ in the $uv$-plane to our region $D$ in the $xy$-plane.

To compute the required integral, we can use the change of variables formula

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dxdy={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(x(u,v),y(u,v))\,|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\text{ }dudv
$$

where $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}$ is the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T.$

To compute the required integral, we proceed as follows:

**Step 1**: Find a suitable change of variables.

The integrand

$$
f(x,y)=2x\operatorname{cos}⁡(x+2y)
$$

suggests that we use the change of variables 

$$
u=2x,\,v=x+2y.
$$

This change of variables gives us the *inverse* function ${T}^{-1},$ that is

$$
{T}^{-1}:[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}u(x,y) \\ v(x,y)\end{aligned}].
$$

**Step 2**: Find $Δ,$ which is the image of $D$ under the action of ${T}^{-1}.$ 

The vertices of our domain $Δ$ in the $uv$-plane are as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{T}^{-1}(1,-\frac{1}{2}) & =(2\cdot 1,1+2(-\frac{1}{2})) \\  & =(2,0) \\ {T}^{-1}(\frac{3}{2},-\frac{3}{4}) & =(2\cdot \frac{3}{2},\frac{3}{2}+2(-\frac{3}{4})) \\  & =(3,0) \\ {T}^{-1}(\frac{3}{2},\frac{\pi -3}{4}) & =(2\cdot \frac{3}{2},\frac{3}{2}+2(\frac{\pi -3}{4})) \\  & =(3,\frac{\pi }{2}) \\ {T}^{-1}(1,\frac{\pi -2}{4}) & =(2\cdot 1,1+2(\frac{\pi -2}{4})) \\  & =(2,\frac{\pi }{2})\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our domain in the $uv$-plane is the following rectangle:

$$
Δ=\{(u,v)\,:\,2\le u\le 3,\,0\le v\le \frac{\pi }{2}\}
$$

![](images/dd/dd628fd99b4684d79e8c3b0f4e6696f72582abaef18eef729f5611711a2e42ec.png)

**Step 3**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}| \\  & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 4**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T:$

$$
\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}={(\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)})}^{-1}=\frac{1}{4}
$$

Note that $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}\ne 0$ everywhere inside $Δ.$ In other words, $T$ has no critical points inside $Δ.$

**Step 5**: Perform the change of variables, and evaluate the integral:

Performing the change of variables, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}2x\operatorname{cos}⁡(x+2y)\,\text{d}x\text{d}y & ={∬}_{Δ}u\operatorname{cos}⁡v\,|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & ={∬}_{Δ}u\operatorname{cos}⁡v\,|\frac{1}{4}|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & =\frac{1}{4}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{2}^{3}u\operatorname{cos}⁡v\,\text{d}u\,\text{d}v \\  & =\frac{1}{4}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{cos}⁡v\,\text{d}v{\int }_{2}^{3}u\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\cdot [\operatorname{sin}⁡v]_{0}^{\pi /2}\cdot {[\frac{1}{2}{u}^{2}]}_{2}^{3}\,\text{d}v \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\cdot 1\cdot \frac{5}{2} \\  & =\frac{5}{8}.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-d3e35845-58c1-5603-a038-b92edbbc2e02" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard] ["answer-field-848b178b-00cd-5964-8724-b50b402d0b68" :answer-field/id #uuid :question/id #uuid "b878a44e-123c-5f2f-a474-6dc1888b9c72"] ["question-b878a44e-123c-5f2f-a474-6dc1888b9c72" :question/math-academy-id "q-160938"] ["question-b878a44e-123c-5f2f-a474-6dc1888b9c72" :question/problem "Use a change of variables to evaluate the double integral 

$$
{∬}_{D}({x}^{2}-xy)\,dxdy,
$$

where $D$ is the quadrilateral region with vertices $(3,2),$ $(5,4),$ $(5,2),$ and $(3,0).$"] ["question-b878a44e-123c-5f2f-a474-6dc1888b9c72" :question/worked-solution "Let's define a transformation $T$ as follows:

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{aligned}]
$$

This transformation maps some region $Δ$ in the $uv$-plane to our region $D$ in the $xy$-plane.

To compute the required integral, we can use the change of variables formula

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dxdy={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(x(u,v),y(u,v))\,|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\text{ }dudv
$$

where $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}$ is the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T.$

To compute the required integral, we proceed as follows:

**Step 1**: Find a suitable change of variables.

The integrand

$$
f(x,y)={x}^{2}-xy=x(x-y)
$$

suggests that we use the change of variables 

$$
u=x,\,v=x-y.
$$

This change of variables gives us the *inverse* function ${T}^{-1},$ that is

$$
{T}^{-1}:[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}u(x,y) \\ v(x,y)\end{aligned}].
$$

**Step 2**: Find $Δ,$ which is the image of $D$ under the action of ${T}^{-1}.$ 

The vertices of our domain $Δ$ in the $uv$-plane are as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{T}^{-1}(3,2) & =(3,3-2) \\  & =(3,1) \\ {T}^{-1}(5,4) & =(5,5-4) \\  & =(5,1) \\ {T}^{-1}(5,2) & =(5,5-2) \\  & =(5,3) \\ {T}^{-1}(3,0) & =(3,3-0) \\  & =(3,3)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our domain in the $uv$-plane is the following rectangle:

$$
Δ=\{(u,v)\,:\,3\le u\le 5,\,1\le v\le 3\}
$$

![](images/e0/e0b810c03e7e3210fcff3a739e3781ad5ff694bfe44d5f73d7782c3b4108a286.png)

**Step 3**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 1 & -1\end{aligned}| \\  & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 4**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T:$

$$
\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}={(\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)})}^{-1}=-1
$$

Note that $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}\ne 0$ everywhere inside $Δ.$ In other words, $T$ has no critical points inside $Δ.$

**Step 5**: Perform the change of variables, and evaluate the integral:

Performing the change of variables, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}({x}^{2}-xy)\,\text{d}x\text{d}y & ={∬}_{D}x(x-y)\,\text{d}x\text{d}y \\  & ={∬}_{Δ}uv\,|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & ={∬}_{Δ}uv\,|-1|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{3}{\int }_{3}^{5}uv\,\text{d}u\,\text{d}v \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{3}v\,\text{d}v{\int }_{3}^{5}u\,\text{d}u \\  & ={[\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}]}_{1}^{3}\cdot {[\frac{1}{2}{u}^{2}]}_{3}^{5} \\  & =4\cdot 8 \\  & =32.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-b878a44e-123c-5f2f-a474-6dc1888b9c72" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard] ["answer-field-e051d3d7-1ee2-505b-957c-b010b42121b8" :answer-field/id #uuid "question-b878a44e-123c-5f2f-a474-6dc1888b9c72"] ["question-e4b188aa-dc23-5bc9-90f6-b5a36b6d8b4b" :question/id #uuid "e4b188aa-dc23-5bc9-90f6-b5a36b6d8b4b"] ["question-e4b188aa-dc23-5bc9-90f6-b5a36b6d8b4b" :question/math-academy-id "q-160902"] ["question-e4b188aa-dc23-5bc9-90f6-b5a36b6d8b4b" :question/problem "Use a change of variables to evaluate the double integral 

$$
{∬}_{D}(2{x}^{2}-xy-{y}^{2})\,dxdy,
$$

where $D$ is the quadrilateral region with vertices $(1,-1),$ $(2,0),$ $(3,-2),$ and $(2,-3).$"] ["question-e4b188aa-dc23-5bc9-90f6-b5a36b6d8b4b" :question/worked-solution "Let's define a transformation $T$ as follows:

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{aligned}]
$$

This transformation maps some region $Δ$ in the $uv$-plane to our region $D$ in the $xy$-plane.

To compute the required integral, we can use the change of variables formula

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dxdy={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(x(u,v),y(u,v))\,|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\text{ }dudv
$$

where $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}$ is the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T.$

To compute the required integral, we proceed as follows:

**Step 1**: Find a suitable change of variables.

The integrand

$$
f(x,y)=2{x}^{2}-xy-{y}^{2}=(2x+y)(x-y)
$$

suggests that we use the change of variables 

$$
u=2x+y,\,v=x-y.
$$

This change of variables gives us the *inverse* function ${T}^{-1},$ that is

$$
{T}^{-1}:[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}u(x,y) \\ v(x,y)\end{aligned}].
$$

**Step 2**: Find $Δ,$ which is the image of $D$ under the action of ${T}^{-1}.$ 

The vertices of our domain $Δ$ in the $uv$-plane are as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{T}^{-1}(1,-1) & =(2(1)+(-1),1-(-1)) \\  & =(1,2) \\ {T}^{-1}(2,0) & =(2(2)+0,2-0) \\  & =(4,2) \\ {T}^{-1}(3,-2) & =(2(3)+(-2),3-(-2)) \\  & =(4,5) \\ {T}^{-1}(2,-3) & =(2(2)+(-3),2-(-3)) \\  & =(1,5)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our domain in the $uv$-plane is the following rectangle:

$$
Δ=\{(u,v)\,:\,1\le u\le 4,\,2\le v\le 5\}
$$

![](images/9f/9f5030bc3437fbc4431dd5350620bc7f9133d2bf910654607c0c5f7ef292f3a3.png)

**Step 3**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 1 & -1\end{aligned}| \\  & =-3.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 4**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T:$

$$
\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}={(\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)})}^{-1}=-\frac{1}{3}
$$

Note that $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}\ne 0$ everywhere inside $Δ.$ In other words, $T$ has no critical points inside $Δ.$

**Step 5**: Perform the change of variables, and evaluate the integral:

Performing the change of variables, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}(2{x}^{2}-xy-{y}^{2})\,\text{d}x\text{d}y & ={∬}_{D}(2x+y)(x-y)\,\text{d}x\text{d}y \\  & ={∬}_{Δ}uv\,|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & ={∬}_{Δ}uv\,|-\frac{1}{3}|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & =\frac{1}{3}{\int }_{2}^{5}{\int }_{1}^{4}uv\,\text{d}u\,\text{d}v \\  & =\frac{1}{3}{\int }_{2}^{5}v\,\text{d}v{\int }_{1}^{4}u\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\cdot {[\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}]}_{2}^{5}\cdot {[\frac{1}{2}{u}^{2}]}_{1}^{4} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\cdot \frac{21}{2}\cdot \frac{15}{2} \\  & =\frac{105}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-e4b188aa-dc23-5bc9-90f6-b5a36b6d8b4b" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard] ["answer-field-1f7c61ba-8de7-54e4-9c9a-0d1e7cbb1333" :answer-field/id #uuid
