Consider a plane lamina that occupies the region $D \subseteq \mathbb{R}^2$ with mass density function $\lambda(x,y),$ (in mass/area), which depends on the position.

By choosing a finite number of points $(x_{ij},y_{ij}),$ where $i=1,2,\ldots,m$ and $j=1,2,\ldots,n,$ we can break the region $D$ into non-overlapping boxes $B_{ij} = [x_{ij}, x_{ij} + \Delta x] \times [y_{ij}, y_{ij} + \Delta y]$ of area $\Delta x \Delta y = \Delta A.$

![](images/c5/c5ac4166ed637b4de525f069673cc6abfaeb2e8e659b3a212d6f2f4d1bf9fc11.png)

For large $m$ and $n,$ the mass density in each box, $B_{ij}$ is approximately constant and equal to the mass density of a point $(x_{ij}^*, y_{ij}^*)$ in the box. Hence, the mass of this part of the lamina is approximately the product of the mass density at this point and the area of the box:

$$
m_{ij} \approx \lambda(x_{ij}^*, y_{ij}^*) \cdot \Delta A
$$

Suppose the function $r(x,y)$ gives the distance of each point $(x,y) \in D$ from a fixed axis $L.$ Then, using the formula for the moment of inertia for a collection of masses, summing over these points, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}I & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}{m}_{i}[r({x}_{ij}^{∗},{y}_{ij}^{∗})]^{2} \\  & ≈{\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}(\lambda ({x}_{ij}^{∗},{y}_{ij}^{∗})\cdot ΔA)[r({x}_{ij}^{∗},{y}_{ij}^{∗})]^{2} \\  & ≈{\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}\lambda ({x}_{ij}^{∗},{y}_{ij}^{∗})[r({x}_{ij}^{∗},{y}_{ij}^{∗})]^{2}ΔA.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, taking the limit as the length and width of the boxes tend to zero, we get an exact representation of the moment of inertia as an integral:

$$
I = \lim\limits_{m,n\to \infty} \sum\limits_{i=1}^m \sum\limits_{j=1}^n \lambda(x_{ij}^*, y_{ij}^*) [r(x_{ij}^*, y_{ij}^*)]^2 \Delta A
= \iint\limits_D \lambda(x,y) [r(x,y)]^2 \:\textrm{d}A.
$$

Therefore, the moment of inertia about a fixed axis $L$ of a plane lamina occupying the region $D$ with mass density $\lambda(x,y)$ is

$$
I_L = \iint\limits_D \lambda(x,y) [r(x,y)]^2 \:\textrm{d}A,
$$

where $r(x,y)$ is the distance from the point $(x,y)$ to the axis $L.$

In this lesson, we'll limit the axis of rotation to the $x$- and $y$-axes. Note that the distance between a point $(x,y)$ and the $x$ and $y$ coordinate axes are $r_x(x,y) = |y|$ and $r_y(x,y) = |x|,$ respectively.

![](images/8a/8a94fcdb8bb1a97e2bc9122e88ca7bd4f441299d2ce3c7bee819e644cf4eae89.png)

Hence, the moments of inertia of a plate with respect to the coordinate axes $x$ and $y,$ denoted $I_x$ and $I_y$, respectively, are 

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{x} & ={∬}_{D}{y}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A \\ {I}_{y} & ={∬}_{D}{x}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

A related concept is the **moment of inertia about the origin** (or **polar moment of inertia**), which deals with the strength of an object when it is rotating. It is defined as

$$
I_0 = \iint\limits_D (x^2+y^2)\lambda(x,y) \:\textrm dA = I_x + I_y.

$$

$$

$$

$$

- The moment of inertia about the $x$-axis is given by

$$
{I}_{x}={∬}_{D}{y}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A.
$$

- The moment of inertia about the $y$-axis is given by

$$
{I}_{y}={∬}_{D}{x}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A.
$$

- The moment of inertia about the origin is given by

$$
{I}_{0}={∬}_{D}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A={I}_{x}+{I}_{y}.
$$

First, notice that $D$ is a type II region with representation

$$
D=\{(x,y)\,:\,y\le x\le 2-{y}^{2},\,\,0\le y\le 1\},
$$

as shown below.

![](images/7a/7a4216a2b1dc3859776c6589459d687981b79b123fa3a5eea638d31529e5cd3a.png)

$$

$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{0} & ={∬}_{D}\lambda (r,\theta )\cdot {r}^{3}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}{\int }_{1}^{2}10r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \cdot {r}^{3}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}{\int }_{1}^{2}10{r}^{4}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =({\int }_{1}^{2}10{r}^{4}\,\text{d}r)({\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta ) \\  & =2{r}^{5}\,{|}_{1}^{2}\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,{|}_{0}^{\pi /4} \\  & =2(32-1)(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}-0) \\  & =31\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}

"![](images/dc/dc61efd6e5ef1fd46fca53f7c1e47394c6b9c95fb2455dc0c798d9936a68631b.png)

A plate occupies the region $D$ enclosed by the $x$-axis, $y$-axis, and the curve $y=\sqrt{4-{x}^{2}}$ in the first quadrant, as shown above. If the mass density function of $D$ is given by $\lambda (x,y)=10y,$ find the moment of inertia of the lamina about the origin." :question/worked-solution "For a plane lamina $D$ with mass density function $\lambda (x,y),$ we have the following definitions:

- The moment of inertia about the $x$-axis is given by

$$
{I}_{x}={∬}_{D}{y}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A.
$$

- The moment of inertia about the $y$-axis is given by

$$
{I}_{y}={∬}_{D}{x}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A.
$$

- The moment of inertia about the origin is given by

$$
{I}_{0}={∬}_{D}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A={I}_{x}+{I}_{y}.
$$

First, notice that $D$ is a type I region with representation

$$
D=\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le 2,\,\,0\le y\le \sqrt{4-{x}^{2}}\},
$$

as shown below.

![](images/62/626cbf8e182d9eebb8b48026f07c5dd012c1096cc9568465f3648710ea0d07a4.png)

Using the formula for ${I}_{0},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{0} & ={∬}_{D}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{4-{x}^{2}}}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})(10y)\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}[{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{4-{x}^{2}}}10{x}^{2}y+10{y}^{3}\,\text{d}y]\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{[5{x}^{2}{y}^{2}+\frac{5}{2}{y}^{4}]}_{y=0}^{y=\sqrt{4-{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}5{x}^{2}(4-{x}^{2})+\frac{5}{2}{(4-{x}^{2})}^{2}\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{5}{2}(4-{x}^{2})(2{x}^{2}+4-{x}^{2})\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{5}{2}{\int }_{0}^{2}16-{x}^{4}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{5}{2}{[16x-\frac{{x}^{5}}{5}]}_{0}^{2} \\  & =\frac{5}{2}(32-\frac{32}{5}) \\  & =64.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "8cc8c4c3-672d-51c1-af40-2419b51ec4f9" :step/next {:db/id 17592186442861}} {:db/id 17592186442858 :step/content {:db/id 17592186281633 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "4c84deba-cb38-5f3b-af0e-58521ec502a3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{2M}{3}\,\text{kg}\cdot {\text{m}}^{2}" :db/id 17592186279280} {:answer/id #uuid "a25defa0-44b9-5bda-a10f-e6ef6a677aaa" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{16M}{3}\,\text{kg}\cdot {\text{m}}^{2}" :db/id 17592186280035} {:answer/id #uuid "ad5bf3b6-9c4b-50ce-879e-8ec79739fdf2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{4M}{3}\,\text{kg}\cdot {\text{m}}^{2}" :db/id 17592186280127} {:answer/id #uuid "ca352098-298f-5e14-a7d7-0c7272084e0f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "8M\,\text{kg}\cdot {\text{m}}^{2}" :db/id 17592186280364} {:answer/id #uuid "cf1d4484-aff6-5376-8a09-a8cd9f6af638" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4M\,\text{kg}\cdot {\text{m}}^{2}" :db/id 17592186280418}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186280127} :answer-field/id #uuid "8a384dc8-494e-5973-bebc-5b4d13e8a8c2" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186281085}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "095d8c09-ff9b-5528-8c3d-3967d18698a1" :question/math-academy-id "q-163204" :question/problem "A rectangular plate of mass $M\,\text{kg}$ and uniform mass density occupies the region
$D=\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le 2,\,\,1\le y\le 3\},$ where $x$ and $y$ are measured in meters. Find the moment of inertia of the plate about the $y$-axis." :question/worked-solution "For a plane lamina $D$ with mass density function $\lambda (x,y),$ we have the following definitions:

- The moment of inertia about the $x$-axis is given by

$$
{I}_{x}={∬}_{D}{y}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A.
$$

- The moment of inertia about the $y$-axis is given by

$$
{I}_{y}={∬}_{D}{x}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A.
$$

- The moment of inertia about the origin is given by

$$
{I}_{0}={∬}_{D}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A={I}_{x}+{I}_{y}.
$$

The area of the rectangular plate $D$ is $A=2\cdot 2=4.$ 

Since the plate has uniform density, every unit of area contains the same amount of mass. Therefore, the mass density is constant and is given by the total mass divided by the total area:

$$
\lambda (x,y)=\frac{M}{A}=\frac{M}{4}.
$$

Using the formula for ${I}_{y},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{y} & ={∬}_{D}{x}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A \\  & =\frac{M}{4}{\int }_{1}^{3}{\int }_{0}^{2}{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{M}{4}{\int }_{1}^{3}{[\frac{1}{3}{x}^{3}]}_{0}^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{M}{4}{\int }_{1}^{3}\frac{8}{3}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{M}{4}{[\frac{8y}{3}]}_{1}^{3} \\  & =\frac{2M}{3}(3-1) \\  & =\frac{4M}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the moment of inertia is $\frac{4M}{3}\,\text{kg}\cdot {\text{m}}^{2}.$"} :step/id #uuid "9a68fb24-0279-5aa2-9378-bef9856a349d" :step/next {:db/id 17592186442859}} {:db/id 17592186442859 :step/content {:db/id 17592186281642 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "17226919-ce93-5049-994f-31d7cd5c10fb" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{7\pi }{6}" :db/id 17592186278798} {:answer/id #uuid "6d3b17cc-de83-57bb-914f-013137289a03" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{5\pi }{12}" :db/id 17592186279586} {:answer/id #uuid "78cff65f-0d69-5e60-9e1c-47253821dc1b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{3\pi }{8}" :db/id 17592186279669} {:answer/id #uuid "8d83c82c-bb2f-532f-ab7d-a58f6e2cc4be" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{9\pi }{4}" :db/id 17592186279853} {:answer/id #uuid "e875a915-69ff-5a94-9c30-f7fd03b5fb84" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{7\pi }{10}" :db/id 17592186280639}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186279586} :answer-field/id #uuid "bf0fe541-fc86-58e2-a9d5-645ba6b20816" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186281172}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "2726afac-54d3-5734-a6e0-8fa5ce77d367" :question/math-academy-id "q-163228" :question/problem "![](images/04/044395de3b30755d0c83d489709c38420827f6984af740bc56a3dc5bfaa33794.png)

First, we compute the expression inside the parentheses:

$$
\dfrac{4}{3} \times ({\color{red}-5} + {\color{red}3})^{-2} + \dfrac{2}{3} = \dfrac{4}{3} \times ({\color{red}-2})^{-2} + \dfrac{2}{3}
$$

Next, notice that

$$
(-2)^{-2}=\dfrac{1}{(-2)^2} = \dfrac{1}{4}
$$

So, we obtain:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{4}{3} \cdot (-2)^{-2} + \frac{2}{3} &=  \\
\frac{4}{3} \cdot \frac{1}{4} + \frac{2}{3} &=  \\
\frac{4 \cdot 1}{3 \cdot 4} + \frac{2}{3} &=  \\
\frac{4 \cdot 1}{3 \cdot 4} + \frac{2}{3} &=  \\
\frac{1}{3} + \frac{2}{3} &=  \\
&= 1
\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186129832 :question/id #uuid "ee923ff1-1614-5d67-a0d6-0d5e7e1dfe3f" :question/math-academy-id "q-68856"} {:db/id 17592186129833 :question/id #uuid "681078d3-db1f-57a2-bcc6-83dda865b685" :question/math-academy-id "q-69340"} {:db/id 17592186129310 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186128872 :question/id #uuid "c6b6a911-843f-5c96-a792-ebd807b5d60e" :question/math-academy-id "e-12875"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "222a5d13-74e9-5f1b-81d5-f38a6b80870c" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186129401 :question/id #uuid "2af8994b-c9e2-5d59-9c51-e7eeafbf6a0d" :question/math-academy-id "q-100300"} {:db/id 17592186129834 :question/id #uuid "5cbb173a-9b62-5ad0-93a2-7271e0aded45" :question/math-academy-id "q-69350"}] :knowledge-point/title "Evaluating Expressions With Both Zero and Negative Exponents"} {:db/id 17592186128872 :question/id #uuid "c6b6a911-843f-5c96-a792-ebd807b5d60e" :question/math-academy-id "e-12875" :knowledge-point/_canonical-example [{:db/id 17592186129310 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "222a5d13-74e9-5f1b-81d5-f38a6b80870c" :knowledge-point/title "Evaluating Expressions With Both Zero and Negative Exponents"}] :question/problem "Find the value of $2 + \left(-4\right)^{-2} \div \left(1.5 + \dfrac{2}{15} \right)^0$." :question/worked-solution "To evaluate the given expression, we use PEMDAS.

$$

$$

$$

Substituting all these values into the expression, we obtain:

$$
\begin{aligned}
2 + (-4)^{-2} \div (1.5 + \frac{2}{15})^{0} &=  \\
2 + \frac{1}{16} \div 1 &=  \\
2 + \frac{1}{16} &=  \\
\frac{32}{16} + \frac{1}{16} &=  \\
&= \frac{33}{16}
\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186129401 :question/id #uuid "2af8994b-c9e2-5d59-9c51-e7eeafbf6a0d" :question/math-academy-id "q-100300"} {:db/id 17592186129834 :question/id #uuid The same rules apply to numerical expressions with zero and negative exponents. To demonstrate, let's compute the value of
$(-3)^0 +2^2 \div 2$.

To evaluate the given expression, we use PEMDAS.

Notice that

$$
\left(-3\right)^{0}=1
$$

So, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}
(-3)^{0} + 2^{2} \div 2 &=  \\
1 + 2^{2} \div 2 &=  \\
1 + 4 \div 2 &=  \\
1 + 2 &=  \\
&= 3 \mid
\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "e2d29fa0-8bcb-537b-bed9-91a9ff109764" :tutorial/math-academy-id 8061 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "32a4a3c3-8cf8-5f85-9674-14a9a3dced4b" :step/math-academy-id 54570 :step/next {:db/id 17592186130285}} {:db/id 17592186130481 :tutorial/content "As we know already, to evaluate numerical expressions with a mix of different operations, we follow the order of operations (PEMDAS).

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x)+g(x) & ={x}^{3}+(1-{x}^{3}) \\  & =({x}^{3}-{x}^{3})+1 \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

So, $C$ is *not* closed under addition.

- Statement II is false. For example, if $f(x)={x}^{3}$ and $k=0,$ then

$$
kf(x)=0\cdot {x}^{3}=0.
$$

- Statement III is false, while statement IV is true. $C$ is *not* a subspace because it's not closed under addition and scalar multiplication.

17592186045486 :db/ident :question.difficulty/hard} :question/problem "Consider the vector space $C[0,1]$ of all continuous functions $f:[0,1]\to R$ and its subset $K$ containing all nonconstant functions.

Which of the following statements are true?

Select all that apply.

- **I.** $K$ is closed under function addition
- **II.** $K$ is closed under scalar multiplication
- **III.** $K$ is a subspace of $C[0,1]$
- **IV.** $K$ is **not** a subspace of $C[0,1]$

*Hint: $f$ is a constant function if $f(x)=\text{constant}$ for all $x\in [0,1].$*" :question/worked-solution "Recall that a subset of a vector space is a subspace if it's closed under addition and scalar multiplication.

With that in mind, let's examine each statement in turn.

- Statement I is false. For example, the functions $f(x)=x+2$ and $f(x)=-x-1$ are in $K$, however

$$
(f+g)(x)=1
$$

for all $x\in [0,1]$ and hence $f+g$ is a constant function. 
So, $K$ is *not* closed under addition.

- Statement II is false. For example, the product of the scalar zero by any function is the constant function zero. So, $K$ is *not* closed under scalar multiplication.

- Statement III is false, while statement IV is true. $K$ is *not* a subspace because it's not closed under addition and scalar multiplication.

Therefore, the correct answer is "IV only.""} {:db/id 17592186446399 :question/id #uuid "33331944-2261-5079-a111-5d0397fe6a4a" :question/math-academy-id "q-107146"} {:db/id 17592186446401 :question/id 17592186045485 :db/ident :question.difficulty/easy} :question/problem "Consider the vector space ${\text{M}}_{2}(R)$ of all $2\times 2$ matrices over $R$ and its subset $E$ containing all $2\times 2$ matrices of the form $\alpha A$ where $A$ is some fixed $2\times 2$ matrix and $\alpha \in R.$

Which of the following statements are true?

Select all that apply.

- **I.** $E$ is closed under matrix addition
- **II.** $E$ is closed under scalar multiplication
- **III.** $E$ is a subspace of ${\text{M}}_{2}(R)$
- **IV.** $E$ is **not** a subspace of ${\text{M}}_{2}(R)$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that a subset of a vector space is a subspace if it's closed under addition and scalar multiplication.

With that in mind, let's examine each statement in turn.

- Statement I is true. If ${A}_{1}={\alpha }_{1}A$ and ${A}_{2}={\alpha }_{2}A$ are two matrices from $E,$ then

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{1}+{A}_{2} & ={\alpha }_{1}A+{\alpha }_{2}A=({\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{2})A,\end{aligned}
$$

which is a matrix from $E.$ So, $E$ is closed under addition.

- Statement II is true. If $B=\alpha A$ is an element of $E$ and $k\in R,$ then 

$$
\begin{aligned}kB & =k\alpha A=(k\alpha )A,\end{aligned}
$$

which is a matrix from $E.$ So, $E$ is closed under scalar multiplication.

- Statement III is true, while statement IV is false. $E$ is a subspace because it's closed under addition and scalar multiplication.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I, II, and III only.""} {:db/id 17592186329725 :question/id #uuid "76fb5f0d-770c-53e0-bb5c-9231d8688147" :question/math-academy-id "q-43776"} {:db/id 17592186360461 17592186045487 :db/ident :question.difficulty/moderate} :question/problem "Consider the vector space ${\text{M}}_{2}(R)$ of all $2\times 2$ matrices over $R$ and its subset $B={[\begin{aligned}0 & a Which of the following statements are true?

Select all that apply.

- **I.** $B$ is closed under matrix addition
- **II.** $B$ is closed under scalar multiplication
- **III.** $B$ is a subspace of ${\text{M}}_{2}(R)$
- **IV.** $B$ is **not** a subspace of ${\text{M}}_{2}(R)$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that a subset of a vector space is a subspace if it's closed under addition and scalar multiplication.

With that in mind, let's examine each statement in turn.

- Statement I is false. For example, if ${A}_{1}={A}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}],$ then

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{1}+{A}_{2} & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}],\end{aligned}

:topic/math-academy-id 1907} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186125348 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125762 :tutorial/content "Given a vector space $V$, any subset $H$ of $V,$ which is itself a vector space, is called a **subspace** of $V$. 

Fortunately, we do not need to check all vector space axioms to determine whether a subset of some vector space is a subspace. Instead, we only need to check the **subspace criterion**, which states the following:

*A subset $H$ of a vector space $V$ is a subspace of $V$ if and only if $H$ is closed under vector addition and scalar multiplication. That is to say, both of the following conditions hold:*

- *If $\mathbf{u}$ and $\mathbf{v}$ lie in $H$, then their sum $\mathbf{u}+\mathbf{v}$ also lies in $H$. Formally,*

$$
\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v} \in H \quad\Rightarrow\quad  \mathbf{u}+\mathbf{v} \in H.
$$

- *If $\mathbf{u}$ lies in $H$, then $k \cdot \mathbf{u}$ also lies in $H$ for any scalar  $k$. Formally,* 

$$
k \in \mathbb{R}, \,\mathbf{u} \in H \quad\Rightarrow\quad  k\cdot\mathbf{u} \in H.
$$

For example, consider the vector space $\mathbb{R}_3[t]$ containing all polynomials of degree at most $3,$ along with the subset 

$$
A = \{ at^2 \:|\: a \in \mathbb{R} \}.
$$

Is $A$ a subspace? Let's check the two subspace criterion conditions: 

- Suppose $p_1(t)=a_1 t^2$ and $p_2(t)=a_2 t^2$ are two polynomials from $A$. Summing the two polynomials, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{p}_{1}(t)+{p}_{2}(t) & =({a}_{1}{t}^{2})+({a}_{2}{t}^{2}) \\  & ={{({a}_{1}+{a}_{2})}_{⏟}}_{a\in R}{t}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

 
Thus, $p_1(t)+p_2(t)$ is a polynomial of the form $at^2,$ which belongs to $A$.

- If $p_1(t)=a_1 t^2 \in A$ and $k \in \mathbb{R},$ then 

$$
\begin{aligned}k{p}_{1}(t) & =k({a}_{1}{t}^{2}) \\  & ={{(k{a}_{1})}_{⏟}}_{a\in R}{t}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

 
Thus, $kp_1(t)$ is a polynomial of the form $at^2,$ which belongs to $A$.

Since both conditions hold, we conclude that $A$ is a subspace $\mathbb{R}_3[t].$" :tutorial/id #uuid "4274a05d-d402-5dfc-a339-e5a6b5a8e5b0" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3205 :tutorial/title "Let's now look at an example of a subset of a vector space that is not a subspace.

Consider the vector space $\mathbb R_2[t]$ of all polynomials in the variable $t$ of degree at most $2,$ and its subset 

$$
B = \big\{ at+b \: | \: a,b  \in\mathbb{Z} \big\}.
$$

Recall that a subset of a vector space is a subspace if it's closed under addition and scalar multiplication.

- $B$ is closed under polynomial addition. Indeed, suppose that $f(t)=a_1t+b_1$ and $g(t)=a_2t+b_2$ are two polynomials from $B.$ Then,

$$
\begin{aligned}f(t)+g(t) & =({a}_{1}t+{b}_{1})+({a}_{2}t+{b}_{2}) \\  & =({a}_{1}+{a}_{2})t+({b}_{1}+{b}_{2}),\end{aligned}
$$

which is a polynomial from $B$ since $a_1+a_2$ and $b_1+b_2$ are in $\Bbb Z.$

- $B$ is *not* closed under scalar multiplication. As a counterexample, consider $f(t)=t$ and $k=0.5,$ then 

$$
\begin{aligned}kf(t) & =0.5t,\end{aligned}
$$

which is *not* a polynomial from $B,$ because $0.5 \notin \Bbb Z.$

![](images/8f/8f4bdd28c709b7f1b162e98ad196547f90c577df74e52fb6eef1d88efa209af9.png)" :question/worked-solution "First, let's denote

![](images/94/948d731d51fff2a1462db9eacab511eefbfdb1634bc9c45b2cf92ca67c4a4d18.png)

We proceed to find an orthogonal basis using the Gram-Schmidt process, as follows.

- **Step 1**: We set ![](images/e8/e8a3c7b01b547745c01f123634ca06ffc966ef9acec682af33f05066e00ceef1.png)

- **Step 2**: Next, we find $\mathbf{v}_2$, using the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{2} & ={a}_{2}-\frac{{a}_{2}\cdot {v}_{1}}{{v}_{1}\cdot {v}_{1}}{v}_{1}.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the formula for $\mathbf v_2$ in our case gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{2} & ={a}_{2}-\frac{(-3)\cdot 1+5\cdot (-1)+2\cdot 2}{{1}^{2}+(-1)^{2}+{2}^{2}}{v}_{1} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 5 \\ 2\end{aligned}]+\frac{2}{3}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-\frac{7}{3} \\ \frac{13}{3} \\ \frac{10}{3}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, ![](images/bb/bb718fb5d9931c6f99268f40bbef401b50dc160304b271bd2035528bddabdec0.png) is an orthogonal basis for $V.$

Finally, $a=-\dfrac 7 3,$ $c=\dfrac{10}{3}$ and  

$$
\dfrac{a}{c} = \dfrac{\left(-\dfrac{7}{3}\right)}{\left(\dfrac{10}{3}\right)} = -\dfrac{7}{10}.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186048893} {:db/id 17592186049811} {:db/id 17592186134309 :question/id #uuid "6cd93368-184b-51ef-8337-6d58bffaad14" :question/math-academy-id "q-40738"} {:db/id 17592186134336 We proceed to find an orthogonal basis using the Gram-Schmidt process, as follows.

**Step 1**: We set ${v}_{1}={a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2 \\ 2\end{aligned}].$

**Step 2**: Next, we find ${v}_{2}$, by using the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{2} & ={a}_{2}-\frac{{a}_{2}\cdot {v}_{1}}{{v}_{1}\cdot {v}_{1}}{v}_{1}.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the formula for ${v}_{2}$ in our case gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{2} & ={a}_{2}-\frac{(-2)\cdot 1+5\cdot (-2)+3\cdot 2}{{1}^{2}+(-2)^{2}+{2}^{2}}{v}_{1} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 5 \\ 3\end{aligned}]+\frac{2}{3}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-\frac{4}{3} \\ \frac{11}{3} \\ \frac{13}{3}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{2} & ={a}_{2}-\frac{{a}_{2}\cdot {v}_{1}}{{v}_{1}\cdot {v}_{1}}{v}_{1}.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the formula for ${v}_{2}$ in our case gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{2} & ={a}_{2}-\frac{4\cdot 2+1\cdot (-1)+1\cdot 2}{{2}^{2}+(-1)^{2}+{2}^{2}}{v}_{1} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -1 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 2 \\ -1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}

First, let's denote

$\,$ ${a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ -2 \\ 2\end{aligned}]\,$ and $\,{a}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 0 \\ -3\end{aligned}].$ 

We proceed to find an orthogonal basis using the Gram-Schmidt process, as follows.

**Step 1**: We set ${v}_{1}={a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ -2 \\ 2\end{aligned}].$

**Step 2**: Next, we find ${v}_{2}$, by using the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{2} & ={a}_{2}-\frac{{a}_{2}\cdot {v}_{1}}{{v}_{1}\cdot {v}_{1}}{v}_{1}.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the formula for ${v}_{2}$ in our case gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{2} & ={a}_{2}-\frac{3\cdot (-1)+0\cdot (-2)+(-3)\cdot 2}{{1}^{2}+(-2)^{2}+{2}^{2}}{v}_{1} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 0 \\ -3\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ -2 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -2 \\ -1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we normalize each vector to get an orthonormal basis:

- ${u}_{1}=\frac{{v}_{1}}{‖{v}_{1}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{{1}^{2}+(-2)^{2}+{2}^{2}}}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ -2 \\ 2\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{3} \\ -\frac{2}{3} \\ \frac{2}{3}\end{aligned}].$

- ${u}_{2}=\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{{2}^{2}+(-2)^{2}+(-1)^{2}}}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -2 \\ -1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{3} \\ -\frac{2}{3} \\ -\frac{1}{3}\end{aligned}].$

Therefore, $B={{u}_{1},{u}_{2}}={[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{3} \\ -\frac{2}{3} \\ \frac{2}{3}\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{3} \\ -\frac{2}{3} \\ -\frac{1}{3}\end{aligned}]}$ is an orthonormal basis for $\text{Col}(A).$

Finally, $a=\frac{2}{3},$ $b=-\frac{2}{3},$ $c=-\frac{1}{3}$ and  

$$
|a|+|b|+|c|=|\frac{2}{3}|+|-\frac{2}{3}|+|-\frac{1}{3}|=\frac{5}{3}.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186272129 :question/id #uuid "3a029be5-b6a5-506a-8947-8d15614953ac" :question/math-academy-id "q-140537"} {:db/id 17592186272130 :question/id #uuid "2e6d1632-87e6-54dd-a8f9-23d096c3bcc7" :question/math-academy-id "q-140539" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186133795 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "ccdefb8e-1bb5-52e9-812d-d2a5bffff731" :knowledge-point/title "Finding an Orthonormal Basis of a Vector Space"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0f0be9bb-0dd7-5727-a685-7067529f3b9f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "2\sqrt{3}" :db/id 17592186269405} {:answer/id #uuid "0fc8fc9a-3735-5af4-ab4b-7a0b06f36be6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\sqrt{3}" :db/id 17592186269410} {:answer/id #uuid "14837d79-0685-5b2f-b7ae-de1bb6acd6e4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\sqrt{2}" :db/id 17592186269449} {:answer/id #uuid "22a41e2d-2e61-5f3e-9b7c-55de1bb113c2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{3}{2}" :db/id 17592186269569} {:answer/id #uuid "a51a7384-da8d-59ed-9c61-4348968fe7f9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\sqrt{6}" :db/id 17592186270746}] :answer-field/correct {:answer/id #uuid "0fc8fc9a-3735-5af4-ab4b-7a0b06f36be6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\sqrt{3}" :db/id 17592186269410} :answer-field/id #uuid "fa412d3d-18c8-523e-8f62-f8bca8e7c4b4" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186271942}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486 :db/ident :question.difficulty/hard} :question/problem "$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{2} & ={a}_{2}-\frac{0\cdot 2+3\cdot (-1)+(-3)\cdot 1}{{2}^{2}+(-1)^{2}+{1}^{2}}{v}_{1} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 3 \\ -3\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 2 \\ -2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}

$\,$ ${a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 0 \\ 3\end{aligned}]\,$ and $\,{a}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}5 \\ -4 \\ 10\end{aligned}].$ 

We proceed to find an orthogonal basis using the Gram-Schmidt process, as follows.

**Step 1**: We set ${v}_{1}={a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 0 \\ 3\end{aligned}].$

**Step 2**: Next, we find ${v}_{2}$, by using the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{2} & ={a}_{2}-\frac{{a}_{2}\cdot {v}_{1}}{{v}_{1}\cdot {v}_{1}}{v}_{1}.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the formula for ${v}_{2}$ in our case gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{2} & ={a}_{2}-\frac{5\cdot 4+(-4)\cdot 0+10\cdot 3}{{4}^{2}+{0}^{2}+{3}^{2}}{v}_{1} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}5 \\ -4 \\ 10\end{aligned}]-2[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 0 \\ 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ -4 \\ 4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}

Now, we normalize each vector to get an orthonormal basis:

- ${u}_{2}=\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{(-3)^{2}+(-4)^{2}+{4}^{2}}}[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ -4 \\ 4\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{3\sqrt{41}}{41} \\ -\frac{4\sqrt{41}}{41} \\ \frac{4\sqrt{41}}{41}\end{aligned}].$

$$

Therefore, $B={{v}_{1},{v}_{2}}={[\begin{aligned}\frac{2\sqrt{5}}{5} \\ 0 \\ \frac{\sqrt{5}}{5}\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{3} \\ \frac{2}{3} \\ \frac{2}{3}\end{aligned}]}$ is an orthonormal basis for $\text{Col}(A).$

Consider the subspace $V$ and an **orthonormal** basis $B$ of $V,$ given above. Given that $B$ is derived from $V$ using the Gram-Schmidt process, what is the value of $|a|+|b|+|c|?$" :question/worked-solution "First, let's denote

$\,$ ${a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-4 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\,$ and $\,{a}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 2 \\ 4\end{aligned}].$ 

We proceed to find an orthogonal basis using the Gram-Schmidt process, as follows.

**Step 1**: We set ${v}_{1}={a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-4 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

**Step 2**: Next, we find ${v}_{2}$, by using the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{2} & ={a}_{2}-\frac{{a}_{2}\cdot {v}_{1}}{{v}_{1}\cdot {v}_{1}}{v}_{1}.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the formula for ${v}_{2}$ in our case gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{2} & ={a}_{2}-\frac{(-3)\cdot (-4)+2\cdot 1+4\cdot 1}{(-4)^{2}+{1}^{2}+{1}^{2}}{v}_{1} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 2 \\ 4\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}-4 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 3\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we normalize each vector to get an orthonormal basis:

- ${u}_{1}=\frac{{v}_{1}}{‖{v}_{1}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{(-4)^{2}+{1}^{2}+{1}^{2}}}[\begin{aligned}-4 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{2\sqrt{2}}{3} \\ \frac{\sqrt{2}}{6} \\ \frac{\sqrt{2}}{6}\end{aligned}].$

- ${u}_{2}=\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{{1}^{2}+{1}^{2}+{3}^{2}}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 3\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}\frac{\sqrt{11}}{11} \\ \frac{\sqrt{11}}{11} \\ \frac{3\sqrt{11}}{11}\end{aligned}].$

Therefore, $B={{u}_{1},{u}_{2}}={[\begin{aligned}\frac{-2\sqrt{2}}{3} \\ \frac{\sqrt{2}}{6} \\ \frac{\sqrt{2}}{6}\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}\frac{\sqrt{11}}{11} \\ \frac{\sqrt{11}}{11} \\ \frac{3\sqrt{11}}{11}\end{aligned}]}$ is an orthonormal basis of $V.$

Finally, $a=\frac{\sqrt{11}}{11},$ $b=\frac{\sqrt{11}}{11},$ $c=\frac{3\sqrt{11}}{11}$ and  

$$
|a|+|b|+|c|=|\frac{\sqrt{11}}{11}|+|\frac{\sqrt{11}}{11}|+|\frac{3\sqrt{11}}{11}|=\frac{5\sqrt{11}}{11}.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186414750 :question/id #uuid "0934e8ac-174d-5792-a7fc-4ab5bbca2aae" :question/math-academy-id "q-41971" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "72cc1442-df79-5623-bff4-42eedddafdb9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{2\sqrt{10}}{5}" :db/id 17592186414732} {:answer/id #uuid "77e7d035-74cb-5a21-8a35-1b0d4898e245" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{\sqrt{10}}{10}" :db/id 17592186414733} {:answer/id #uuid "9aa54ac6-f50b-5137-953c-f00902b1d420" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{3\sqrt{10}}{10}" :db/id 17592186414738} {:answer/id #uuid "be937ae3-0668-5fe5-9548-61b224487acf" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{\sqrt{10}}{5}" :db/id 17592186414741} {:answer/id #uuid "c38c74ea-a21b-5c0e-bb44-84641a158c8e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\sqrt{10}" :db/id 17592186414742}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186414732} :answer-field/id #uuid "969beab5-314b-57a6-99da-182f476a0e29" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186414749}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/problem "$$

**Step 1**: We set ${v}_{1}={a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1 \\ 3\end{aligned}].$

**Step 2**: Next, we find ${v}_{2}$, by using the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{2} & ={a}_{2}-\frac{{a}_{2}\cdot {v}_{1}}{{v}_{1}\cdot {v}_{1}}{v}_{1}.\end{aligned}

:activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186134684 :step/content {:db/id 17592186135054 :tutorial/content "The **Gram-Schmidt process** is an algorithm that we can use to construct an *orthogonal* basis if we are given a non-orthogonal basis to start with.

For example, consider the basis $\{ \mathbf{a}_1, \mathbf{a}_2 \}$ for the subspace $V=\textrm{Span} \{ \mathbf{a}_1, \mathbf{a}_2 \},$ where

$$
[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]
$$

We can use the above basis to construct an *orthogonal* basis for the given $2$-dimensional subspace. To do this, we use the Gram-Schmidt process, which involves $2$ steps:

- **Step 1:** Set ${\color{blue}\mathbf{v}_1}=\mathbf{a}_1.$

- **Step 2:** Find a vector $\color{blue}\mathbf{v}_2$ in $V$ that's orthogonal to $\color{blue}\mathbf{v}_1.$ This can be achieved by computing

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{2} & ={a}_{2}\,-\,{\text{proj}}_{{v}_{1}}\,{a}_{2} \\  & ={a}_{2}-\frac{{a}_{2}\cdot {v}_{1}}{{v}_{1}\cdot {v}_{1}}{v}_{1}.\end{aligned}
$$

![](images/67/678cc056e3c9d3fbf17423ac591b3e85d84ee8060c0637840fe1c4c9e87aa878.png)

Notice that $\color{blue}\mathbf{v}_2$ is written as a linear combination of $\mathbf{a}_1(={\color{blue}\mathbf{v}_1})$ and $\mathbf{a}_2.$ So this means that ${\color{blue}\mathbf{v}_2} \in V,$ and also ${\color{blue}\mathbf{v}_2} \perp {\color{blue}\mathbf{v}_1}.$
Moreover, 

$$
\textrm{Span}\{\mathbf{a}_1,\mathbf{a}_2\} = V = \textrm{Span}\{ {\color{blue}\mathbf{v}_1}, {\color{blue}\mathbf{v}_2} \}.
$$

After applying the Gram-Schmidt process, we get the set $\mathcal{B}=\{{\color{blue}\mathbf{v}_1}, {\color{blue}\mathbf{v}_2}\},$ which is an orthogonal basis for $V.$

So, in our example, we start by setting $[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]$ Then, we find the vector $\mathbf{v}_2$ that's orthogonal to $\textrm{Span}\{\mathbf{v}_1\}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{2} & ={a}_{2}-\frac{{a}_{2}\cdot {v}_{1}}{{v}_{1}\cdot {v}_{1}}{v}_{1} \\  & ={a}_{2}-\frac{4\cdot 1+6\cdot (-1)}{{1}^{2}+(-1)^{2}}{v}_{1} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 6\end{aligned}]-(-1)\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 5\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]$ is an orthogonal basis for $V.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "3b833ab7-f6d4-5c93-8709-37ecf29bf023" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3631 :tutorial/title To do this, we simply execute the Gram-Schmidt process as before to obtain an orthogonal basis $\{\mathbf{v}_1, \mathbf{v}_2\},$ and then we normalize each vector in this basis to get the orthonormal basis $\{\mathbf{u}_1, \mathbf{u}_2\},$ where

$$
\mathbf{u}_1 = \dfrac{\mathbf{v}_1}{\Vert \mathbf{v}_1 \Vert},
	\quad
	\mathbf{u}_2 = \dfrac{\mathbf{v}_2}{\Vert \mathbf{v}_2 \Vert}.
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "1ea8b19b-f7a8-5339-abd4-3069e18b2555" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3632 :tutorial/title "Using the Gram-Schmidt Process to Find an Orthonormal Basis"} :step/id #uuid "881045a6-4243-5fbd-8617-d6520ecad604" :step/math-academy-id 20260 :step/next {:db/id 17592186134688}} {:db/id 17592186134688 :step/content {:db/id 17592186133795 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186133604 :question/id #uuid "60dbc829-01fc-5283-8741-68af483d5313" :question/math-academy-id "e-5583"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "ccdefb8e-1bb5-52e9-812d-d2a5bffff731" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186134310} {:db/id 17592186134311} {:db/id 17592186272129} {:db/id 17592186272130} {:db/id 17592186326874} {:db/id 17592186351265} {:db/id 17592186354526} {:db/id 17592186354527} {:db/id 17592186366118} {:db/id 17592186366386} {:db/id 17592186414750}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding an Orthonormal Basis of a Vector Space"} :step/id #uuid "5c0057df-8020-54b5-b1ba-1011db749edc" :step/math-academy-id 20261} {:db/id 17592186134770 :step/content {:db/id 17592186135089 :tutorial/content "Sometimes it's helpful to "clean up" the result of a Gram-Schmidt process by scaling the resulting vectors.

For example, suppose that the set $\mathcal B,$ given by

$$
[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]
$$

is an orthogonal basis for $\textrm{Span} \{ \mathbf{v}_1, \mathbf{v}_2 \}.$

Since the vector $\mathbf{v}_2$ lies in $\textrm{Span} \{ \mathbf{v}_1, \mathbf{v}_2 \}$ and $\mathbf{v}_1 \perp \mathbf{v}_2,$ the vector $3\mathbf{v}_2$ also lies in $\textrm{Span} \{ \mathbf{v}_1, \mathbf{v}_2 \}$ and $\mathbf{v}_1 \perp 3\mathbf{v}_2.$ Therefore, taking 

$$
[\begin{aligned}-7 \\ 13 \\ 10\end{aligned}]
$$

instead of $\mathbf{v}_2,$ we again obtain an orthogonal basis for $\textrm{Span} \{ \mathbf{v}_1, \mathbf{v}_2 \}\mathbin{:}$

$$
[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]
$$

But this time, the second vector in the basis looks slightly nicer and is probably easier to work with." :tutorial/id #uuid "00f219fa-5ae3-5e1d-acd0-7b7df752a433" :tutorial/math-academy-id 4351 :tutorial/title "Scaling the Vectors After the Gram-Schmidt Process"} :step/id #uuid "8e33ff42-ffc9-57ae-941b-8a447aded2e4" :step/math-academy-id 26458 :step/next {:db/id 17592186134686}}] :activity/title "The Gram-Schmidt Process for Two Vectors" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186134006} {:db/id 17592186134684 :step/content {:db/id 17592186135054 :tutorial/content "The **Gram-Schmidt process** is an algorithm that we can use to construct an *orthogonal* basis if we are given a non-orthogonal basis to start with.

For example, consider the basis $\{ \mathbf{a}_1, \mathbf{a}_2 \}$ for the subspace $V=\textrm{Span} \{ \mathbf{a}_1, \mathbf{a}_2 \},$ where

$$
[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]
$$

We can use the above basis to construct an *orthogonal* basis for the given $2$-dimensional subspace. To do this, we use the Gram-Schmidt process, which involves $2$ steps:

- **Step 1:** Set ${\color{blue}\mathbf{v}_1}=\mathbf{a}_1.$

- **Step 2:** Find a vector $\color{blue}\mathbf{v}_2$ in $V$ that's orthogonal to $\color{blue}\mathbf{v}_1.$ This can be achieved by computing

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{2} & ={a}_{2}\,-\,{\text{proj}}_{{v}_{1}}\,{a}_{2} \\  & ={a}_{2}-\frac{{a}_{2}\cdot {v}_{1}}{{v}_{1}\cdot {v}_{1}}{v}_{1}.\end{aligned}
$$

![](images/67/678cc056e3c9d3fbf17423ac591b3e85d84ee8060c0637840fe1c4c9e87aa878.png)

Notice that $\color{blue}\mathbf{v}_2$ is written as a linear combination of $\mathbf{a}_1(={\color{blue}\mathbf{v}_1})$ and $\mathbf{a}_2.$ So this means that ${\color{blue}\mathbf{v}_2} \in V,$ and also ${\color{blue}\mathbf{v}_2} \perp {\color{blue}\mathbf{v}_1}.$
Moreover, 

$$
\textrm{Span}\{\mathbf{a}_1,\mathbf{a}_2\} = V = \textrm{Span}\{ {\color{blue}\mathbf{v}_1}, {\color{blue}\mathbf{v}_2} \}.
$$

After applying the Gram-Schmidt process, we get the set $\mathcal{B}=\{{\color{blue}\mathbf{v}_1}, {\color{blue}\mathbf{v}_2}\},$ which is an orthogonal basis for $V.$

So, in our example, we start by setting $[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]$ Then, we find the vector $\mathbf{v}_2$ that's orthogonal to $\textrm{Span}\{\mathbf{v}_1\}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{2} & ={a}_{2}-\frac{{a}_{2}\cdot {v}_{1}}{{v}_{1}\cdot {v}_{1}}{v}_{1} \\  & ={a}_{2}-\frac{4\cdot 1+6\cdot (-1)}{{1}^{2}+(-1)^{2}}{v}_{1} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 6\end{aligned}]-(-1)\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 5\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]$ is an orthogonal basis for $V.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "3b833ab7-f6d4-5c93-8709-37ecf29bf023" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3631 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "e23dc2ed-aace-586d-8f71-e7621bc6d386" :step/math-academy-id 20257 :step/next {:db/id 17592186134685}} {:db/id 17592186135054 :tutorial/content "The **Gram-Schmidt process** is an algorithm that we can use to construct an *orthogonal* basis if we are given a non-orthogonal basis to start with.

A=[\begin{aligned}-2 & -3 \\ 1 & 2 \\ 2 & 5\end{aligned}],\,B={[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 1 \\ 2\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}a \\ b \\ c\end{aligned}]}
$$

Consider the subspace $\text{Col}(A)$ and an orthogonal basis $B$ of $\text{Col}(A),$ where $A$ and $B$ are given above. Given that $B$ is derived from $\text{Col}(A)$ using the Gram-Schmidt process, what is the value of $\frac{b}{a}?$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that $\text{Col}(A)$ is the span of the columns of $A.$  

First, let's denote

$\,$ ${a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]\,$ and $\,{a}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 2 \\ 5\end{aligned}].$ 

We proceed to find an orthogonal basis using the Gram-Schmidt process, as follows.

**Step 1**: We set ${v}_{1}={a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 1 \\ 2\end{aligned}].$

**Step 2**: Next, we find ${v}_{2}$, by using the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{2} & ={a}_{2}-\frac{{a}_{2}\cdot {v}_{1}}{{v}_{1}\cdot {v}_{1}}{v}_{1}.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the formula for ${v}_{2}$ in our case gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{2} & ={a}_{2}-\frac{(-3)\cdot (-2)+2\cdot 1+5\cdot 2}{(-2)^{2}+{1}^{2}+{2}^{2}}{v}_{1} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 2 \\ 5\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}-4 \\ 2 \\ 4\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $B={{v}_{1},{v}_{2}}={[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 1 \\ 2\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]}$ is an orthogonal basis for $\text{Col}(A).$

Finally, $a=1,$ $b=0,$ and  

$$
\frac{b}{a}=\frac{0}{1}=0.
$$"} :step/id #uuid "22215345-cf56-5cf6-8ec7-0d0ddc7f81fb"} {:db/id 17592186414755 :step/content {:db/id 17592186414750 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "72cc1442-df79-5623-bff4-42eedddafdb9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{2\sqrt{10}}{5}" :db/id 17592186414732} {:answer/id #uuid "77e7d035-74cb-5a21-8a35-1b0d4898e245" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{\sqrt{10}}{10}" :db/id 17592186414733} {:answer/id #uuid "9aa54ac6-f50b-5137-953c-f00902b1d420" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{3\sqrt{10}}{10}" :db/id 17592186414738} {:answer/id #uuid "be937ae3-0668-5fe5-9548-61b224487acf" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{\sqrt{10}}{5}" :db/id 17592186414741} {:answer/id #uuid "c38c74ea-a21b-5c0e-bb44-84641a158c8e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\sqrt{10}" :db/id 17592186414742}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186414732} :answer-field/id #uuid "969beab5-314b-57a6-99da-182f476a0e29" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186414749}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "0934e8ac-174d-5792-a7fc-4ab5bbca2aae" :question/math-academy-id "q-41971" :question/problem "$$
V=\text{Span}{[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1 \\ 3\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 4 \\ 2\end{aligned}]},\,B={[\begin{aligned}\frac{\sqrt{14}}{7} \\ \frac{\sqrt{14}}{14} \\ \frac{3\sqrt{14}}{14}\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}a \\ b \\ c\end{aligned}]}
$$

Consider the subspace $V$ and an **orthonormal** basis $B$ of $V,$ given above. Given that $B$ is derived from $V$ using the Gram-Schmidt process, what is the value of $|a|+|b|+|c|?$" :question/worked-solution "First, let's denote

$\,$ ${a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1 \\ 3\end{aligned}]\,$ and $\,{a}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 4 \\ 2\end{aligned}].$ 

We proceed to find an orthogonal basis using the Gram-Schmidt process, as follows.

**Step 1**: We set ${v}_{1}={a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1 \\ 3\end{aligned}].$

**Step 2**: Next, we find ${v}_{2}$, by using the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{2} & ={a}_{2}-\frac{{a}_{2}\cdot {v}_{1}}{{v}_{1}\cdot {v}_{1}}{v}_{1}.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the formula for ${v}_{2}$ in our case gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{2} & ={a}_{2}-\frac{2\cdot 2+4\cdot 1+2\cdot 3}{{2}^{2}+{1}^{2}+{3}^{2}}{v}_{1} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 4 \\ 2\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1 \\ 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 3 \\ -1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we normalize each vector to get an orthonormal basis.

- ${u}_{1}=\frac{{v}_{1}}{‖{v}_{1}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{{2}^{2}+{1}^{2}+{3}^{2}}}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1 \\ 3\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}\frac{\sqrt{14}}{7} \\ \frac{\sqrt{14}}{14} \\ \frac{3\sqrt{14}}{14}\end{aligned}].$

- ${u}_{2}=\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{{0}^{2}+{3}^{2}+(-1)^{2}}}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 3 \\ -1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ \frac{3\sqrt{10}}{10} \\ -\frac{\sqrt{10}}{10}\end{aligned}].$

Therefore, $B={{u}_{1},{u}_{2}}={[\begin{aligned}\frac{\sqrt{14}}{7} \\ \frac{\sqrt{14}}{14} \\ \frac{3\sqrt{14}}{14}\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}0 \\ \frac{3\sqrt{10}}{10} \\ -\frac{\sqrt{10}}{10}\end{aligned}]}$ is an orthonormal basis for $V.$

Finally, $a=0,$ $b=\frac{3\sqrt{10}}{10},$ $c=-\frac{\sqrt{10}}{10}$ and

First, let's denote

$\,$ ${a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ -2 \\ 2\end{aligned}]\,$ and $\,{a}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 0 \\ -3\end{aligned}].$ 

We proceed to find an orthogonal basis using the Gram-Schmidt process, as follows.

**Step 1**: We set ${v}_{1}={a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ -2 \\ 2\end{aligned}].$

**Step 2**: Next, we find ${v}_{2}$, by using the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{2} & ={a}_{2}-\frac{{a}_{2}\cdot {v}_{1}}{{v}_{1}\cdot {v}_{1}}{v}_{1}.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the formula for ${v}_{2}$ in our case gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{2} & ={a}_{2}-\frac{3\cdot (-1)+0\cdot (-2)+(-3)\cdot 2}{{1}^{2}+(-2)^{2}+{2}^{2}}{v}_{1} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 0 \\ -3\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ -2 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -2 \\ -1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we normalize each vector to get an orthonormal basis:

- ${u}_{1}=\frac{{v}_{1}}{‖{v}_{1}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{{1}^{2}+(-2)^{2}+{2}^{2}}}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ -2 \\ 2\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{3} \\ -\frac{2}{3} \\ \frac{2}{3}\end{aligned}].$

$$

"$$
A=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 3 \\ -2 & 0 \\ 2 & -3\end{aligned}],\,B={{u}_{1},{u}_{2}}={[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{3} \\ -\frac{2}{3} \\ \frac{2}{3}\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}a \\ b \\ c\end{aligned}]}
$$

Consider the subspace $\text{Col}(A)$ and an **orthonormal** basis $B$ of $\text{Col}(A),$ where $A$ and $B$ are given above. Given that $B$ is derived from $\text{Col}(A)$ using the Gram-Schmidt process, what is the value of $|a|+|b|+|c|?$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that $\text{Col}(A)$ is the span of the columns of $A.$  

First, let's denote

$\,$ ${a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ -2 \\ 2\end{aligned}]\,$ and $\,{a}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 0 \\ -3\end{aligned}].$ 

We proceed to find an orthogonal basis using the Gram-Schmidt process, as follows.

**Step 1**: We set ${v}_{1}={a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ -2 \\ 2\end{aligned}].$

**Step 2**: Next, we find ${v}_{2}$, by using the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{2} & ={a}_{2}-\frac{{a}_{2}\cdot {v}_{1}}{{v}_{1}\cdot {v}_{1}}{v}_{1}.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the formula for ${v}_{2}$ in our case gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{2} & ={a}_{2}-\frac{3\cdot (-1)+0\cdot (-2)+(-3)\cdot 2}{{1}^{2}+(-2)^{2}+{2}^{2}}{v}_{1} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 0 \\ -3\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ -2 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -2 \\ -1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we normalize each vector to get an orthonormal basis:

- ${u}_{1}=\frac{{v}_{1}}{‖{v}_{1}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{{1}^{2}+(-2)^{2}+{2}^{2}}}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ -2 \\ 2\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{3} \\ -\frac{2}{3} \\ \frac{2}{3}\end{aligned}].$

- ${u}_{2}=\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{{2}^{2}+(-2)^{2}+(-1)^{2}}}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -2 \\ -1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{3} \\ -\frac{2}{3} \\ -\frac{1}{3}\end{aligned}].$

Therefore, $B={{u}_{1},{u}_{2}}={[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{3} \\ -\frac{2}{3} \\ \frac{2}{3}\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{3} \\ -\frac{2}{3} \\ -\frac{1}{3}\end{aligned}]}$ is an orthonormal basis for $\text{Col}(A).$

Finally, $a=\frac{2}{3},$ $b=-\frac{2}{3},$ $c=-\frac{1}{3}$ and  

$$
|a|+|b|+|c|=|\frac{2}{3}|+|-\frac{2}{3}|+|-\frac{1}{3}|=\frac{5}{3}.
$$"} :step/id #uuid "84989845-fb61-500c-b47d-0a19bc3d185f" :step/next {:db/id 17592186414755}} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "012fe31e-f759-58b8-9e32-2deea745562c" :answer/type {:db/id $$

$$
\begin{aligned}[D\,|\,b] & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & -3 & -2 & 1 \\ -2 & -2 & 6 & 4 & 4 \\ 2 & 2 & 1 & 1 & 8 \\ 1 & 6 & 5 & -1 & 6\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+2{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & -3 & -2 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 & 6 \\ 2 & 2 & 1 & 1 & 8 \\ 1 & 6 & 5 & -1 & 6\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}-3{x}_{3}-2{x}_{4}=1 \\ 0=6 \\ 2{x}_{1}+2{x}_{2}+{x}_{3}+{x}_{4}=-8 \\ {x}_{1}+6{x}_{2}+5{x}_{3}-{x}_{4}=6.\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}[A\,|\,b] & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & -8 & -2 \\ 0 & -1 & 4 & 2 \\ 2 & 0 & -4 & 2\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+(-2){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & -8 & -2 \\ 0 & -1 & 4 & 2 \\ 0 & -6 & 12 & 6\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+(-6){R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & -8 & -2 \\ 0 & -1 & 4 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & -12 & -6\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we have the system

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+3{x}_{2}-8{x}_{3}=-2 \\ -{x}_{2}+4{x}_{3}=2 \\ -12{x}_{3}=-6.\end{aligned}
$$

From the third equation, we get ${x}_{3}=\frac{1}{2}.$ Substituting it into the second equation gives 

$$
\begin{aligned}-{x}_{2}+4(\frac{1}{2}) & =2 \\ -{x}_{2}+2 & =2 \\ {x}_{2} & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, from the first equation, we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+3(0)-8(\frac{1}{2}) & =-2 \\ {x}_{1}-4 & =-2 \\ {x}_{1} & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Since we have a solution, the equation $Ax=b$ is consistent, which implies that $b\in \text{Col}(A).$ 

Moreover, there is exactly one solution, so we have exactly one way to write $b$ as a linear combination of ${a}_{1},$ ${a}_{2},$ and ${a}_{3}:$

$$
{{[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 2 \\ 2\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{b}=2\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 2\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{a}_{1}}+0\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{a}_{2}}+\frac{1}{2}\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}-8 \\ 4 \\ -4\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{a}_{3}}
$$

Finally, we get ${x}_{1}\cdot {x}_{2}\cdot {x}_{3}=2\cdot 0\cdot \frac{1}{2}=0.$"} {:db/id 17592186430001 :question/id #uuid "6e653566-d375-5ee1-b745-3dfd829381b0" :question/math-academy-id 1850} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186120680 :step/content {:db/id 17592186121037 :tutorial/content "The **column space** of a matrix $A$ is denoted $\text{Col}(A)$ and is the span of the columns of $A$ (i.e., the set of all possible linear combinations of columns of $A$). For example, consider the matrix

![](images/6c/6c03ab3dfd7b75c9a89defe102f33946da200fb88d26139e54c889a90467068a.svg)
where we denote its columns by $\color{red}\mathbf{a}_1$ and ${\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_2},$ respectively. The column space of this matrix is given by
![](images/5f/5faad23bc77f821d42223beaca06364e38c7f0ba8a4869cb138e0e923e90b8f7.svg)

Now, suppose we would like to determine whether the vector ![](images/45/45349edee356334c54ad85a6d60757a6a7833a392962086815a2436446e323dc.svg) lies in $\textrm{Col}(A).$ In other words, we need to check if $\mathbf{b} \in \textrm{Span}\{ {\color{red}\mathbf{a}_1}, {\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_2} \}.$ So, we need to determine whether $\mathbf{b}$ can be written as some linear combination of $\color{red}\mathbf{a}_1$ and ${\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_2}\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}{a}_{1}+{x}_{2}{a}_{2}=b\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that the equation above can be written as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}{a}_{1} & {a}_{2}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =b \\ {{[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ 2 & -1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{A}{{[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{\text{x}} & ={{[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -3\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{\text{b}}\end{aligned}
$$

So, the equation is equivalent to $A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{b}.$ To solve the equation, let's find the row echelon form of the augmented matrix $[A \,|\, \mathbf{b}]$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}[A\,|\,b] & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & 2 \\ 2 & -1 & -3\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-2){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & 2 \\ 0 & -7 & -7\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we have the system

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+3{x}_{2}=2 \\ -7{x}_{2}=-7.\end{aligned}
$$

From the second equation, we get $x_2=1.$ Substituting into the first equation, we get $x_1=-1.$

Since we have a solution, the equation $A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{b}$ is consistent, which implies that $\mathbf{b} \in \textrm{Col}(A).$

Moreover, there is exactly one solution, so we have exactly one way to write $\mathbf{b}$ as a linear combination of $\color{red}\mathbf{a}_1$ and ${\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_2}\mathbin{:}$
![](images/a3/a3965a53b3b3cfda2e11c4a68ba882631dc2763f32de67de30b4751aca76f2e5.svg)" :tutorial/id #uuid "f65da145-207a-50c6-b59e-8756d247cc71" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3201 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "e2b22098-86e0-53ea-bbc9-fc31b60b4152" :step/math-academy-id 17489 :step/next {:db/id 17592186120681}} {:db/id 17592186120681 :step/content {:db/id 17592186119810 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186119621 :question/id #uuid "244793f6-41c3-5920-9264-bec32cda9c9c" :question/math-academy-id "e-4807"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "5c8e217c-252d-529f-a810-84787e2ee886" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186048315}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186120313} {:db/id 17592186120339} {:db/id 17592186247182} {:db/id 17592186247183} {:db/id 17592186247185} {:db/id 17592186317417} {:db/id 17592186342180} {:db/id 17592186408163} {:db/id 17592186430002}] :knowledge-point/title "Determining if a Vector is in the Column Space of a Matrix"} :step/id #uuid "415a39b4-7da9-55ac-afde-f8932b3c0813" :step/math-academy-id 17491 :step/next {:db/id 17592186120749}} {:db/id 17592186120682 :step/content {:db/id 17592186121038 :tutorial/content "The column space is defined for matrices of *any* dimensions. In general, if ${\color{black}\mathbf{a}_1}, {\color{black}\mathbf{a}_2}, \ldots, {\color{black}\mathbf{a}_n}$ are the columns of a matrix $A,$ that is to say,
![](images/d9/d9d3fd7384b4375895d234c22c9d81f30358439f7e04ee8db055de9d5d7f1174.svg)
then $\textrm{Col}(A) = \textrm{Span} \{ {\color{black}\mathbf{a}_1}, {\color{black}\mathbf{a}_2}, \ldots, {\color{black}\mathbf{a}_n} \}.$

The column space satisfies the following properties:

- If $A$ is an ${\color{blue}m}\times n$ matrix, then $\textrm{Col}(A)$ is a subspace of $\mathbb{R}^{\color{blue}m}.$ This is because each column has ${\color{blue}m}$ entries.

- $\mathbf{b}\in\textrm{Col}(A)$ if and only if the equation $A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{b}$ is consistent (has a solution).

- If the equation $A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{b}$ is inconsistent (has no solution), then $\mathbf{b}\not\in\textrm{Col}(A).$

These hold for any $m\times n$ matrix, and the matrix does not necessarily have to be square." :tutorial/id #uuid "f33b7df2-b0c3-5b23-b26b-50509cefd3a3" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3203 :tutorial/title :tutorial/content "The **column space** of a matrix $A$ is denoted $\text{Col}(A)$ and is the span of the columns of $A$ (i.e., the set of all possible linear combinations of columns of $A$). For example, consider the matrix

![](images/6c/6c03ab3dfd7b75c9a89defe102f33946da200fb88d26139e54c889a90467068a.svg)
where we denote its columns by $\color{red}\mathbf{a}_1$ and ${\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_2},$ respectively. The column space of this matrix is given by
![](images/5f/5faad23bc77f821d42223beaca06364e38c7f0ba8a4869cb138e0e923e90b8f7.svg)

Now, suppose we would like to determine whether the vector ![](images/45/45349edee356334c54ad85a6d60757a6a7833a392962086815a2436446e323dc.svg) lies in $\textrm{Col}(A).$ In other words, we need to check if $\mathbf{b} \in \textrm{Span}\{ {\color{red}\mathbf{a}_1}, {\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_2} \}.$ So, we need to determine whether $\mathbf{b}$ can be written as some linear combination of $\color{red}\mathbf{a}_1$ and ${\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_2}\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}{a}_{1}+{x}_{2}{a}_{2}=b\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that the equation above can be written as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}{a}_{1} & {a}_{2}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =b \\ {{[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ 2 & -1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{A}{{[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{\text{x}} & ={{[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -3\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{\text{b}}\end{aligned}
$$

So, the equation is equivalent to $A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{b}.$ To solve the equation, let's find the row echelon form of the augmented matrix $[A \,|\, \mathbf{b}]$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}[A\,|\,b] & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & 2 \\ 2 & -1 & -3\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-2){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & 2 \\ 0 & -7 & -7\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we have the system

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+3{x}_{2}=2 \\ -7{x}_{2}=-7.\end{aligned}
$$

From the second equation, we get $x_2=1.$ Substituting into the first equation, we get $x_1=-1.$

Since we have a solution, the equation $A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{b}$ is consistent, which implies that $\mathbf{b} \in \textrm{Col}(A).$

Moreover, there is exactly one solution, so we have exactly one way to write $\mathbf{b}$ as a linear combination of $\color{red}\mathbf{a}_1$ and ${\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_2}\mathbin{:}$
![](images/a3/a3965a53b3b3cfda2e11c4a68ba882631dc2763f32de67de30b4751aca76f2e5.svg)" :tutorial/id #uuid "f65da145-207a-50c6-b59e-8756d247cc71" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3201 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "e2b22098-86e0-53ea-bbc9-fc31b60b4152" :step/math-academy-id 17489 :step/next {:db/id 17592186120681}} {:db/id 17592186121037 :tutorial/content "The **column space** of a matrix $A$ is denoted $\text{Col}(A)$ and is the span of the columns of $A$ (i.e., the set of all possible linear combinations of columns of $A$). In general, if ${\color{black}\mathbf{a}_1}, {\color{black}\mathbf{a}_2}, \ldots, {\color{black}\mathbf{a}_n}$ are the columns of a matrix $A,$ that is to say,
![](images/d9/d9d3fd7384b4375895d234c22c9d81f30358439f7e04ee8db055de9d5d7f1174.svg)
then $\textrm{Col}(A) = \textrm{Span} \{ {\color{black}\mathbf{a}_1}, {\color{black}\mathbf{a}_2}, \ldots, {\color{black}\mathbf{a}_n} \}.$

The column space satisfies the following properties:

- If $A$ is an ${\color{blue}m}\times n$ matrix, then $\textrm{Col}(A)$ is a subspace of $\mathbb{R}^{\color{blue}m}.$ This is because each column has ${\color{blue}m}$ entries.

- $\mathbf{b}\in\textrm{Col}(A)$ if and only if the equation $A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{b}$ is consistent (has a solution).

- If the equation $A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{b}$ is inconsistent (has no solution), then $\mathbf{b}\not\in\textrm{Col}(A).$

These hold for any $m\times n$ matrix, and the matrix does not necessarily have to be square." :tutorial/id #uuid "f33b7df2-b0c3-5b23-b26b-50509cefd3a3" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3203 :tutorial/title "Properties of the Column Space of a Matrix"} :step/id #uuid "65ce55e4-127b-59e8-96ab-fabcdc24aef9" :step/math-academy-id 17493 :step/next {:db/id 17592186120683}} {:db/id 17592186121038 :tutorial/content "The column space is defined for matrices of *any* dimensions. A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & -8 \\ 0 & -1 & 4 \\ 2 & 0 & -4\end{aligned}],\,b=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 2 \\ 2\end{aligned}]
$$" :question/worked-solution "In order to determine whether $b$ lies in $\text{Col}(A),$ we need to check if the equation $Ax=b$ is consistent. So, let's find the row echelon form of the augmented matrix $[A\,|\,b]$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}[A\,|\,b] & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & -8 & -2 \\ 0 & -1 & 4 & 2 \\ 2 & 0 & -4 & 2\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+(-2){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & -8 & -2 \\ 0 & -1 & 4 & 2 \\ 0 & -6 & 12 & 6\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+(-6){R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & -8 & -2 \\ 0 & -1 & 4 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & -12 & -6\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we have the system

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+3{x}_{2}-8{x}_{3}=-2 \\ -{x}_{2}+4{x}_{3}=2 \\ -12{x}_{3}=-6.\end{aligned}
$$

From the third equation, we get ${x}_{3}=\frac{1}{2}.$ Substituting it into the second equation gives 

$$
\begin{aligned}-{x}_{2}+4(\frac{1}{2}) & =2 \\ -{x}_{2}+2 & =2 \\ {x}_{2} & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, from the first equation, we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+3(0)-8(\frac{1}{2}) & =-2 \\ {x}_{1}-4 & =-2 \\ {x}_{1} & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Since we have a solution, the equation $Ax=b$ is consistent, which implies that $b\in \text{Col}(A).$ 

Moreover, there is exactly one solution, so we have exactly one way to write $b$ as a linear combination of ${a}_{1},$ ${a}_{2},$ and ${a}_{3}:$

$$

$$
\left(5^2\right)^{1/3} = \sqrt[3]{5^2}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186152698 :question/id #uuid "ea07c67e-0a31-5aaf-93ff-c5510fb4655f" :question/math-academy-id "q-69159"} {:db/id 17592186152700 :question/id #uuid "b0a552b0-c4bf-5977-8e56-e73ff43c51af" :question/math-academy-id "q-69161"} {:db/id 17592186152129 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186151931 :question/id #uuid "a7466252-b70d-5a77-83d5-28390c82c820" :question/math-academy-id "e-4903"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "bb7b6041-4844-5476-9980-d0851c95b7d0" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186152696 :question/id #uuid "105f1142-80ed-54af-b165-464334ec040c" :question/math-academy-id "q-69157"} {:db/id 17592186152703 :question/id #uuid "f9c78f2d-9022-5de0-974d-0664100fd96b" :question/math-academy-id "q-69244"}] :knowledge-point/title "Converting a Radical to a Fractional Exponent"} {:db/id 17592186151931 :question/id #uuid "a7466252-b70d-5a77-83d5-28390c82c820" :question/math-academy-id "e-4903" :knowledge-point/_canonical-example [{:db/id 17592186152129 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "bb7b6041-4844-5476-9980-d0851c95b7d0" :knowledge-point/title "Converting a Radical to a Fractional Exponent"}] :question/problem "Express $\sqrt[3]{4^2}$ using a fractional exponent." :question/worked-solution "The radical $\sqrt[n]{x}$ can be written using a fractional exponent as $x^{1/n}$.

:step/content {:db/id 17592186153346 :tutorial/content "So far, we know the following:

- To find the square root of a number, we need to find another that multiplies by itself $2$ times to give the original number. For example,
$\sqrt{9} = \sqrt{3 \cdot 3} = \sqrt{3^2} = 3$.
- To find the cube root of a number, we need to find another that multiplies by itself $3$ times to give the original number. For example,
$\sqrt[3]{8} = \sqrt[3]{2 \cdot 2 \cdot 2} = \sqrt[3]{2^3} = 2$.

We can extend this to any root. In general, to find the $n$th root of a number, we needed to find another number that multiplies by itself $n$ times to give the original number. We express the $n$th root as the radical $\sqrt[n]{\phantom{0}}$. For instance,

$$
\sqrt[{\color{blue}4}]{16} = \sqrt[{\color{blue}4}]{\underbrace{2\cdot 2\cdot 2\cdot 2}_{{\color{blue}4}\text{times}}} = \sqrt[{\color{blue}4}]{2^4} = 2
$$

Given a radical $\sqrt[n]{x}$, we can write an equivalent expression using the fractional exponent $x^{1/n}$. To demonstrate, let's write an equivalent expression for $\sqrt[7]{3}$.

Comparing $\sqrt[n]{x}$ with $\sqrt[7]{3}$, we get $x = 3$ and $n = 7$. Therefore,

$$
\sqrt[7]{3} = 3^{1/7}
$$

The reverse is also true: the fractional exponent $x^{1/n}$ can be written as the radical $\sqrt[n]{x}$.

**Note:** Remember that the square root of a number corresponds to the case of $n=2$. So, for example, we have

$$
\sqrt{3} = 3^{1/2}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "ace9adb3-54cf-5410-b2e4-d0e8ae4fb000" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3293 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "47028c77-f8df-57f6-ad0c-476649be1dd4" :step/math-academy-id 18077 :step/next {:db/id 17592186153012}}] :activity/title "Radicals as Fractional Exponents" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186152321} {:db/id 17592186153014 :step/content {:db/id 17592186153346 :tutorial/content "So far, we know the following:

$$
f(x,y) =\dfrac{xy}2, \qquad
D = \big\{ (x,y) \: : \: 0 \leq x \leq 2y, \: 0 \leq y \leq 4 \big\}.
$$

According to the mean value theorem for double integrals, there exists a point $(a,b) \in D$ such that the volume of the solid enclosed between the surface $z=f(x,y)$ and the $xy$-plane over the region $D$ equals the volume of the right cylinder with base $D$ and height $f(a,b).$ Find $a$ given that $b=2.$" :question/worked-solution "According to the mean value theorem for double integrals, there exists a point $(a,b) \in D$ such that

$$
\iint\limits_D f(x,y) \: \textrm{d}A = f(a,b) \cdot \textrm{Area}(D).
$$

Evaluating the integral on the left-hand side, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{D}\frac{xy}{2}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{4}{\int }_{0}^{2y}\frac{xy}{2}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{4}[\frac{{x}^{2}y}{4}]_{x=0}^{x=2y}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{4}{y}^{3}\,\text{d}y \\  & =[\frac{{y}^{4}}{4}]_{y=0}^{y=4} \\  & =64.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Area}(D) & ={∬}_{D}\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{4}{\int }_{0}^{2y}\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{4}[x]_{x=0}^{x=2y}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{4}2y\,\text{d}y \\  & ={[{y}^{2}]}_{y=0}^{y=4} \\  & =16.\end{aligned}
$$

Also, we are told that $b=2.$ So, our initial equation simplifies to

$$
\begin{aligned}64 & =f(a,2)\cdot 16 \\ 64 & =\frac{a\cdot 2}{2}\cdot 16 \\ 64 & =16a \\ a & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that $\left( 4,2 \right) \in D.$ Therefore, the answer is $a = 4.$"} {:db/id 17592186049280} {:db/id 17592186049997} {:db/id 17592186050264} {:db/id 17592186167132 :question/id #uuid $1$ centered at the origin, where $x\geq 0,$ and $y \leq 0.$" :question/worked-solution "First, let's sketch our region $D\mathbin{:}$ 

![](images/a3/a381fede820f9fc5ba08bb9569906d41a3e8f779de38b446c4f271ceef3a5ccd.png)

Notice that 

$$
\textrm{Area}(D) = \dfrac{1}{4} \cdot \pi \cdot 1^2 = \dfrac\pi 4.
$$

The average value of the function over a region $D$ is given by

$$
f_{\textrm{ave}} = \dfrac{1}{\textrm{Area}(D)} \, \iint\limits_D f(x,y) \: \textrm{d}A.
$$

We will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
\iint\limits_{D} f(x,y) \ \mathrm d A = \iint\limits_{\Delta} \ f(r\cos\theta, r\sin\theta) \:  r \ \mathrm d r \mathrm d \theta.
$$

In polar coordinates $(r, \theta),$ the region can be expressed as 

$$
\Delta = \left\{ (r,\theta) \: : \: 0 \leq r \leq 1, \: \dfrac{3\pi}{2} \leq \theta \leq 2\pi\right\}.
$$

Using the change of variables formula, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}15x{y}^{2}\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}15r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \cdot (r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2}\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{3\pi /2}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{1}15{r}^{4}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta {sin}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{3\pi /2}^{2\pi }3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta {sin}^{2}⁡\theta {\int }_{0}^{1}5{r}^{4}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{3\pi /2}^{2\pi }3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta {sin}^{2}⁡\theta \,{[{r}^{5}]}_{0}^{1}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{3\pi /2}^{2\pi }3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta {sin}^{2}⁡\theta ({1}^{5}-0)\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{3\pi /2}^{2\pi }3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta {sin}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={[{sin}^{3}⁡\theta ]}_{3\pi /2}^{2\pi } \\  & =({sin}^{3}⁡(2\pi )-{sin}^{3}⁡(\frac{3\pi }{2})) \\  & =(0-(-1)) \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
f_{\textrm{ave}} = \dfrac{4}{\pi} \cdot 1 = \dfrac{4}{\pi}.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186049084} {:db/id 17592186167136 :question/id #uuid "49e12370-95b6-55a6-adbd-181ce8b9aebf" :question/math-academy-id "q-163067"} {:db/id 17592186167137 :question/id #uuid at the origin, where $x\le 0.$" :question/worked-solution "First, let's sketch our region $D:$ 

![](images/25/25c1f00e588ddaa130f854d9f4e9dfe9b1158d7952a01bae8108ea4b94d3c347.png)

Notice that 

$$
\text{Area}(D)=\frac{1}{2}\cdot \pi \cdot {3}^{2}=\frac{9\pi }{2}.
$$

The average value of the function over a region $D$ is given by

$$
{f}_{\text{ave}}=\frac{1}{\text{Area}(D)}\,{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A.
$$

We will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .
$$

In polar coordinates $(r,\theta ),$ the region can be expressed as 

$$
Δ={(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le 3,\,\frac{\pi }{2}\le \theta \le \frac{3\pi }{2}}.
$$

Using the change of variables formula, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\frac{2}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+1}\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}\frac{2}{(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2}+1}\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{3\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{3}\frac{2r}{{r}^{2}+1}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{3\pi /2}[\operatorname{ln}⁡({r}^{2}+1)]_{0}^{3}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{3\pi /2}(\operatorname{ln}⁡10-\operatorname{ln}⁡1)\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡10{\int }_{\pi /2}^{3\pi /2}\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡10[\theta ]_{\pi /2}^{3\pi /2} \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡10(\frac{3\pi }{2}-\frac{\pi }{2}) \\  & =\pi \operatorname{ln}⁡10.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
{f}_{\text{ave}}=\frac{2}{9\pi }\cdot \pi \operatorname{ln}⁡10=\frac{2\operatorname{ln}⁡10}{9}.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186281654 :question/id #uuid "9c6dbd46-16b0-53ac-9c25-a6637f9ce3ed" :question/math-academy-id "q-163261"} {:db/id 17592186281662 :question/id #uuid {:db/id 17592186167791}} {:db/id 17592186167791 :step/content {:db/id 17592186168149 :tutorial/content "Recall that the average value of a continuous function $f(x)$ on a closed interval $D = [a,b]$ is given by

$$
f_\textrm{ave} = \dfrac{1}{\textrm{Length}(D)}\int_a^b f(x) \: \textrm{d}x.
$$

There is an analogous definition for functions of two variables, stated below:

> *Suppose $D$ is a closed and bounded region in $\mathbb{R}^2$ which has non-zero finite area $\textrm{Area}(D).$ If $f (x, y)$ is a continuous function on $D,$ then **the average value of $\boldsymbol f$ on $\boldsymbol D$** is given by*
> 
> 
> $$
> f_{\textrm{ave}} =\dfrac{1}{\textrm{Area}(D)} \, \iint\limits_D f(x,y) \: \textrm{d}A.
> $$

For example, let's find the average value of the function 

\[
f(x,y) =x+3y^2+2
\]

over the region 

\[
D = \big\{ (x,y) \: : \: 0 \leq x \leq 2, \: 0 \leq y \leq 2 \big\}.
\] 

Earlier, we found that 

\[
\iint\limits_D f(x,y) \: \textrm{d}A = 28, \qquad \textrm{Area}(D) = 4.
\]

Therefore, the average value of the function over [math]D[/math] is

\begin{align*}
f_{\textrm{ave}}  	

&= \dfrac{1}{\textrm{Area}(D)} \, \iint\limits_D f(x,y) \: \textrm{d}A \\[5pt]

&= \dfrac{1}{4} \cdot 28 \\[5pt]

&=  7. 
\end{align*}" :tutorial/id #uuid "c862ff42-4e5b-5bbb-aed6-3d9760d339b1" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7770 :tutorial/title "The Average Value of a Function"} :step/id #uuid interval $[a, b],$ the mean value theorem for integrals guarantees that there exists a number $c \in [a,b]$ such that

$$
\int_a^b f(x)\, \textrm d x = f(c) \cdot (b-a),
$$

which can be visualized as shown below.

![](images/0a/0afb9b15787eb89f73f322290bdbe2288027c54924d274c438773ce151a17291.png)

We have a similar theorem for functions with two variables. The so-called **mean value theorem for double integrals** states:

> *If the function $f(x,y)$ is continuous on a closed and bounded region $D,$ then there exists a point $(a,b) \in D$ such that*
> 
> 
> $$
> \iint\limits_D f(x,y) \: \textrm{d}A = f(a,b) \cdot \textrm{Area}(D).
> $$

This has a nice geometrical interpretation when $f$ is non-negative on $D.$ In this case, the theorem tells us that there exists a point $(a,b) \in D$ such that the volume of the solid enclosed between the surface $z=f(x,y)$ and the $xy$-plane over the region $D$ equals the volume of the right cylinder with base $D$ and height $f(a,b).$ 

The diagram below shows the case when $D$ is rectangular, and the corresponding cylinder is a rectangular solid.

![](images/8e/8ed477207ee61fbdaf963ed8a127e3f1d4cf76707d2eeb4b450fd49f78e15b7e.png)

In general, the point $(a,b)$ mentioned in the theorem is not unique. Let's see an example." :tutorial/id #uuid "b65eeb5f-8a44-55b9-819c-1c6c0d979d1e" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7778 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "037c5a22-eee3-557c-b683-370d2389ad82" :step/math-academy-id 45031 :step/next {:db/id 17592186167795}} {:db/id 17592186167795 :step/content {:db/id 17592186168151 :tutorial/content "Consider the continuous function 

$$
f(x,y) = x+3y^2+2
$$

and the region $D$ given by

$$
D = \big\{ (x,y) \: : \: 0 \leq x \leq 2, \: 0 \leq y \leq 2 \big\}.
$$

According to the mean value theorem for double integrals, there exists a point $(a,b) \in D$ such that

$$
\iint\limits_D f(x,y) \: \textrm{d}A = f(a,b) \cdot \textrm{Area}(D).
$$

Evaluating the integral on the left-hand side, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{D}(x+3{y}^{2}+2)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{2}(x+3{y}^{2}+2)\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{[xy+{y}^{3}+2y]}_{y=0}^{y=2}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}(2x+12)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={[{x}^{2}+12x]}_{x=0}^{x=2} \\  & =28.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we have

$$
\textrm{Area}(D) = 2 \cdot 2 = 4.
$$

So, our mean-value equation simplifies to

$$
\begin{aligned}28 & =f(a,b)\cdot 4 \\ 7 & =f(a,b) \\ 7 & =a+3{b}^{2}+2 \\ a & =5-3{b}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

This equation describes part of a parabola in the $xy$-plane, as shown below.

![](images/46/46873c4ecb290380488e589082fc0759324d3540494f5b83e2d64db5d9cdf62a.png)

To find a particular point that satisfies the mean value theorem, we can set, for example, $b=1 \in [0,2]$ and obtain $a=2.$ So, the point $(2,1)$ satisfies the mean value theorem for double integrals. Consequently, the two solids below must have the same volume.

$$
f_\textrm{ave} = \dfrac{1}{\textrm{Length}(D)}\int_a^b f(x) \: \textrm{d}x.
$$

There is an analogous definition for functions of two variables, stated below:

> *Suppose $D$ is a closed and bounded region in $\mathbb{R}^2$ which has non-zero finite area $\textrm{Area}(D).$ If $f (x, y)$ is a continuous function on $D,$ then **the average value of $\boldsymbol f$ on $\boldsymbol D$** is given by*
> 
> 
> $$
> f_{\textrm{ave}} =\dfrac{1}{\textrm{Area}(D)} \, \iint\limits_D f(x,y) \: \textrm{d}A.
> $$

For example, let's find the average value of the function 

\[
f(x,y) =x+3y^2+2
\]

over the region 

\[
D = \big\{ (x,y) \: : \: 0 \leq x \leq 2, \: 0 \leq y \leq 2 \big\}.
\] 

Earlier, we found that 

\[
\iint\limits_D f(x,y) \: \textrm{d}A = 28, \qquad \textrm{Area}(D) = 4.
\]

Therefore, the average value of the function over [math]D[/math] is

\begin{align*}
f_{\textrm{ave}}  	

&= \dfrac{1}{\textrm{Area}(D)} \, \iint\limits_D f(x,y) \: \textrm{d}A \\[5pt]

&= \dfrac{1}{4} \cdot 28 \\[5pt]

&=  7. 
\end{align*}" :tutorial/id #uuid "c862ff42-4e5b-5bbb-aed6-3d9760d339b1" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7770 :tutorial/title "The Average Value of a Function"} :step/id #uuid "c77b7ad4-9d8d-58f4-bd79-4c0b0b47cfea" :step/math-academy-id 44981 :step/next {:db/id 17592186167792}} {:db/id 17592186168149 :tutorial/content "Recall that the average value of a continuous function $f(x)$ on a closed interval $D = [a,b]$ is given by

"Let's take a number, say, $-3$. We can depict it on a number line as follows:

![](images/de/ded8743284f207bff35eba24617fd4245a69d439ed151d09eed564813f9d72fb.png)

The *distance* between the number $-3$ and $0$ is known as the **absolute value** of $-3$. We write it as

$$
\mid -3 \mid = {\color{red}3}
$$

Similarly, $\mid \,2\, \mid$, the absolute value of the number $2$, is the distance between $2$ and $0$:

![](images/f4/f44fcd05fb0932083d48c8b11892247d8de8fbc46ccf7186fb12843702181aea.png)

We write

$$
\mid \,2\, \mid = {\color{red}2}
$$

So, the absolute value simply

- *removes the minus sign*, if the number is negative, or
- does nothing, if the number is non-negative.

Sometimes, we can be asked to evaluate an expression involving the absolute value function, like $\mid x +1 \mid + 5$ when $x=-3$. In this case, we evaluate the expression inside the absolute value before simplifying the rest of the expression:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mid x + 1 \mid + 5 &=  \\
\mid (-3) + 1 \mid + 5 &=  \\
\mid - 2 \mid + 5 &=  \\
2 + 5 &=  \\
&= 7
\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "3325f9a7-d389-562e-ac1b-4eb26671f84b" :tutorial/math-academy-id 8817 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "2ecbe2d3-3bf6-5c94-9e47-13b35a557d38" :step/math-academy-id 147765 :step/next {:db/id 17592186055549}} {:db/id 17592186055549 :step/content {:db/id 17592186054626 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186054470 :question/id #uuid "af2c36f6-7258-56b3-aabc-c0736bdfb6a5" :question/math-academy-id "e-14209"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "2a5017c8-1933-515c-980a-c4b6a8a46334" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186048599} {:db/id 17592186049688} {:db/id 17592186050127}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186055102} {:db/id 17592186055113} {:db/id 17592186055175}] :knowledge-point/title "Evaluating an Expression With One Absolute Value"} :step/id #uuid "4957b9ec-7c2c-553a-b341-f367fd1d5e59" :step/math-academy-id 147766 :step/next {:db/id 17592186055550}} {:db/id 17592186055550 :step/content {:db/id 17592186054627 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186054471 :question/id #uuid "2af15364-dc4d-52c1-a519-02e8568279ae" :question/math-academy-id "e-14212"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "9d29b448-4fd6-51bc-b2f0-92e3d909f299" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186055103} {:db/id 17592186055104} {:db/id 17592186055114}] :knowledge-point/title "Evaluating an Expression With Two Absolute Values"} :step/id #uuid "ea43903e-13f4-5326-a1ae-670194c48ad9" :step/math-academy-id 147770}] :activity/title "Absolute Value Expressions" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186054936} {:db/id 17592186055548 :step/content {:db/id 17592186056066 :tutorial/content "Let's take a number, say, $-3$. $$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & =x\cdot {q}_{1} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2\sqrt{10} \\ \frac{\sqrt{10}}{2} \\ -\frac{\sqrt{10}}{2}\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}} \\ \frac{3}{\sqrt{10}}\end{aligned}] \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}-\frac{3}{2} \\  & =-2.\end{aligned}

$$

$\mathbf{x}$ and any subspace $W$ in $\mathbb{R}^n,$ we can always write $\mathbf{x}$ as a sum of a vector from $W$ and a vector from $W^{\perp}.$ This fact is known as the **orthogonal decomposition theorem.** We can state it formally as follows:

> *Let $W$ be a subspace of $\mathbb{R}^n.$ Then each $\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^n$ can be written uniquely in the form
> 
> 
> $$
> \mathbf{x}= \mathbf{y}+\mathbf{z}
> $$
> 
> 
> where $\mathbf{y} \in W$ and $\mathbf{z} \in W^{\perp}.$*

> *Moreover, since $\mathbf y$ is the orthogonal projection of $\mathbf x$ onto the subspace $W,$ if $\{\mathbf{u}_1\,\dots,\mathbf{u}_p\}$ is any orthogonal basis of $W,$ then*
> 
> 
> $$
> \begin{aligned}y & ={\text{proj}}_{W}\,x \\  & ={\text{proj}}_{{u}_{1}}\,x+{\text{proj}}_{{u}_{2}}\,x+⋯+{\text{proj}}_{{u}_{p}}\,x \\  & =\frac{x\cdot {u}_{1}}{{u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{1}}{u}_{1}+\frac{x\cdot {u}_{2}}{{u}_{2}\cdot {u}_{2}}{u}_{2}+⋯+\frac{x\cdot {u}_{p}}{{u}_{p}\cdot {u}_{p}}{u}_{p}.\end{aligned}
> $$" :tutorial/id #uuid "789dc38d-c1e0-5bdc-9f01-5940371a326b" :tutorial/math-academy-id 4304 :tutorial/title "The Orthogonal Decomposition Theorem"} :step/id #uuid "450eea64-01cc-591d-9042-fba21e4feb99" :step/math-academy-id 26173}] :activity/title "The Components of a Vector with Respect to an Orthogonal or Orthonormal Basis" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186157482} {:db/id 17592186158103 :step/content {:db/id 17592186158470 :tutorial/content "Given an orthogonal basis $\mathcal{B}=\{\mathbf{q}_1, \mathbf{q}_2, \ldots, \mathbf{q}_n\}$ of $S=\textrm{Span}\{\mathcal{B}\},$ there is an easy way to find the components of a vector $\mathbf{x}\in S$ with respect to this basis.
